(CBS12) — A misplaced cellphone in a school cafeteria sparked a weapon rumor at Vero Beach High School on Monday morning, but school officials said there was no credible threat. The School District of Indian River County said a student left a cellphone in the cafeteria and rushed back to retrieve it. During the confusion, inaccurate information spread and developed into a rumor involving a weapon. Officials said the reported threat was not credible. See also: Florida woman killed after firing at officers, striking patrol vehicle Principal Serra Finnegan updated families about the misunderstanding, the district said. The district thanked the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office for its continued partnership and urged families to help share accurate information. Dog lovers from across South Florida are heading to Fort Pierce this weekend for the Treasure Coast Kennel Club's Pirate Cluster, a four-day event featuring dock diving, FastCAT racing, agility, frisbee competitions, and other canine sports.The event is taking place Oct. Lucie County Fairgrounds, where visitors can watch trained canine athletes compete or give their own dogs an opportunity to try several activities. According to Treasure Coast Kennel Club President Lisa Root, many of the events offer same-day participation."It has to do with all kinds of sporting events that we do with our dogs, so dock diving, FastCAT, agility, UpDog (frisbee catching). It's fun," she said.Admission and parking are free for spectators. Fees apply for participants entering dogs into individual events.One of the most popular attractions is dock diving, where dogs run down a platform and launch themselves into a pool in pursuit of a toy.Competitors say many dogs recognize the venue before they even leave the vehicle."Once they start competing, they know what this dock means," said dock-diving participant Janet. "You'll see them when they start coming in. They just roll past the dock, and they'll start barking in the cars and stuff because they know that they get to get up here and just jump."Organizers say the excitement surrounding dock diving often becomes contagious for owners and spectators alike.In addition to the sporting events, the Pirate Cluster includes vendors, raffles and opportunities for families to spend time with fellow dog lovers.The event highlights the growing popularity of dog sports as a way for owners to stay active, build stronger relationships with their pets and connect with others in the community.Whether someone owns a highly trained competitor or simply wants to learn more about canine activities, organizers say the weekend provides an opportunity to see what these sports are all about.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Jupiter HarbourFest is returning to Harbourside Place this Friday and Saturday, offering two days of live music, local food, vendors and family-friendly fun along the Jupiter waterfront.The festival, presented by Jupiter Medical Center and organized by the Palm Beach North Chamber of Commerce, is free to attend for general admission guests this year."It's a great event," said Brian of the Palm Beach North Chamber of Commerce. "Thanks to our sponsors, we're able to put on the event for free for general admission."In addition to free admission, attendees can purchase tickets for special experiences, including the festival's Tastings event and VIP areas.Organizers describe HarbourFest as a coastal country music festival featuring food trucks, local restaurants, vendors and performances spread across two stages.Among the participating restaurants are Tommy Bahama and the Wyndham, both of which showcased dishes ahead of the event.Tommy Bahama will offer some of its most popular menu items, including its coconut shrimp and house-made key lime pie."We're going to feature two dishes, kind of the fan favorites of Tommy Bahama," said Kyle from Tommy Bahama.The Wyndham plans to feature a braised beef shank prepared with Mediterranean spices, saffron cream sauce and orzo pasta.Live music will also be a major part of the festival experience. Local band BOXELDER will perform during the event, bringing its signature sound to the waterfront celebration.Festival organizers say HarbourFest aims to combine music, food and community while highlighting the businesses, restaurants and attractions that make Jupiter a popular destination in northern Palm Beach County.More information, including VIP ticket options, can be found at JupiterHarbourFest.org.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. With an 18-5 record heading into the playoffs, The Kings Academy volleyball team in Palm Beach County is one of the favorites to win the Florida state championship — and could also claim a seventh straight district title.Coming into this volleyball season, few teams in the state were talked about more than The Kings Academy, and for good reason.WATCH BELOW: Kings Academy volleyball team eyes state title"This year has been a year of expectations to win some stuff because our team is so well-rounded," setter Jordan Molnar said.Winning "some stuff" might be an understatement. The girls opened the season as one of the top teams in Palm Beach County and one of the favorites to win the state crown. Instead of feeding into the hype, the team came together with shared expectations."It's called the core covenant, and anytime they get a little sidetracked, we go back and refocus on those things that they said they wanted to do," head coach Bethafor Avila said. They wanted to get over the hump of losing in regional play and win a state championship, and while they're primed to do just that, the girls are taking it one day at a time and focusing on district play, where they could win their seventh straight district title."A lot of the girls on the team have been for a while, so we've got to experience a lot of those district wins. It's just special that we get to do it for such an amazing school," middle hitter Ava Maldonado said.At 18-5, the school might be amazing, but so are the Kings Academy volleyball team, who fully expect to put the entire state on notice."It's a lot of energy around because we know that we can do something big this year and we’re all just working hard to get to that," Molnar said."It's been fun; we have a great group of girls put together, and I think it's really nice to come together and compete with them," Maldonado said.

The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office (PBSO) has identified the robbery suspect involved in a deadly deputy-involved shooting incident Wednesday that shut down a major Boynton Beach roadway for several hours.PBSO identified the suspect as Gregory Dobkins, 51, of West Palm Beach.The incident unfolded Wednesday afternoon near Woolbright Road, where a large law enforcement presence prompted the closure of the roadway in both directions. PBSO previously confirmed that the encounter involved deputies and resulted in a death.WATCH WPTV REPORTER MICHAEL HOFFMAN'S REPORT BELOW:PBSO Sheriff Ric Bradshaw said the investigation began after a pizza delivery driver was robbed around 10 p.m. The suspect allegedly ordered a pizza to a Lake Worth location and told the driver he only had a $100 bill. When the driver pulled out money to make change, the suspect allegedly grabbed him, and the two struggled over the cash.The delivery driver provided investigators with a description of the suspect's vehicle and a license plate number, Bradshaw said.Investigators entered that information into license plate readers and received an alert Tuesday that the vehicle was in the Lake Park area.PBSO tactical units located the vehicle and conducted surveillance to confirm the registered owner was driving, according to Bradshaw. When deputies attempted a traffic stop, the driver fled, Bradshaw said.The pursuit traveled south on Interstate 95, with the Florida Highway Patrol becoming involved, before ending near Jog and Woolbright roads. Bradshaw said the driver crossed a median, apparently blew multiple tires and crashed into a fence.A PBSO helicopter was overhead as the man got out of the vehicle and began running along Jog Road, Bradshaw said. Something was wrapped around his right hand, and deputies in the helicopter believed he might have been holding a firearm.Bradshaw said the man attempted to take cover behind concrete light poles as deputies tried to stop him using two types of less-lethal weapons. Three less-lethal rounds struck him but had no effect, according to the sheriff.Bradshaw said the man repeatedly yelled at deputies, "You're gonna have to kill me."When the man reached a second pole, Bradshaw said he got into a kneeling position and raised his hands in what appeared to be a shooting position.A deputy then opened fire, striking the man. He died at the scene.Officials said the investigation remains active and ongoing.The Florida Department of Law Enforcement, the Palm Beach County State Attorney's Office and PBSO's Violent Crimes Division are investigating the incident.

Palm Beach County has recorded five deputy-involved shootings since the start of 2026, all of which ended in fatalities, including a deputy-involved shooting Tuesday that left a 54-year-old man dead.The latest shooting remains under investigation by the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, the Palm Beach County State Attorney's Office and its Violent Crimes Division, according to the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office.The number of deadly deputy-involved shootings this year comes as law enforcement agencies continue to face heightened scrutiny over use-of-force incidents and transparency in investigations following fatal encounters.WATCH BELOW: Palm Beach County records 5 deadly deputy-involved shootings in 2026The first deadly deputy-involved shooting of the year occurred Feb. Secret Service agents and a Palm Beach County Sheriff's deputy fatally shot 21-year-old Austin Tucker Martin near Mar-a-Lago.According to Palm Beach County Sheriff Ric Bradshaw, Martin breached the inner security perimeter while armed."He put down the gas can, raised the gun at a shooting position," Bradshaw said following the incident. "At that point in time, the deputy and the two (Secret Service) agents fired their weapons and neutralized the threat. He is deceased at the scene."Just days later, on Feb. 25, a Palm Beach County Sheriff's deputy fatally shot 44-year-old Charles Curtis McCloud Jr. in Pahokee.According to the sheriff's office, McCloud was accused of killing two men and injuring a third before attempting to strike a deputy with a vehicle and allegedly trying to fire a weapon at law enforcement.Sheriff Bradshaw later praised the deputy's actions."His training kicked in," Bradshaw said. "What really kicked in was his courage and his will to survive and not let this guy get out of the car with the gun and shoot him on the ground."On Aug. 6, two Palm Beach County Sheriff's deputies shot and killed an 18-year-old man in unincorporated West Palm Beach. Authorities said the teenager was attacking his father with a butcher knife when deputies responded.The fourth deadly deputy-involved shooting happened on Sept. 16 outside a South Palm Beach fire station.According to investigators, Rex Magann, 32, allegedly attacked a deputy, attempted to take her patrol vehicle and tried to wrestle her firearm away during a violent struggle."She was able to get her firearm and shoot the guy to stop the assault on her, which was very, very violent," Sheriff Ric Bradshaw said during a news conference.The fifth deadly deputy-involved shooting occurred Tuesday and resulted in the death of a 54-year-old man.The deputy involved has been placed on administrative leave, which is standard protocol following deputy-involved shootings, according to the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office.State investigators are reviewing the circumstances surrounding the shooting. The Florida Department of Law Enforcement and the Palm Beach County State Attorney's Office are conducting independent investigations.Additional details about the events leading up to Tuesday's shooting have not yet been released.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. It’s a long way from Washington, has a small population and hasn't backed a Democrat for Senate in nearly 20 years.Yet President Donald Trump on Tuesday devoted a big chunk of his dwindling time ahead of crucial midterm elections to head to Alaska — attempting to bolster a Republican incumbent senator in another sign of GOP fears about retaining control of Congress after Election Day on Nov. 3.Trump headlined a rally for Sen. Dan Sullivan in Wasilla, about 45 miles north of Anchorage — famous for being the hometown of former Republican vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin and the headquarters of the Iditarod sled dog race across the state.Trump's stop is part of a western swing also taking him to rallies in Arizona and Montana on Wednesday.The president noted to the crowd that he had flown eight hours to rally for Sullivan, whom he called “one of the best and most respected senators in D.C.” Sullivan, seeking a third term, faces Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman who is running to put “Alaska first” and emphasizing cost-of-living issues.During Tuesday's rally, Trump announced that Taiwan would purchase gas from a proposed mega-gas project that he has been highlighting amid Sullivan's campaign and that it would invest more than $4 billion. There was no immediate confirmation from Taiwan, the self-governing island that China claims as its own. The White House did not immediately provide further details.Trump also said the Federal Communications Commission would vote in the coming weeks on investing an additional $162 million in expanding high-speed internet access in Alaska. And he announced pardons for two men who had pleaded guilty in 2022 to Clean Air Act violations for tampering with federally mandated monitoring devices on certain vehicles.Trump and Vance have been trying to boost Sullivan repeatedlyDemocrats last won a Senate seat in Alaska in 2008, and the state hasn’t elected a governor from that party since 1998. The only time Alaska didn’t vote Republican for president was during Lyndon B. Johnson’s landslide 1964 reelection.Yet high gasoline prices from the Iran war and persistently elevated inflation have damaged Trump’s approval ratings enough to leave Democrats dreaming of Alaska upsets.Alaska pollster Ivan Moore said he's seen a decline in Trump's support statewide that mirrors the president's falling approval ratings nationally. That means the Senate race may be decided by Trump 2024 voters who are now unsure they still back him.“The visit is certainly appropriate. Whether the visit will be effective or not is another matter," said Moore, who said when he first heard that Trump would visit Alaska, he didn't believe it would actually happen.The Trump administration has prioritized expanding oil and gas drilling in the state. Vice President JD Vance last week campaigned in Fairbanks for Sullivan and Republican Rep. Nick Begich.Sullivan recently joined Trump in the Oval Office, where the president announced a $54 billion investment by South Korea's government into the proposed Alaska gas project. That's despite South Korea saying the deal, and its total value, haven't been finalized.Versions of a gas project have been proposed in Alaska for decades.Trump trekking four time zones west to get to Sullivan’s home turf — an unusually long trip so close to the midterms — is his strongest show of support for the incumbent.Trump last campaigned in Alaska to try to defeat a fellow RepublicanAlaska is home to around 740,000 people, making it slightly less populous than Denver. It ranks 48th out of 50 states in population, smaller than all but Vermont and Wyoming.Trump nonetheless headlined a 2022 rally in Anchorage opposing Republican Alaska Sen. Lisa Murkowski after she voted to convict him on a charge of incitement of insurrection during his second impeachment trial, following the attack on the U.S. Capitol by a mob of his supporters on Jan. 6, 2021.Trump endorsed Kelly Tshibaka, who challenged Murkowski that year, but that didn't stop incumbent Murkowski from winning reelection.In Wasilla, Max Christensen was waiting in line for the rally and said he hoped to hear more specifics from Trump about the natural gas project, and said he was “really curious just to see how he’s going to handle things like inflation and gas prices and things like that.”Christensen, 22, said he thinks Trump has been a great president “despite all his flaws and stuff," adding, “I think he really does genuinely care about the people of the United States of America.”This year, there are two Dan Sullivans on the ballotTrump has complained about Alaska’s unique elections system. The state has open primaries, in which the four top vote-getters — regardless of party affiliation — advance to the general election, which uses ranked choice voting.RELATED STORY | Republicans are flooding Senate races with ad money, but paying a premiumThat's led to a scenario where there also will be another Dan Sullivan on the November ballot: retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan, whom Trump and other allies of Sen. Sullivan have called a sham candidate. Sullivan has denied this, but Trump continued to hammer the other Sullivan at his rally.“They found a guy named Dan Sullivan, they put him up to get things a little confused,” Trump said, as he repeatedly urged his supporters to vote for “the real Dan Sullivan.”Trump also touted Begich, who is facing a competitive challenge from Bill Hill, an independent.Alaska has a history of rewarding candidates with an independent streak — something Vance acknowledged during his trip to Fairbanks last week."In very deep red years, Alaska is competitive. In very deep blue years, Alaska is still competitive,” Vance said. “I think it’s just a reality of the politics of the state.”Independence has been hard to find in the Republican Party, where Trump for years has had total control. Some Republicans facing tough elections have begun tiptoeing away from the president on key issues such as Iran and tariffs, but not Sullivan, who has been vocal in supporting both.Trump also questioned why three Republicans were running against a Democrat for governor and endorsed Bernadette Wilson, who finished third in the August primary but was the top vote-getting Republican. This came at the same time state GOP leaders — including outgoing Gov. Mike Dunleavy — are urging voters to rank Republicans on the ballot.Many Republicans — despite reservations with ranked voting — have seen a ranking strategy in that race as crucial for Republicans trying to win the seat.Trump's trade war with Canada may also be a factorTrump has also triggered a trade war with Canada, which shares a 1,500-plus-mile border with Alaska and is among the state's most important trading partners.The U.S. banned nearly $1 billion worth of imports from its neighbor — including alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motorcycles — after previously imposing 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian products. Canada has responded with reciprocal bans and its own import levies, and the back-and-forth could raise prices for Alaska consumers.RELATED STORY | 'I had the flu': Talarico returns to campaign trail, dismisses online rumorsMaking Canada an enemy of sorts is "discomforting" for many Alaskans, said pollster Moore.“We associate, I think, probably more closely with the Canadians — more than a lot of the Lower 48," he said.

Lucie family is seeking justice after their German shepherd, Titus, was struck and killed by a truck in a hit-and-run incident last Tuesday on Goodman Avenue. "I want justice served because you didn’t stop; you killed my dog after you hit him," Michelle Baker, Titus' owner, said. Michelle and Dillon Baker, parents of two young children, are struggling to explain the loss to their 11-year-old son and 2-year-old daughter. The incident occurred around noon when the family’s dogs hopped the fence and ran down the road. Despite efforts to track them using GPS collars, the Bakers were unable to locate the dogs in time. "He knew he hit something because he stopped, then he kept going," Dillon Baker said. Surveillance footage shows a silver truck hitting Titus, stopping briefly, and then continuing to drag the dog down the road before running him over. "My dog did not deserve to go out like that," Michelle Baker said. The driver did not return to the scene, and animal control is investigating the incident as a hit-and-run. The family believes the act constitutes animal cruelty. "That’s a crime, that’s a full-on crime, it’s murder," Michelle Baker said. Back at the Baker home, Gypsy, who witnessed the incident, has not been the same since Titus’ death. The family has a message for the driver. "Pay attention, pay attention and care about what’s on the road in front of you," Michelle Baker said. WPBF contacted animal control for further comment on the incident; as of Monday night, they have not responded. WPTV Morning Anchor Ashley Glass is following up at the Resource Depot in West Palm Beach, home to a Let's Hear It community meet-up, and learning that the non-profit, which focuses on recycling and repurposing everyday items, just received a major boost in community support. "This place is amazing," Craig Goldenfarb, Esq., Founder and CEO of GOLDLAW, said. WATCH Local non-profit all about recycling gets community boostThe Resource Depot is one of 65 local non-profit organizations benefiting from the law firm's GOLDEN 100 program, in which $100,000 in funding was donated. "To support my community is really special," Goldenfarb said. "Putting money back into the non-profit is something that strikes me close to the heart.”Staff at the Resource Depot take in 20,000 pounds of donated materials each month and repurpose them for sale. Glass asked the Resource Depot's Executive Director, Jennifer O'Brien, how the funding will be used. "AI training for our staff," she responded. "We have a small but mighty staff, and we’re looking for ways we might work more efficiently.”O'Brien also told Glass that when the community is invested, it gives her entire staff the energy to keep pushing forward with their non-profit work and saving an immeasurable amount of what could be trash from landfills.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier highlighted the recent conviction of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms at a press conference Wednesday, calling it the first major outcome from the state's newly created public corruption unit and warning that more investigations are underway across Florida.Speaking at the Attorney General's Office in West Palm Beach, Uthmeier said public officials who abuse their positions for personal gain will face increased scrutiny from his office and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement (FDLE)."Public officials are held to an even higher standard," Uthmeier said. "If you work in a city hall, serve on a commission, if you hold public office or work for a state agency, you have a duty to serve the public and not use your job to enrich yourself."Last week, a St. Lucie County jury found Mimms guilty of official misconduct, a third-degree felony, but acquitted him on a bid-tampering charge. The case centered on a city-owned parcel near the historic Lincoln Theater in Fort Pierce. Prosecutors alleged that in 2024, Mimms used his position to benefit a nonprofit organization on whose board his niece served by helping secure the land deal and later concealing his involvement. During the trial, prosecutors presented evidence that Mimms failed to disclose his familial relationship and took steps to influence and cover up the transaction.Uthmeier said the case represented the type of conduct the state's public corruption unit was created to investigate."The facts make clear that shenanigans took place to ensure that that nonprofit ended up with the award, and ultimately the city manager covered it up," Uthmeier said.According to Uthmeier, the nonprofit later received hundreds of thousands of dollars in grant funding from a Catholic charitable organization for planned development on the property, though he said the infrastructure project never materialized."We'll keep digging," Uthmeier said. "I think more facts will come to light as to where that money was going."Uthmeier said since the public corruption unit was launched, investigators have opened more than 25 active public corruption investigations or cases statewide."This is the first big announcement," he said. "You'll see many to come in the weeks ahead as we wrap up our evidence and begin to press charges against people that have abused their office, that have abused the public trust."FDLE Larry Keefe said the agency is making public corruption investigations a top priority."When the people of Florida lose their sense of trust in their institutions, it's death by a thousand cuts," Keefe said. Sentencing for Mimms is expected at a later date."This will be the first of many, sadly," Uthmeier said. "I hope we don't have to do too many, but we'll do as many as necessary to ensure the public knows that we are protecting their trust, that we are protecting taxpayers, and that we are going to hold public officials to the oaths that they take."

Many Americans say they’ve been confused or even fooled by political ads using artificial intelligence this campaign season, and want more rules governing how the technology is used, according to a new Scripps News/Talker Research poll.More than four-in-ten registered voters say they’ve seen something they thought was real in a political ad, only to later find it was AI-generated. Another 30% said they saw something they weren’t sure was real or AI.Some of the most talked about ads of the campaign have featured AI-generated candidates like Sen. Jon Ossoff in a beauty salon, James Talarico reciting old quotes out of context, and Sherrod Brown overstaying his welcome at a birthday party.More than half of survey respondents (56%) said they have seen Republicans using AI ads, compared with 49% saying they have seen ads for Democrats.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | 'I had the flu': Talarico returns to campaign trail, dismisses online rumorsAnd more than three-quarters of voters say there should be rules around how the technology is used in politics.In the absence of federal regulation, states have passed their own laws aimed at curbing the influence of AI or deepfakes in campaign advertising. Some states require disclosures or bar deepfake videos from being published in the weeks leading up to Election Day. But many of the regulations fail to keep up with the evolving use of what can be a cheap and effective new tool.An analysis from the Wesleyan Media Project from early September found AI tools had been used in at least 164 ads, 69% of which did not disclose AI was used. Eighty percent were from Republicans or Republican-leaning groups.Still, a similar amount of voters in both parties say there should be rules around how the technology is used, according to the Scripps News/Talker Research poll, including 77% of Democrats and 79% of Republicans.Concerns about how AI could impact areas outside politics also cut across party lines. Large swaths of the country worry about the impact AI could have on their jobs (61%), government institutions (83%), financial institutions (81%), and their physical safety (57%).Nearly 80% say they see content they believe was generated by AI at least once per day.This random double-opt-in online survey of 1,000 U.S. registered voters was commissioned by Scripps News and conducted by market research company Talker Research, in accordance with the Market Research Society’s code of conduct. Data was collected from Sept. The margin of error is +/- 2.2 points with 95% confidence

A suspected drug trafficker linked to a deadly fentanyl overdose investigation is behind bars after investigators say he fled from detectives, hit a law enforcement vehicle and led authorities on a high-speed chase on I-95 in St. Lucie and Martin counties.Investigators said the arrest of James Arthur Green, 43, came after a weeks-long narcotics investigation that also uncovered a suspected connection to a fatal fentanyl overdose.According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, detectives with the Special Investigations Division conducted multiple undercover purchases of drugs, gathering evidence during those operations that identified Green as the suspected supplier of fentanyl to a person who later died from an overdose.On Oct. 13, detectives used the deceased victim's cellphone during another controlled narcotics operation and placed an order for fentanyl. Investigators said Green returned to the victim's residence, delivered about two grams of fentanyl and sent a photograph showing where he left the drugs.Later that day, detectives conducted a separate undercover operation in which Green allegedly participated in a transaction involving about two ounces of fentanyl and one pound of methamphetamine.When detectives attempted to arrest him, Green fled, allegedly hitting a sheriff's office vehicle and fleeing onto southbound I-95.Authorities said the pursuit reached speeds of approximately 115 mph. During the chase, detectives reported seeing Green throw suspected narcotics and a cellphone out of his vehicle.The Florida Highway Patrol and Martin County Sheriff's Office joined the pursuit as it entered Martin County. Troopers deployed stop sticks before performing a PIT maneuver near Kanner Highway, bringing the chase to an end.Investigators recovered the one pound of methamphetamine and two ounces of fentanyl associated with the controlled purchase, along with an additional 22 grams of methamphetamine, two grams of crack cocaine and one gram of fentanyl.As part of the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office investigation, Green faces charges including trafficking of fentanyl, trafficking of cocaine, four counts of trafficking methamphetamine, sale of cocaine and unlawful use of a two-way communication device.The Florida Highway Patrol also charged Green with two counts of aggravated battery on a law enforcement officer, trafficking of fentanyl, trafficking of methamphetamine, two counts of fleeing and eluding, tampering with evidence, reckless driving, dangerous excessive speeding and resisting an officer without violence.According to the sheriff's office, Green was already out on bond in an unrelated Miami-Dade County case at the time of his arrest. Lucie County Jail without bond.The fatal overdose investigation remains active.

A major stretch of South Ocean Boulevard in Palm Beach is scheduled to close Friday morning until further notice, prompting traffic changes for residents and commuters in the area. According to the Town of Palm Beach's website, South Ocean Boulevard (State Road A1A) will close between South County Road and Southern Boulevard beginning at 5 a.m. The closure will remain in effect until further notice.Town officials said information about traffic checkpoints, modified bridge-opening schedules and temporary marine security zones is available on the town's Planned Traffic Impacts webpage.The closure announcement comes as federal aviation officials issued a Temporary Flight Restriction, or TFR, for VIP movement in the West Palm Beach area. The notice is scheduled to take effect Saturday, Oct. 17, and remain in place through Sunday, Oct. 18.Similar road and airspace restrictions have been implemented in the past during visits by President Donald Trump to his Mar-a-Lago residence.At this time, neither the Town of Palm Beach nor federal authorities have publicly confirmed whether Trump is expected to be in Palm Beach this weekend.Motorists are encouraged to plan ahead and expect delays in the area surrounding the closure.

Lucie family is turning unimaginable loss into hope after choosing organ donation following the death of their 14-year-old son, who was struck by a vehicle while walking to school, according to police.Port St. Lucie police said the teen was walking along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near Squirrel Avenue on Oct. 7 when he was struck from behind. He died from his injuries two days later.WATCH: Port St. Lucie Teen's Legacy Lives On Through DonationNow, the family's decision to donate his organs could help multiple people waiting for lifesaving transplants while creating a lasting legacy in his memory.Organ donation advocates say the family's choice highlights an ongoing need for registered donors. According to transplant advocates, more than 100,000 people nationwide are currently waiting for an organ transplant, and 15 lives are lost each day while patients remain on waiting lists.The teen's family chose organ donation in the days following his death, a decision supporters say can have a profound impact on recipients and their families."It's a courageous thing for them to do, and I think it's the right thing," said St. Lucie County Tax Collector Chris Craft.Craft has worked with Donate Life Florida through the tax collector's office to encourage organ donor registration and raise awareness about the need for donors.For Tyre Gray, a kidney transplant recipient and the chief administrative and legal officer for South Florida Donor Network, the family's decision carries special meaning."Organ donation is one of the few places where grief and gratitude exist in the same place," Gray told WPTV.Gray said he spent five years waiting for a kidney transplant before receiving the life-saving organ he needed."I know for a fact that I wouldn't be here without a family making that election in their deepest moment of despair," he said.Gray described years of uncertainty while waiting for a match."That's five years of uncertainty, five years of being paralyzed, five years of not being able to grow," he said.Organ donation advocates say the need for donors continues across Florida and the United States.Gray noted that a single donor has the potential to save multiple lives and help many more patients through tissue donation."One donor is to save upwards of nine lives and to be able to heal another 75 lives," Gray said.Behind those numbers are people awaiting a second chance, he said."Let's all be heroes and save lives," Gray added.Advocates say organ donation often allows families to find meaning during some of life's most difficult moments."I would hope that they could see the lasting impact that a selfless act can make on others," Craft said. "If you can help somebody else, it's an amazing thing."For transplant recipients, organ donation can mean more time with family, additional milestones and opportunities.In the midst of tragedy, one Port St. Lucie family's decision could now help save lives and ensure their son's legacy continues through the people he may help.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. If you've ever wondered what the world looks like through your dog's eyes or how your cat experiences its surroundings, a new exhibit at the Cox Science Center & Aquarium in West Palm Beach aims to provide answers.The new Cats & Dogs exhibition opened Oct. 10 and runs through April 16, 2027. According to the Cox Science Center & Aquarium, the interactive experience allows visitors to explore how cats and dogs see, hear, smell, communicate, and move through the world.The exhibition combines science, animal behavior, and hands-on activities designed to help guests better understand their four-legged companions. Visitors can compare their height to various dog breeds, test their balance by walking like a cat or dog, navigate agility challenges, and participate in games that highlight the unique abilities of household pets.One of the exhibit's central themes is encouraging visitors to "step into their pets' paws."Guests can explore sensory experiences that demonstrate how animals perceive the world differently than humans. Interactive stations examine body language, communication, physical abilities, and the ways cats and dogs use their senses to gather information about their surroundings.The exhibit also highlights the remarkable differences among breeds, allowing visitors to compare themselves to everything from Great Danes to smaller companion dogs and learn how physical traits affect behavior and movement.The exhibit was created to make science relatable through animals that many families already know and love.Visitors can participate in agility activities, balance challenges, and interactive games while learning more about animal intelligence, awareness, and communication. WPTV has been reporting extensively on the growth at the Vero Beach Regional Airport when it comes to flights.But on Tuesday, Vero Beach City Council approved a lease agreement to bring a four-story, 116-room Marriott hotel to the airport."We've been in negotiations with this for the last three years,” Brian Dembeck, interim airport director, said. "This is something that is going to dramatically improve the passenger experience."Dembeck took WPTV to the site, which sits just outside the gates of the terminal along Aviation Boulevard."They're going to have a hotel right next door that they can come, they can stay, wait for their flight, and then go right over to the terminal."But the lodging is more than just for passengers.Brian Cartland, vice-president of economic development for the Indian River County Chamber of Commerce, said the hotel could attract more businesses to the city of Vero Beach and beyond."The hotel is going to serve multiple purposes,” said Cartland. "This hotel is going to help target industry growth by giving those companies that are looking at the area some additional alternatives for some great high-end options."While the hotel is close to the airport, Chad Maxey, senior vice president of Diversified Companies, the developer of the project, said one big need for the extra lodging is just down the street at the Jackie Robinson Training Complex."We feel this is a great location to have a hotel that's going to be able to provide amenities to the airport and also to the families and kids that are going to play baseball,” Maxey said.Maxey said the hotel will also feature a “homerun dugout amenity” for families."Kids can play virtual baseball in the hotel as they're getting ready to go across the street and actually hit the diamond over there and play with the Major League Baseball players,” Maxey said.Developers said the hotel will break ground next year and is expected to be completed by the end of 2028.

A major stretch of South Ocean Boulevard in Palm Beach is scheduled to close Friday morning until further notice, prompting traffic changes for residents and commuters in the area. Many Americans say they’ve been confused or even fooled by political ads using artificial intelligence this campaign season, and want more rules governing how the technology is used, according to a new Scripps News/Talker Research poll.More than four-in-ten registered voters say they’ve seen something they thought was real in a political ad, only to later find it was AI-generated. Another 30% said they saw something they weren’t sure was real or AI.Some of the most talked about ads of the campaign have featured AI-generated candidates like Sen. Jon Ossoff in a beauty salon, James Talarico reciting old quotes out of context, and Sherrod Brown overstaying his welcome at a birthday party.More than half of survey respondents (56%) said they have seen Republicans using AI ads, compared with 49% saying they have seen ads for Democrats.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | 'I had the flu': Talarico returns to campaign trail, dismisses online rumorsAnd more than three-quarters of voters say there should be rules around how the technology is used in politics.In the absence of federal regulation, states have passed their own laws aimed at curbing the influence of AI or deepfakes in campaign advertising. Some states require disclosures or bar deepfake videos from being published in the weeks leading up to Election Day. But many of the regulations fail to keep up with the evolving use of what can be a cheap and effective new tool.An analysis from the Wesleyan Media Project from early September found AI tools had been used in at least 164 ads, 69% of which did not disclose AI was used. Eighty percent were from Republicans or Republican-leaning groups.Still, a similar amount of voters in both parties say there should be rules around how the technology is used, according to the Scripps News/Talker Research poll, including 77% of Democrats and 79% of Republicans.Concerns about how AI could impact areas outside politics also cut across party lines. Large swaths of the country worry about the impact AI could have on their jobs (61%), government institutions (83%), financial institutions (81%), and their physical safety (57%).Nearly 80% say they see content they believe was generated by AI at least once per day.This random double-opt-in online survey of 1,000 U.S. registered voters was commissioned by Scripps News and conducted by market research company Talker Research, in accordance with the Market Research Society’s code of conduct. Data was collected from Sept. The margin of error is +/- 2.2 points with 95% confidence

Republicans are spending hundreds of millions of dollars on advertising in battleground Senate races as they scramble to defend increasingly competitive GOP seats in the final stretch of the midterms.But when it comes to how far they can stretch a dollar, they’re effectively paying premium prices at Whole Foods while Democrats are shopping deals at Costco.RELATED STORY | Trump is heading all the way to Alaska in a sign of just how close its Senate race may beAcross nine of the most competitive Senate races last month, Republicans cumulatively outspent Democrats on broadcast TV ads by nearly 100% more, $233 million to $121 million, according to AdImpact data, but only saw about 40% more rating points.The disparity comes down to a difference in strategy. Republicans are relying heavily on outside groups, like super PACs, that pay elevated rates for ads and are making big buys late in the campaign, when inventory is stretched.By contrast, Democrats are taking advantage of discounted rates for candidates and earlier, less expensive reservations.At this stage in the game, Republicans are spending more to get less, which means the “shock and awe” of their massive dollar advantage isn’t necessarily translating to an actual impact on the ground, according to veteran Republican strategist John Thomas.A better metric, he said, is to consider the gross rating points, or GRPs, a unit advertisers use to measure the reach and frequency of an ad campaign, independent of how much was paid for it.In those nine races – where outside groups accounted for about 9 in 10 Republican ad dollars, compared to about half for Democrats – Democrats paid $201 per GRP, while Republicans paid about $274.In some races in September, Democrats actually outpaced Republicans in GRPs, completely overcoming their spending edge.In North Carolina, for example, Republicans outspent Democrats by about $17 million to $14 million on TV ads in September, as former Gov. Roy Cooper poses a major threat to former RNC Chair Michael Whatley and the GOP chances of holding Sen. But Democrats got more than 71,000 GRPs from their spend while Republicans got about 58,000. And at the beginning of October – recognizing the costly, difficult road ahead for Whatley – Republicans actually began cutting their remaining ad bookings by about $15 million.Democrats were also outspent last month by Republicans in Maine by about 32%, another premier battleground race where former state Sen. Troy Jackson is looking to unseat veteran GOP incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, who has received major backing from national Republicans. But here, again, despite being outspent, Democrats got 6% more GRPs for their money.Even in Texas – where Democrats were blasted by Republican ad money in September, outspent more than 4 times over – the GRP gap was proportionally much smaller. Republicans got only 2.6 times more GRPs.A GOP super PAC had to spend more than $22 million to air its top ad, touting Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s record as a prosecutor, about 15,500 times in September. Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico’s campaign spent a little under $4 million to air its most aired ad, casting Paxton as “the most corrupt politician in Texas,” about 8,000 times. That amounts to less than one-fifth the spending for about half the airtime.Lauren French, communications director for Senate Majority PAC, a leading Democratic super PAC, also emphasized that buying TV late in the cycle becomes exorbitantly expensive. “The nitty-gritty of campaigning is that not all ad space costs the same,” she said.“If you are buying something in February, it’s going to be a lot cheaper, and you’re going to get a lot more bang for your buck than, say, if you’re buying it in September. So that’s why you’re seeing this huge disconnect between what Republicans are paying and what Democrats are paying on average in some of these races,” French said.In seven of the top nine Senate races by total TV and radio ad spending in September, Democrats paid less per GRP than Republicans.The two exceptions were New Hampshire and Alaska. Confident in their nominees, Republicans were able to secure comparable or better rates in both states’ key markets. In New Hampshire, this was reinforced by Republicans allocating relatively more to cheaper secondary markets.“Broadly speaking, Republicans are using their money pretty ineffectively, and public polling is saying that people are not seeing their ads as much as one would expect. So, by that definition alone, some of their money is being set on fire. We are being outspent in a lot of these states, which means we have to make more strategic decisions,” French said.Thomas said that Texas, in particular, was emblematic of this effect, with GOP outside groups mounting an urgent rescue effort for Paxton and pouring money into the state. He noted that Paxton allies had taken to buying ad time on national NFL broadcasts because local markets had grown so crowded. That’s why people across the country are seeing Texas Senate ads in games that don’t include the Dallas Cowboys or Houston Texans.RELATED STORY | Barack Obama to campaign with Ohio Democrats as he expands his outreach ahead of Election Day“In some cases, because the commercial rate is so high in a local, like a Houston spot, it actually sometimes can be cheaper to buy a national spot,” he said.Democrats’ efficiency advantage might have been much greater, given their candidates have consistently raised more money their Republican opponents on a campaign-to-campaign basis, allowing them to spend more directly on their own ads at cheap rates.But thanks to a recent Supreme Court ruling, for the first time this year, national party committees can take advantage of candidate ad rates through coordinated buys.This means well-funded national committees like the National Republican Congressional Committee or National Republican Senate Committee can team up with candidates – like Mike Rogers in Michigan or Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio – and foot the bill for pricey ad campaigns while getting candidate discounts.The expansion of coordinated buying has allowed Republicans to blunt the Democratic candidate fundraising advantage. Democrats can do the same, but the GOP has taken to it far more aggressively: In September, GOP advertisers spent more than $30 million on coordinated ad buys, compared to about $5 million from Democrats.Outside groups like super PACs still play a dominant role, however, due to their unique ability to accept unlimited donations and make unlimited expenditures.“The money is actually very, very inefficient, but the benefit, even with the inefficiency of a super PAC, is one or two people can cut checks and fund the whole thing,” Thomas said.

Lucie Boulevard say more needs to be done to protect pedestrians as construction continues on the busy road. Their concerns come after a 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student died from injuries he suffered when he was hit by an SUV while walking to school. Police say the freshman was walking along the edge of Southwest Port St. Lucie Boulevard near Squirrel Avenue on the morning of Oct. 7 when he was struck from behind. He was pronounced clinically deceased two days later. His family chose to donate his organs . Much of the roadway remains under construction, and there are no sidewalks along large sections of the corridor. Recent heavy rain also left portions of the shoulder flooded, further limiting space for pedestrians. "He was just going to school," said neighbor Irene Ange. "He was just starting his high school year. He had the right to be safe." Irene Ange, who has lived near the boulevard for more than two decades, says students often walk or bike close to traffic, sometimes before sunrise. The stretch of road is dangerous, Ange said. It’s very dark, and drivers are not following the speed limits. Ange said she saw first responders rushing to the crash site and was heartbroken for the student and his family. See also: Suspect booked into Martin County Jail after undercover drug sting, sheriff says The teen’s mother told CBS12 by phone that her son was a people person who made friends easily. She said the family does not want this to happen to another child. The Florida Department of Transportation is widening the southern portion of Port St. Lucie Boulevard from two lanes to four and adding sidewalks on both sides of the road. FDOT says the sidewalks will be eight to 10 feet wide. The project is expected to be completed in winter 2028, with an estimated cost of about $25.6 million. CBS 12 saw crews building sidewalks several blocks from where the crash happened. FDOT did not respond to questions about what pedestrian safety measures are in place while construction continues. "No accountability with that response because now there's another death," Ange said. Ange says more needs to be done now to keep children safe on their way to school. "This did not have to happen to this family," Ange said. The family now have to mourn him." The driver initially told officers he believed he had struck a construction barrel and has been cooperating with investigators. It remains unclear whether any charges will be filed.

Fort Pierce police are searching for a driver who they say hit and killed a man riding a scooter before fleeing the scene, crashing into a salon and running away on foot Sunday night. The deadly crash happened shortly before 9 p.m. on October 11 along Okeechobee Road, just west of South 25th Street. According to Major Michael Santiago with the Fort Pierce Police Department , a man riding a scooter was stopped at a red light behind a Toyota pickup truck when a white van traveling eastbound failed to stop and struck him from behind. "That in turn led to a domino effect where the motorcyclist was ejected from the scooter itself and was thrown into the vehicle in front of the scooter," Santiago said. Obtained 911 recordings capture the frantic moments following the crash. In one call, a person inside the Toyota pickup truck described the aftermath. "We got hit, and it's like, there's blood all over our car," the caller told a dispatcher. Another caller reported seeing the white van crash into the nearby building while trying to get away. Lucie County Fire District officials said crews were dispatched at 8:51 p.m. and arrived four minutes later. The scooter rider was pronounced dead at the scene. No other patients were transported. But investigators say the van driver did not remain at the scene. See also: No lawyer, no law degree: Port St. Lucie man takes on Flock cameras in federal court Instead, Santiago said the driver reversed, made a U-turn, briefly traveled westbound in the eastbound lanes of Okeechobee Road, crossed the median and lost control before crashing into Kings & Queens Unisex Salon. "After he crashed into the business, he fled on foot," Santiago said. According to a police news release, the driver ran northbound after crashing into the salon, located at 2508 Okeechobee Road. Police responded to multiple 911 calls reporting the crash around 8:52 p.m. and immediately established a perimeter, searching for the driver using K-9 units and assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office aviation unit. Despite their efforts, they were unable to locate him. Two additional vehicles involved in the crash remained at the scene, according to police. The department's Traffic Homicide Unit, Crime Scene Investigations and other personnel processed the scene as part of the ongoing investigation. By Monday afternoon, the van had been removed, but significant damage remained. Broken concrete and debris were piled outside the entrance, which was boarded up and surrounded by caution tape. Salon owner Sheila Hampton said she received a phone call about the crash and arrived to find extensive damage to her business. "They just called me at the last minute and I just seen a hole in my wall. Hampton said she was unable to open the salon Monday and was concerned about when she would be allowed to resume business. And I'm just hoping tomorrow will be a better day," she said. Despite the damage to her business, Hampton also expressed sympathy for the family of the man who died. "My condolences from King and Queen Salon. We give out our condolences to the family," she said. "This shouldn't have ever happened." Police searching for driver Santiago said witnesses described the driver as a Hispanic man wearing a dark top and light-colored pants or shorts. Investigators believe he may have been injured in the crash, based on evidence recovered at the scene. Police have recovered the van and identified its registered owner, but have not confirmed who was driving. Santiago said the registered owner lives approximately one to one-and-a-half miles from the crash scene. He also said the owner stopped communicating with investigators after officers began asking who had access to the vehicle. Police have not ruled anyone out as they continue pursuing leads. Investigators are also searching for surveillance footage that could help identify the driver. As of Monday afternoon, Santiago said they had not obtained video showing the suspect himself. "We are desperately needing the public's help in identifying who was behind the wheel of this box van," Santiago said. He urged anyone who saw the white van in the area Sunday night, recognized someone who may have been driving it or captured video of the incident to come forward. Police said the victim's identity had not yet been confirmed as of Monday, and confirmation was still pending before next of kin could be notified. No arrest had been announced as of Monday afternoon. Anyone with information about the crash or the driver's whereabouts is asked to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or submit a tip through Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers .

Police are searching for a hit-and-run cargo van driver accused of fatally striking a 44-year-old man riding a gas scooter before he crashed into a nearby business and ran away in Fort Pierce. On Tuesday, the victim was identified as Andy Ramon Martinez-Pantoja. Police officers received multiple 911 calls just before 9 p.m. Sunday about a vehicle crash involving a motorcycle, which later was identified as a gas scooter, close to the intersection of Okeechobee Road and 25th Street, near HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. A white cargo van was behind the scooter, traveling east on Okeechobee Road, Maj. Michael Santiago told WPBF's Angela Rozier at a briefing Monday afternoon. The van driver fled the scene and made a U-turn to drive in the wrong direction across the median on Okeechobee Road, but he crashed into the side of a building, the Kings Queens Unisex Salon. The man then ran from the scene. Salon owner Sheila Hampton showed the damage, and is thankful no one was inside at the time. Hampton said she feels for the victim and his family. "His family told me he was just leaving from one of his friend's houses and just going home," she said. A second vehicle, a Toyota pickup truck, was also struck, but no one was injured. Lucie County Sheriff's Office K-9 Unit and Aviation Unit assisted Fort Pierce police and the K-9 Unit in efforts to locate the driver. They are in possession of the van. Police described the driver as a Hispanic man wearing a dark-colored top with light-colored pants or shorts. "So, that in itself proves intent that that person knew exactly what they were doing at the time and was just trying to simply get away," Santiago said. Anyone with information should call the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-8477. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

A nurse at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie is under investigation after allegedly stealing fentanyl from a critically ill patient’s IV bag on June 24 and 25, according to police. "They did an internal investigation where the Department of Health was then notified, in turn notifying PSLPD where we started our investigation in early August," said Officer Brittany McNally, public information officer for the Port St. Police said a family member of the patient reported seeing 54-year-old Leslie Pope use a syringe to withdraw fluid from the patient’s fentanyl infusion, place the syringe in her pocket, and leave the room. "That’s not standard procedure, from what I understand at the hospital," McNally said. "But again, she’s not even assigned that patient. And there was no initial justification for her to even be in that room at the time." Investigators said Pope returned the following evening and approached the IV equipment again, but the family member intervened and stopped her. Hospital video reportedly showed Pope manipulating protective caps on the IV equipment, but investigators said she did not remove any fluid during the second incident. And this individual had this monitor that had video recordings, which was a key piece of evidence in this case and completely contradicted what her recollection was," McNally said. Police said Pope denied the allegations and did not admit to using the fentanyl for personal consumption. "From my understanding, she did not admit that she was using it for personal consumption and essentially denied all the allegations that were made, but there was an overwhelming amount of evidence to prove otherwise," McNally said. Cleveland Clinic released a statement regarding the arrest, saying, "We take these allegations very seriously. The individual no longer works with us, and we are fully cooperating with law enforcement. Because this is an active investigation, we are unable to comment further at this time." The investigation remains ongoing.

Just days after MARTY public bus services abruptly shut down in Martin County, county commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to allow the county administrator to negotiate a new contract with a company that could restore service. The vote gives county administration the green light to begin negotiations with MTM Transit, a company that previously operated the county’s public bus system. For former MARTY bus driver Bill Lawrence, Tuesday’s decision offered a sign of hope after he and several other drivers suddenly lost their jobs last Thursday. “I’m hoping that we get this back on the road soon. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work,” Lawrence said. Lawrence was among the drivers impacted when Martin County Transit LLC, the company previously operating MARTY, abruptly stopped services last Thursday. The company cited rising operating costs, including fuel and maintenance, as reasons for its decision to discontinue service. During Tuesday’s county commission meeting, Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton explained that county officials had spent the past several days exploring options to restore service. “We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us,” Gorton said. According to Gorton, the county evaluated several proposals before identifying MTM Transit as its preferred option. Under the county’s emergency procurement rules, the proposed agreement would be a one-year contract costing approximately $3 million. During that year, county officials would work toward establishing a standard multi-year contract through the county’s normal competitive bidding process. One of the county’s priorities during negotiations is bringing back the drivers who lost their jobs following last week’s shutdown. “We absolutely want to use those same drivers and get them back to work as quickly as possible,” Gorton said. Jupiter Fire Rescue began its first day of municipal service Thursday by responding to four calls after midnight and unveiling Jupiter's first ladder truck, which carries a tribute to FDNY Ladder 10 and the six members who died in the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.Fire Chief Darrel Donatto said the department's first calls unfolded as its members had prepared."They went perfectly, exactly as planned," Donatto said. "We've been planning for this moment for three years, and everything is perfect."The launch marks a new chapter for public safety in Jupiter, with locally controlled fire rescue and emergency medical services operating from stations serving the town's eastern, central and western communities.Jupiter's new ladder truck is based at Station 10, located at 500 N. Highway 1 near Burt Reynolds Park. It is the first ladder truck based in Jupiter, according to Donatto.Donatto said the equipment is important because of the town's oceanfront high-rises and multi-story residential developments."Jupiter has a lot of high-rise buildings all along the oceanfront here, plus a lot of three-story type townhomes all through the Abacoa community," Donatto said. "And so a ladder truck is vital to protecting those, those type of occupancies."Palm Beach County Fire Rescue continues to serve nearby unincorporated areas, including county pockets near the Jupiter Inlet, DuBois Park and Jonathan's Landing, Donatto said.Jupiter's first ladder truck features an American flag design and imagery of the Jupiter Lighthouse. The truck carries the number 10 as a tribute to FDNY Ladder 10, whose firehouse sits across from the World Trade Center site in New York City.Following the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, FDNY Ladder 10's replacement truck was wrapped in an American flag design honoring the firefighters who responded that day. Before adopting the tribute, Town of Jupiter officials contacted FDNY Ladder 10 to seek their blessing.Rodman Leas, a firefighter with Jupiter Fire Rescue, explained the significance behind the tribute."Today marks a brand new chapter in Jupiter fire history as we roll out 10 Truck, our community is, like you said, our community's very first ladder truck ever," Leas said. "It carries the number 10 badge ... as we honor FDNY Truck 10, whose firehouse stands directly across from the Sept. 11th World Trade Center site." Leas said six members of FDNY Ladder 10 made the ultimate sacrifice on Sept. 11."I took an inspiration from their American flag design as well ... as a constant reminder of the bravery, courage, brotherhood that defined the fire service," Leas said.Battalion Chief Jason Bohan said Jupiter Fire Rescue worked with Palm Beach Gardens as crews prepared for the new department's launch."We've had an incredible partnership with Palm Beach Gardens," Bohan said. "We've been using their training facility, and because of that partnership over the last couple of months, they and us have been training, getting ready for today."That preparation includes learning to put on approximately 60 pounds of protective equipment quickly when an emergency call comes in.Bohan said the most exciting part of launch day was bringing the new department together around its public service mission."Getting us all together, knowing what we're called to do, which is to protect and save people," Bohan said. "So now that it finally came today, we're all really excited."For Lt. Christian Lainhart, joining Jupiter Fire Rescue also represents a personal homecoming. Lainhart previously worked for Martin County Fire Rescue and described himself as a sixth-generation Jupiter pioneer."I'm super excited, very blessed to be here," Lainhart said.Lainhart said his family's roots in the Jupiter area extend to the 1890s. He grew up and attended school in Jupiter and is now raising his family there."It's just truly remarkable," Lainhart said. They're excited to serve the town of Jupiter."By 5 a.m. Thursday, Jupiter Fire Rescue's firefighters and paramedics had already answered four calls while introducing the community to the people and equipment behind the new department.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives announced Friday it will no longer enforce National Firearms Act registration and approval requirements for suppressors, short-barreled rifles and short-barreled shotguns.The move eliminates what was often a months-long process that required buyers to obtain federal approval, register the items with the government and pay a tax stamp before taking possession. Federal background checks are still required.For firearm retailers in West Palm Beach, the change is already having an impact.At We Kick Brass, owner Mike Perez said customers previously had to navigate a lengthy approval process to legally purchase suppressors and certain firearms regulated under the National Firearms Act."People were legally able to own these firearms," Perez said. "They just had to wait a longer process. It had to get ATF approval."For decades, suppressors and short-barreled rifles and shotguns were subject to National Firearms Act requirements that included registration, federal approval and a tax stamp.The ATF announced Friday it will no longer enforce those requirements for those items.The move follows a federal court ruling in Texas involving National Firearms Act registration requirements and comes after Congress reduced the tax stamp fee from $200 to zero.Perez said the biggest change is the amount of paperwork buyers no longer have to complete."The biggest change is less paperwork," Perez said. "It's a lot easier for someone to come in here and purchase a firearm and feel safe about it and secure about it."He said some customers who once faced waits stretching nine months, 14 months or longer may now be able to take possession much sooner."They no longer have to wait 14 months, or nine months, or even more than a day if they have a concealed weapon firearm permit," Perez said. "They can leave with that same day and start training immediately and empower themselves and be able to protect themselves or their family."Perez said interest surged almost immediately after the federal announcement.When WPTV's Michael Hoffman visited We Kick Brass, several customers were at the shop picking up suppressors.Perez believes the changes will make firearms and accessories that were already legal to own more accessible to law-abiding buyers.Perez also has personal experience with short-barreled rifles. In 2018, he was involved in a self-defense shooting in which he used one."I used a short-barreled rifle to save my mother's life," Perez said. "They are just simply put the best and most effective tools."Asked what could happen if a future administration attempted to reverse the policy, Perez said he believes current owners would likely be protected."I imagine that they would be grandfathered in," Perez said. "You can't make millions of Americans felons overnight by the flick of a pen. It just makes no sense."The ATF's policy change does not eliminate all National Firearms Act regulations.Machine guns and destructive devices, including bombs, rockets and grenades, remain subject to federal requirements.Customers purchasing firearms must also continue to undergo background checks and comply with all applicable federal and state laws.For those concerned about expanded access to suppressors and short-barreled firearms, Perez said the changes affect law-abiding citizens."We are just allowing people, law-abiding citizens, the ability to protect themselves with the right firearm to do so," Perez said.Florida gun owners should also be aware that state law prohibits short-barreled rifles and short-barreled shotguns unless they are lawfully owned under federal law. The ATF has said it cannot provide guidance on whether an unregistered firearm would satisfy that requirement under Florida law.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI.
