Fort Pierce police are searching for a driver who they say hit and killed a man riding a scooter before fleeing the scene, crashing into a salon and running away on foot Sunday night. The deadly crash happened shortly before 9 p.m. on October 11 along Okeechobee Road, just west of South 25th Street. According to Major Michael Santiago with the Fort Pierce Police Department , a man riding a scooter was stopped at a red light behind a Toyota pickup truck when a white van traveling eastbound failed to stop and struck him from behind. "That in turn led to a domino effect where the motorcyclist was ejected from the scooter itself and was thrown into the vehicle in front of the scooter," Santiago said. Obtained 911 recordings capture the frantic moments following the crash. In one call, a person inside the Toyota pickup truck described the aftermath. "We got hit, and it's like, there's blood all over our car," the caller told a dispatcher. Another caller reported seeing the white van crash into the nearby building while trying to get away. Lucie County Fire District officials said crews were dispatched at 8:51 p.m. and arrived four minutes later. The scooter rider was pronounced dead at the scene. No other patients were transported. But investigators say the van driver did not remain at the scene. See also: No lawyer, no law degree: Port St. Lucie man takes on Flock cameras in federal court Instead, Santiago said the driver reversed, made a U-turn, briefly traveled westbound in the eastbound lanes of Okeechobee Road, crossed the median and lost control before crashing into Kings & Queens Unisex Salon. "After he crashed into the business, he fled on foot," Santiago said. According to a police news release, the driver ran northbound after crashing into the salon, located at 2508 Okeechobee Road. Police responded to multiple 911 calls reporting the crash around 8:52 p.m. and immediately established a perimeter, searching for the driver using K-9 units and assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office aviation unit. Despite their efforts, they were unable to locate him. Two additional vehicles involved in the crash remained at the scene, according to police. The department's Traffic Homicide Unit, Crime Scene Investigations and other personnel processed the scene as part of the ongoing investigation. By Monday afternoon, the van had been removed, but significant damage remained. Broken concrete and debris were piled outside the entrance, which was boarded up and surrounded by caution tape. Salon owner Sheila Hampton said she received a phone call about the crash and arrived to find extensive damage to her business. "They just called me at the last minute and I just seen a hole in my wall. Hampton said she was unable to open the salon Monday and was concerned about when she would be allowed to resume business. And I'm just hoping tomorrow will be a better day," she said. Despite the damage to her business, Hampton also expressed sympathy for the family of the man who died. "My condolences from King and Queen Salon. We give out our condolences to the family," she said. "This shouldn't have ever happened." Police searching for driver Santiago said witnesses described the driver as a Hispanic man wearing a dark top and light-colored pants or shorts. Investigators believe he may have been injured in the crash, based on evidence recovered at the scene. Police have recovered the van and identified its registered owner, but have not confirmed who was driving. Santiago said the registered owner lives approximately one to one-and-a-half miles from the crash scene. He also said the owner stopped communicating with investigators after officers began asking who had access to the vehicle. Police have not ruled anyone out as they continue pursuing leads. Investigators are also searching for surveillance footage that could help identify the driver. As of Monday afternoon, Santiago said they had not obtained video showing the suspect himself. "We are desperately needing the public's help in identifying who was behind the wheel of this box van," Santiago said. He urged anyone who saw the white van in the area Sunday night, recognized someone who may have been driving it or captured video of the incident to come forward. Police said the victim's identity had not yet been confirmed as of Monday, and confirmation was still pending before next of kin could be notified. No arrest had been announced as of Monday afternoon. Anyone with information about the crash or the driver's whereabouts is asked to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or submit a tip through Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers .

A 54-year-old man suspected of robbing a pizza delivery driver was fatally shot by a Palm Beach County sheriff's deputy Tuesday after a pursuit ended near Jog and Woolbright roads, Sheriff Ric Bradshaw said.Bradshaw said the investigation began after a pizza delivery driver was robbed around 10 p.m. The suspect allegedly ordered a pizza to a Lake Worth location and told the driver he only had a $100 bill. When the driver pulled out money to make change, the suspect allegedly grabbed him, and the two struggled over the cash.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The delivery driver provided investigators with a description of the suspect's vehicle and a license plate number, Bradshaw said.Investigators entered that information into license plate readers and received an alert Tuesday that the vehicle was in the Lake Park area.PBSO tactical units located the vehicle and conducted surveillance to confirm the registered owner was driving, according to Bradshaw. When deputies attempted a traffic stop, the driver fled, Bradshaw said.The pursuit traveled south on Interstate 95, with the Florida Highway Patrol becoming involved, before ending near Jog and Woolbright roads. Bradshaw said the driver crossed a median, apparently blew multiple tires and crashed into a fence.BREAKING NEWS: Deputy fatally shoots robbery suspect after chaseA PBSO helicopter was overhead as the man got out of the vehicle and began running along Jog Road, Bradshaw said. Something was wrapped around his right hand, and deputies in the helicopter believed he might have been holding a firearm.Bradshaw said the man attempted to take cover behind concrete light poles as deputies tried to stop him using two types of less-lethal weapons. Three less-lethal rounds struck him but had no effect, according to the sheriff.Bradshaw said the man repeatedly yelled at deputies, "You're gonna have to kill me."When the man reached a second pole, Bradshaw said he got into a kneeling position and raised his hands in what appeared to be a shooting position.A deputy then opened fire, striking the man. He died at the scene.Bradshaw later confirmed investigators did not find a firearm on the man.The sheriff said the 54-year-old was a convicted felon whose criminal history included carjacking, robbery, kidnapping, assault and drug offenses.The man's identity has not been released pending notification of his next of kin.Jog Road was shut down in both directions between Woolbright Road and Grand Isle Drive during the investigation. the road is back open.Bradshaw said additional information, including a more detailed timeline and information about the suspect, will be released as the investigation continues.

WPTV has been reporting extensively on the growth at the Vero Beach Regional Airport when it comes to flights.But on Tuesday, Vero Beach City Council approved a lease agreement to bring a four-story, 116-room Marriott hotel to the airport."We've been in negotiations with this for the last three years,” Brian Dembeck, interim airport director, said. "This is something that is going to dramatically improve the passenger experience."Dembeck took WPTV to the site, which sits just outside the gates of the terminal along Aviation Boulevard."They're going to have a hotel right next door that they can come, they can stay, wait for their flight, and then go right over to the terminal."But the lodging is more than just for passengers.Brian Cartland, vice-president of economic development for the Indian River County Chamber of Commerce, said the hotel could attract more businesses to the city of Vero Beach and beyond."The hotel is going to serve multiple purposes,” said Cartland. "This hotel is going to help target industry growth by giving those companies that are looking at the area some additional alternatives for some great high-end options."While the hotel is close to the airport, Chad Maxey, senior vice president of Diversified Companies, the developer of the project, said one big need for the extra lodging is just down the street at the Jackie Robinson Training Complex."We feel this is a great location to have a hotel that's going to be able to provide amenities to the airport and also to the families and kids that are going to play baseball,” Maxey said.Maxey said the hotel will also feature a “homerun dugout amenity” for families."Kids can play virtual baseball in the hotel as they're getting ready to go across the street and actually hit the diamond over there and play with the Major League Baseball players,” Maxey said.Developers said the hotel will break ground next year and is expected to be completed by the end of 2028.

Lucie City Council approved three major site plans for projects along the Southern Grove, a developing jobs corridor in the city. One of those plans: the long-awaited Costco retail store. “This is something that we have been looking forward to for a long time,” Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Samples and Wes McCurry, president and CEO of the St. Lucie County Economic Development Council, said the 163,000-square-foot store is just the beginning for a new phase of growth in western Port St. “This is getting closer to the finish line,” Samples said. The Costco will join other companies like Amazon, Tamco and Cheney Brothers, calling the Southern Grove area home. McCurry said since the jobs are now here, new commercial development will follow. “They see all the development that’s occurring here, along with the demographics that they like to see,” said McCurry. “It only makes sense that Costco opens a retail store here.” City council approved two other major site plans for the area, including a 5.5-acre site making up the first phase of the Tradition Entertainment District set to bring restaurants and retail. “This area has historically been largely underserved by restaurants and retail, and especially entertainment facilities,” McCurry said. “It’s kind of catching up to the rooftops that are happening. You know, rooftops always drive that demand, but there’s more to come.” The other plan is space for an acute care rehabilitation hospital, featuring inpatient and outpatient services with 42 beds in a more than 55,000-square-foot building. “A growing area needs services, and that’s just another component of services that are coming into the area is expanded healthcare access,” McCurry said. McCurry said the plans for retail, healthcare and entertainment are fulfilling the city’s master plan for what Southern Grove was destined to become. “The plan is coming together. The vision is coming together. What everyone saw 20 years ago is now starting to happen,” McCurry said. Samples said Costco still must close on the land, move on to construction design planning and permitting before any shovels hit the ground.

Martin County commissioners have approved emergency measures aimed at restoring MARTY bus service after an abrupt shutdown last week left hundreds of riders without transportation and dozens of drivers without jobs.County leaders voted Tuesday to terminate their contract with Martin County Transit and begin negotiating an emergency one-year operating agreement with MTM Transit, a company that previously operated the county's transit system.WATCH: Martin County moves to restore MARTY busesThe move comes as the county works to quickly restore public transportation service for residents who rely on MARTY buses to get to work, medical appointments and other essential destinations.The emergency action follows last week's sudden shutdown of MARTY bus service, which county officials say disrupted transportation across the community."We're doing it under our emergency procurement rules, and we will have a one-year contract," said Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton.The proposed agreement with MTM Transit would serve as a temporary solution while county leaders develop a longer-term plan for public transportation service.County officials say restoring service is a top priority."The next vendor needs to have a contract to be able to hire the drivers back," Gorton said.The shutdown has created uncertainty for employees who suddenly found themselves without work."It was shocking. This company has pulled out and left 28 employees unemployed, and not knowing what tomorrow is going to be like is very devastating," said Joey Acevedo, president of ATU Local 1577.Former MARTY bus driver Bill Lawrence said workers are eager to get back behind the wheel and resume serving the community."I'm very hopeful. We have people behind us that give us hope," Lawrence said.Martin County officials say they are moving quickly to finalize an agreement with MTM Transit and restore operations."Our goal is to get them finalized this week and try to stand up the service next week. It's an aggressive goal," Gorton said.For drivers like Lawrence, the timeline is critical as they wait for paychecks and benefits to resume."We have no income right now. I'm going to lose it if I don't have my insurance," Lawrence said.Despite the challenges, Lawrence remains optimistic."So we need to get everything rolling, so we all can get back to work," he said.County leaders are continuing negotiations with MTM Transit and hope to finalize an emergency operating contract in the coming days.If approved, officials say service could return as early as next week, restoring a transportation option for riders across Martin County and providing a pathway for former drivers to return to work.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Martin County commissioners voted Tuesday unanimously to move forward with a one-year moratorium on data centers as county leaders consider how to handle future development of the facilities.Martin County Commissioner Edward Ciampi explained it's "an opportunity to say, 'pause,' let's hear from people, let’s have the opportunity for experts to come and speak to us on both sides.”Watch report from Cassandra Garcia:Commissioners explained they would consider extending the moratorium later if they need more time.“If it takes a year, a year and a half, two years, whatever it takes, whatever it takes, we should be doing this,” said Martin County Commissioner Eileen Vargas.Tuesday's vote marked the first of two hearings scheduled this month on the proposed moratorium.PREVIOUS COVERAGE: Martin County eyes pause on data center developmentCommissioners are expected to revisit the issue on Oct. 27, when another vote will be required.Residents are now hoping the county will use the time to consider their concerns.“For me it’s wildlife so these areas are in largely rural or large plots of land and so you take that area and develop it and these facilities are massive—millions and millions of square feet, no animals can live there anymore, or the hum is going to affect the animals,” said Sergei Kelley, who spoke at the meeting.Martin County resident Scott Butler added, "The fear of the use of all this water we have [...] and understanding what these data center[s] are going to use.”The discussion comes as Martin County has already received an application for a data center. The county received the application Monday, one day before commissioners considered the moratorium. It’s the first data center proposed in unincorporated Martin County. The application is considered a hyper-scale data center, at over 950-thousand square feet proposed on a lot off Kanner Highway west of I-95. Because the application was submitted before the proposed moratorium, it would not be affected by the measure.The proposal comes amid residents' concerns about the future of data center development in Martin County.One resident at the meeting told commissioners, "Once land is converted into industrial use, the consequences can remain long after."Ann Vandersteel, another resident, added, "We need to have serious studies completed in order to go forward with something of this consideration."WPTV continues to hear from residents about those concerns as commissioners consider what restrictions, if any, to place on future data center development.

WPTV has been reporting extensively on the growth at the Vero Beach Regional Airport when it comes to flights. But on Tuesday, Vero Beach City Council approved a lease agreement to bring a four-story, 116-room Marriott hotel to the airport. "We've been in negotiations with this for the last three years,” Brian Dembeck, interim airport director, said. "This is something that is going to dramatically improve the passenger experience." Dembeck took WPTV to the site, which sits just outside the gates of the terminal along Aviation Boulevard. "They're going to have a hotel right next door that they can come, they can stay, wait for their flight, and then go right over to the terminal." But the lodging is more than just for passengers. Brian Cartland, vice-president of economic development for the Indian River County Chamber of Commerce, said the hotel could attract more businesses to the city of Vero Beach and beyond. "The hotel is going to serve multiple purposes,” said Cartland. "This hotel is going to help target industry growth by giving those companies that are looking at the area some additional alternatives for some great high-end options." While the hotel is close to the airport, Chad Maxey, senior vice president of Diversified Companies, the developer of the project, said one big need for the extra lodging is just down the street at the Jackie Robinson Training Complex. "We feel this is a great location to have a hotel that's going to be able to provide amenities to the airport and also to the families and kids that are going to play baseball,” Maxey said. Maxey said the hotel will also feature a “homerun dugout amenity” for families. "Kids can play virtual baseball in the hotel as they're getting ready to go across the street and actually hit the diamond over there and play with the Major League Baseball players,” Maxey said. Developers said the hotel will break ground next year and is expected to be completed by the end of 2028.

Martin County commissioners have approved emergency measures aimed at restoring MARTY bus service after an abrupt shutdown last week left hundreds of riders without transportation and dozens of drivers without jobs.County leaders voted Tuesday to terminate their contract with Martin County Transit and begin negotiating an emergency one-year operating agreement with MTM Transit, a company that previously operated the county's transit system.WATCH: Martin County moves to restore MARTY busesThe move comes as the county works to quickly restore public transportation service for residents who rely on MARTY buses to get to work, medical appointments and other essential destinations.The emergency action follows last week's sudden shutdown of MARTY bus service, which county officials say disrupted transportation across the community."We're doing it under our emergency procurement rules, and we will have a one-year contract," said Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton.The proposed agreement with MTM Transit would serve as a temporary solution while county leaders develop a longer-term plan for public transportation service.County officials say restoring service is a top priority."The next vendor needs to have a contract to be able to hire the drivers back," Gorton said.The shutdown has created uncertainty for employees who suddenly found themselves without work."It was shocking. This company has pulled out and left 28 employees unemployed, and not knowing what tomorrow is going to be like is very devastating," said Joey Acevedo, president of ATU Local 1577.Former MARTY bus driver Bill Lawrence said workers are eager to get back behind the wheel and resume serving the community."I'm very hopeful. We have people behind us that give us hope," Lawrence said.Martin County officials say they are moving quickly to finalize an agreement with MTM Transit and restore operations."Our goal is to get them finalized this week and try to stand up the service next week. It's an aggressive goal," Gorton said.For drivers like Lawrence, the timeline is critical as they wait for paychecks and benefits to resume."We have no income right now. I'm going to lose it if I don't have my insurance," Lawrence said.Despite the challenges, Lawrence remains optimistic."So we need to get everything rolling, so we all can get back to work," he said.County leaders are continuing negotiations with MTM Transit and hope to finalize an emergency operating contract in the coming days.If approved, officials say service could return as early as next week, restoring a transportation option for riders across Martin County and providing a pathway for former drivers to return to work.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie County Fire District board member is calling on Fire Chief Jeff Lee to resign after firefighters delivered an overwhelming vote of no confidence in district leadership, the latest fallout from a hazing investigation that led to the firing of three veteran firefighters.More than 74% of firefighters who participated in the union vote said they had no confidence in Lee. About 92% said they had no confidence in Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez, while 97% said the same of district attorney Kim Sabol.WATCH BELOW: St. Lucie County fire chief faces calls to resign after no-confidence vote"I think it's a wake-up call," Fire Board member and St. Lucie County Commissioner James Clasby told WPTV Investigates. "They've sent their message, and now it's, again, up for the board to take action." When investigative reporter Kate Hussey asked whether he believed that action should include Lee's resignation, Clasby said yes."I don't know how you could possibly recover from getting such an overwhelming vote of no confidence," he said.The vote is the latest fallout from an investigation earlier this year into videos involving firefighters at Station 1A.A third-party investigator concluded the videos depicted hazing. One showed firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary employees.Veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin were fired following the investigation.The three have maintained the activity was consensual and "all in good fun.""It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson previously told WPTV."We're all still friends," Boudrias said.Their terminations sparked pushback from firefighters and members of the community, which eventually led to the union's no-confidence vote."The amount that voted no confidence really sends a message that we have, in their opinion, a lack of confidence in their leadership," union representative Ryan Sapp said.Sapp is representing the three firefighters in their fight for reinstatement. With previous settlement offers now off the table, Sapp said he recently met with Lee and district leadership to ask how they planned to respond to the vote."His response was that he doesn't feel a change in leadership would change the confidence issue or the morale," Sapp said.The vote comes as the district is already undergoing changes in leadership.Sabol has submitted notice of her retirement, effective in December. Meanwhile, a reassignment notice obtained by WPTV Investigates shows Gonzalez is being moved from assistant chief to battalion chief.Clasby questioned the decision, particularly given the no-confidence vote against Gonzalez."I have lots of questions about why this move happened, why you would move somebody that received over 90% no confidence into a training position that will now train everybody in the district," Clasby said.The district told WPTV that Gonzalez and Lee agreed the reassignment was in the district's best interest and said the move had been under discussion "for some time prior to recent events."In a statement, the district said it "recognizes" the results of the no-confidence vote and the importance of listening to its personnel.The district said it remains committed to addressing workplace concerns and taking "appropriate action" to protect the safety, well-being and trust of its firefighters.Sapp said rebuilding that trust could prove difficult."I think it's hard whenever you see those staggering numbers, that lack confidence in leadership, to rebound it back," he said.The Fire Board is also weighing whether it has the authority to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin while working to overhaul how complaints against district leadership are handled.That work is expected to continue at the board's Oct. 21 meeting.Sapp said their last settlement offer, an offer to reinstate the three firefighters with a three-shift suspension, was not accepted. "I do want to say, this is a great department," Sapp added. We have great men and women that work here. In light of all this bad publicity we've had, I promise you these members, these employees that I have, they genuinely enjoy serving this community and do the absolute best they can do." A 54-year-old man suspected of robbing a pizza delivery driver was fatally shot by a Palm Beach County sheriff's deputy Tuesday after a pursuit ended near Jog and Woolbright roads, Sheriff Ric Bradshaw said.Bradshaw said the investigation began after a pizza delivery driver was robbed around 10 p.m. The suspect allegedly ordered a pizza to a Lake Worth location and told the driver he only had a $100 bill. When the driver pulled out money to make change, the suspect allegedly grabbed him, and the two struggled over the cash.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The delivery driver provided investigators with a description of the suspect's vehicle and a license plate number, Bradshaw said.Investigators entered that information into license plate readers and received an alert Tuesday that the vehicle was in the Lake Park area.PBSO tactical units located the vehicle and conducted surveillance to confirm the registered owner was driving, according to Bradshaw. When deputies attempted a traffic stop, the driver fled, Bradshaw said.The pursuit traveled south on Interstate 95, with the Florida Highway Patrol becoming involved, before ending near Jog and Woolbright roads. Bradshaw said the driver crossed a median, apparently blew multiple tires and crashed into a fence.BREAKING NEWS: Deputy fatally shoots robbery suspect after chaseA PBSO helicopter was overhead as the man got out of the vehicle and began running along Jog Road, Bradshaw said. Something was wrapped around his right hand, and deputies in the helicopter believed he might have been holding a firearm.Bradshaw said the man attempted to take cover behind concrete light poles as deputies tried to stop him using two types of less-lethal weapons. Three less-lethal rounds struck him but had no effect, according to the sheriff.Bradshaw said the man repeatedly yelled at deputies, "You're gonna have to kill me."When the man reached a second pole, Bradshaw said he got into a kneeling position and raised his hands in what appeared to be a shooting position.A deputy then opened fire, striking the man. He died at the scene.Bradshaw later confirmed investigators did not find a firearm on the man.The sheriff said the 54-year-old was a convicted felon whose criminal history included carjacking, robbery, kidnapping, assault and drug offenses.The man's identity has not been released pending notification of his next of kin.Jog Road was shut down in both directions between Woolbright Road and Grand Isle Drive during the investigation. the road is back open.Bradshaw said additional information, including a more detailed timeline and information about the suspect, will be released as the investigation continues.

Fort Pierce police are searching for a driver who they say hit and killed a man riding a scooter before fleeing the scene, crashing into a salon and running away on foot Sunday night. The deadly crash happened shortly before 9 p.m. on October 11 along Okeechobee Road, just west of South 25th Street. According to Major Michael Santiago with the Fort Pierce Police Department , a man riding a scooter was stopped at a red light behind a Toyota pickup truck when a white van traveling eastbound failed to stop and struck him from behind. "That in turn led to a domino effect where the motorcyclist was ejected from the scooter itself and was thrown into the vehicle in front of the scooter," Santiago said. Obtained 911 recordings capture the frantic moments following the crash. In one call, a person inside the Toyota pickup truck described the aftermath. "We got hit, and it's like, there's blood all over our car," the caller told a dispatcher. Another caller reported seeing the white van crash into the nearby building while trying to get away. Lucie County Fire District officials said crews were dispatched at 8:51 p.m. and arrived four minutes later. The scooter rider was pronounced dead at the scene. No other patients were transported. But investigators say the van driver did not remain at the scene. See also: No lawyer, no law degree: Port St. Lucie man takes on Flock cameras in federal court Instead, Santiago said the driver reversed, made a U-turn, briefly traveled westbound in the eastbound lanes of Okeechobee Road, crossed the median and lost control before crashing into Kings & Queens Unisex Salon. "After he crashed into the business, he fled on foot," Santiago said. According to a police news release, the driver ran northbound after crashing into the salon, located at 2508 Okeechobee Road. Police responded to multiple 911 calls reporting the crash around 8:52 p.m. and immediately established a perimeter, searching for the driver using K-9 units and assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office aviation unit. Despite their efforts, they were unable to locate him. Two additional vehicles involved in the crash remained at the scene, according to police. The department's Traffic Homicide Unit, Crime Scene Investigations and other personnel processed the scene as part of the ongoing investigation. By Monday afternoon, the van had been removed, but significant damage remained. Broken concrete and debris were piled outside the entrance, which was boarded up and surrounded by caution tape. Salon owner Sheila Hampton said she received a phone call about the crash and arrived to find extensive damage to her business. "They just called me at the last minute and I just seen a hole in my wall. Hampton said she was unable to open the salon Monday and was concerned about when she would be allowed to resume business. And I'm just hoping tomorrow will be a better day," she said. Despite the damage to her business, Hampton also expressed sympathy for the family of the man who died. "My condolences from King and Queen Salon. We give out our condolences to the family," she said. "This shouldn't have ever happened." Police searching for driver Santiago said witnesses described the driver as a Hispanic man wearing a dark top and light-colored pants or shorts. Investigators believe he may have been injured in the crash, based on evidence recovered at the scene. Police have recovered the van and identified its registered owner, but have not confirmed who was driving. Santiago said the registered owner lives approximately one to one-and-a-half miles from the crash scene. He also said the owner stopped communicating with investigators after officers began asking who had access to the vehicle. Police have not ruled anyone out as they continue pursuing leads. Investigators are also searching for surveillance footage that could help identify the driver. As of Monday afternoon, Santiago said they had not obtained video showing the suspect himself. "We are desperately needing the public's help in identifying who was behind the wheel of this box van," Santiago said. He urged anyone who saw the white van in the area Sunday night, recognized someone who may have been driving it or captured video of the incident to come forward. Police said the victim's identity had not yet been confirmed as of Monday, and confirmation was still pending before next of kin could be notified. No arrest had been announced as of Monday afternoon. Anyone with information about the crash or the driver's whereabouts is asked to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or submit a tip through Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers .

Just days after MARTY public bus services abruptly shut down in Martin County, county commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to allow the county administrator to negotiate a new contract with a company that could restore service. The vote gives county administration the green light to begin negotiations with MTM Transit, a company that previously operated the county’s public bus system. For former MARTY bus driver Bill Lawrence, Tuesday’s decision offered a sign of hope after he and several other drivers suddenly lost their jobs last Thursday. “I’m hoping that we get this back on the road soon. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work,” Lawrence said. Lawrence was among the drivers impacted when Martin County Transit LLC, the company previously operating MARTY, abruptly stopped services last Thursday. The company cited rising operating costs, including fuel and maintenance, as reasons for its decision to discontinue service. During Tuesday’s county commission meeting, Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton explained that county officials had spent the past several days exploring options to restore service. “We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us,” Gorton said. According to Gorton, the county evaluated several proposals before identifying MTM Transit as its preferred option. Under the county’s emergency procurement rules, the proposed agreement would be a one-year contract costing approximately $3 million. During that year, county officials would work toward establishing a standard multi-year contract through the county’s normal competitive bidding process. One of the county’s priorities during negotiations is bringing back the drivers who lost their jobs following last week’s shutdown. “We absolutely want to use those same drivers and get them back to work as quickly as possible,” Gorton said. Commissioners also authorized county administration to move forward with terminating its previous contract with Martin County Transit LLC. County officials say they are hopeful negotiations with MTM Transit can be finalized by the end of this week, potentially allowing buses to begin operating again next week. Fort Pierce city commissioners voted unanimously to end their lease with the former operator of Crabby's Dockside and begin searching for a new operator for the waterfront restaurant. The restaurant, located along Avenue A at the Fort Pierce Marina, closed in February. The city said its operator, Winking Starfish, owed more than $418,000 in rent, taxes, and late fees. After recalculating the balance, the city now says the amount owed is nearly $334,000. Winking Starfish identified a potential new operator for the restaurant, but city officials said the proposal sought favorable terms. City Manager Richard Chess told commissioners that the city would allow interested restaurateurs to compete for the location. The city plans to set requirements for potential operators, with the city commission making the final decision. "Our marina is very, very successful, and we're very proud of it, and that location, that Crabby's location, is a very critical part of the marina," Mayor Linda Hudson said. Chess also said during the meeting that a new agreement would combine rent and other payments into one amount, based on the property's market value. Local leaders joined housing advocates in West Palm Beach on Tuesday to discuss rising homeowners association fees and condo assessments that they say are putting financial pressure on residents, particularly seniors and people struggling to remain in their homes.WATCH BELOW: Palm Beach County leaders tackle rising HOA feesThe panel, organized by U.S. Lois Frankel, focused on potential solutions including more financial assistance for seniors, greater state oversight of homeowners associations and limits on attorney fees charged to condo owners."This is really tough," state Sen. "But we don’t want another Surfside, but at the same time what we want to do is create new affordable housing."Florida condominium owners have faced increased financial pressures following reforms adopted in response to the 2021 Surfside condominium collapse. The reforms included inspection and reserve requirements intended to address building safety.The discussion comes as Florida communities rank among those with the nation's highest HOA burdens. A Realtor.com analysis previously covered by WPTV found seven of the nation's 10 metro areas with the highest HOA fees relative to estimated mortgage payments were in Florida. Lucie ranked fifth, while the Sebastian-Vero Beach area ranked ninth.Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said questions about transparency are adding to homeowners' concerns."What we're seeing is a lot of transparency issues, questioning each other, are these fees necessary or not necessary," Flores said.Panelists also discussed reports of condo owners being forced from their homes as association costs become unaffordable.Among the potential solutions raised Tuesday were additional financial assistance for seniors and more state oversight of HOAs.Flores said keeping seniors in their homes should be part of the discussion."More dollars coming to help these seniors stay in their homes because if they don’t stay in their homes we have to find another solution of where will they go to live," Flores said.The panel also discussed controlling attorney fees charged to condo owners.For Florida homeowners, the issue goes beyond association dues. Rising HOA fees can add to other major housing expenses, including property taxes and insurance. Tuesday's discussion highlighted the challenge facing policymakers: ensuring condominium buildings have the money needed to address safety concerns while finding ways to prevent those costs from pricing residents out of their homes.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Martin County commissioners voted Tuesday unanimously to move forward with a one-year moratorium on data centers as county leaders consider how to handle future development of the facilities.Martin County Commissioner Edward Ciampi explained it's "an opportunity to say, 'pause,' let's hear from people, let’s have the opportunity for experts to come and speak to us on both sides.”Watch report from Cassandra Garcia:Commissioners explained they would consider extending the moratorium later if they need more time.“If it takes a year, a year and a half, two years, whatever it takes, whatever it takes, we should be doing this,” said Martin County Commissioner Eileen Vargas.Tuesday's vote marked the first of two hearings scheduled this month on the proposed moratorium.PREVIOUS COVERAGE: Martin County eyes pause on data center developmentCommissioners are expected to revisit the issue on Oct. 27, when another vote will be required.Residents are now hoping the county will use the time to consider their concerns.“For me it’s wildlife so these areas are in largely rural or large plots of land and so you take that area and develop it and these facilities are massive—millions and millions of square feet, no animals can live there anymore, or the hum is going to affect the animals,” said Sergei Kelley, who spoke at the meeting.Martin County resident Scott Butler added, "The fear of the use of all this water we have [...] and understanding what these data center[s] are going to use.”The discussion comes as Martin County has already received an application for a data center. The county received the application Monday, one day before commissioners considered the moratorium. It’s the first data center proposed in unincorporated Martin County. The application is considered a hyper-scale data center, at over 950-thousand square feet proposed on a lot off Kanner Highway west of I-95. Because the application was submitted before the proposed moratorium, it would not be affected by the measure.The proposal comes amid residents' concerns about the future of data center development in Martin County.One resident at the meeting told commissioners, "Once land is converted into industrial use, the consequences can remain long after."Ann Vandersteel, another resident, added, "We need to have serious studies completed in order to go forward with something of this consideration."WPTV continues to hear from residents about those concerns as commissioners consider what restrictions, if any, to place on future data center development.

Fort Pierce police are searching for a driver who they say fled after a crash that killed a motorcyclist Sunday night.The crash happened around 8:52 p.m. near South 25th Street and Okeechobee Road. Officers responded after receiving multiple 911 calls about a crash involving a motorcycle.According to preliminary information from the Fort Pierce Police Department, a white box van traveling east on Okeechobee Road struck a blue motorcycle and attempted to leave the scene.Police said the van's driver made a U-turn in the eastbound lanes while fleeing, crossed the westbound lanes and crashed into Kings and Queens Unisex Salon at 2508 Okeechobee Road.The driver then got out of the van and fled north on foot, police said.When officers arrived, they found the motorcyclist in the outside eastbound lane of Okeechobee Road and determined the person had died. Lucie County Fire Rescue also responded.The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office K-9 and Aviation units assisted Fort Pierce police in searching for the driver, but police said he had not been located as of Monday. Two other vehicles involved in the crash remained at the scene.Police described the driver as an adult Hispanic man wearing a dark-colored top and light-colored pants or shorts.The identity of the person killed has not been confirmed.The Fort Pierce Police Department's Traffic Homicide Unit and Crime Scene Investigations are investigating.Anyone with information about the crash or the driver's identity or whereabouts is asked to contact Fort Pierce police at 772-462-6800 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

A nurse at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie is under investigation after allegedly stealing fentanyl from a critically ill patient’s IV bag on June 24 and 25, according to police. "They did an internal investigation where the Department of Health was then notified, in turn notifying PSLPD where we started our investigation in early August," said Officer Brittany McNally, public information officer for the Port St. Police said a family member of the patient reported seeing 54-year-old Leslie Pope use a syringe to withdraw fluid from the patient’s fentanyl infusion, place the syringe in her pocket, and leave the room. "That’s not standard procedure, from what I understand at the hospital," McNally said. "But again, she’s not even assigned that patient. And there was no initial justification for her to even be in that room at the time." Investigators said Pope returned the following evening and approached the IV equipment again, but the family member intervened and stopped her. Hospital video reportedly showed Pope manipulating protective caps on the IV equipment, but investigators said she did not remove any fluid during the second incident. And this individual had this monitor that had video recordings, which was a key piece of evidence in this case and completely contradicted what her recollection was," McNally said. Police said Pope denied the allegations and did not admit to using the fentanyl for personal consumption. "From my understanding, she did not admit that she was using it for personal consumption and essentially denied all the allegations that were made, but there was an overwhelming amount of evidence to prove otherwise," McNally said. Cleveland Clinic released a statement regarding the arrest, saying, "We take these allegations very seriously. The individual no longer works with us, and we are fully cooperating with law enforcement. Because this is an active investigation, we are unable to comment further at this time." The investigation remains ongoing.

Lucie City Council approved three major site plans for projects along the Southern Grove, a developing jobs corridor in the city.One of those plans: the long-awaited Costco retail store.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie City Council approves site plan for Costco"This is something that we have been looking forward to for a long time,” Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said.Samples and Wes McCurry, president and CEO of the St. Lucie County Economic Development Council, said the 163,000-square-foot store is just the beginning for a new phase of growth in western Port St. Lucie."This is getting closer to the finish line," Samples said.The Costco will join other companies like Amazon, Tamco and Cheney Brothers, calling the Southern Grove area home.McCurry said since the jobs are now here, new commercial development will follow."They see all the development that's occurring here, along with the demographics that they like to see,” said McCurry. "It only makes sense that Costco opens a retail store here."City council approved two other major site plans for the area, including a 5.5-acre site making up the first phase of the Tradition Entertainment District set to bring restaurants and retail."This area has historically been largely underserved by restaurants and retail, and especially entertainment facilities,” McCurry said. "It's kind of catching up to the rooftops that are happening. A Florida prisoner who said he killed his cellmate specifically to get on death row was executed Tuesday, nearly 18 years after the attack.James Robertson, 63, declined to offer any last words before receiving a three-drug injection and was pronounced dead about 10 minutes later. It was a stark contrast to the failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee two weeks ago, where she was rushed to the hospital after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital.Robertson’s execution, the first in Florida since Pike, comes at a time of escalating attention on the death penalty in the United States. The Pentagon said last week that it would livestream the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan, drawing criticism from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers.“Florida has a sound lethal injection process and protocol,” Jordan Kirkland, a state Department of Corrections spokesperson, said at a news conference before the execution. Although he couldn’t speak to Tennessee’s lethal injection procedure, he said Florida would make sure its process was “humane and dignified.”Florida executes people by injecting them with a sedative, a paralytic, and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.Robertson had pleaded guilty to first-degree murder for strangling Frank Hart while he slept in 2008, and waived all appeals. He told investigators that he did it so he wouldn't have to live out his days in prison.Hart was killed just eight days before he was due to be released, his daughter, Rebecca Hart, told reporters at Florida State Prison. She stressed that her father was not just a piece of Robertson’s story.“When someone you love is taken from you in such a violent way, the world keeps moving, even when a part of yours feels like it has stopped,” she read. “Other people go on with their lives, but you carry your loss into every tomorrow.”Robertson was 17 years old when he went to prison in 1980 for burglary and assault. Years of convictions for escape, battery and weapons while in prison kept adding time to his total sentence. Hart had been sent to prison in 2003 following a sexual battery conviction.Robertson was supposed to be one of two executions carried out by Florida on Tuesday, but Gov. Ron DeSantis withdrew a death warrant last week for William Lee Thompson. The Republican governor did not provide a reason but had temporarily stayed the execution last month pending a psychiatric evaluation.Records show this was the first time DeSantis withdrew a death warrant. Thompson, 74, will remain on death row, and a new death warrant could be signed in the future. His attorneys say he has dementia and failing health, and they want him transferred to a medical facility.DeSantis is the third Florida governor to sign a death warrant for Thompson. Bob Graham and Bob Martinez both scheduled executions for Thompson in the 1980s, but years of appeals and stays allowed him to avoid the electric chair, the state's method of execution at the time.Thompson was convicted of first-degree murder, kidnapping and sexual battery in the 1976 killing of 23-year-old Sally Ivester.DeSantis oversaw 19 executions in 2025, more than any other Florida governor in a single year since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Robertson was the state’s 17th execution of 2026, with two more already scheduled, not counting Thompson.DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has made few public comments about the unprecedented number of executions but explained previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out.William Reaves, 77, is scheduled to be executed on Oct. 20, followed by Jesse Guardado, 64, on Nov. Reaves was convicted of fatally shooting a deputy after dropping a gun in front of the law enforcement officer in 1986. Guardado was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half the 31 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.

After years of infertility, pregnancy loss and unanswered questions, one Jupiter mother is turning her personal journey into a source of hope for others.The inaugural Hope Rising 5K and Fun Walk will take place Oct. 17 at Carlin Park, bringing together families, wellness providers and community partners with a shared goal: ensuring that no one facing infertility or pregnancy loss feels alone.WATCH: Jupiter woman creates Hope Rising after infertility journeyFor founder Kimberly Malik, the event grew from her own experience navigating five miscarriages and four years of infertility."When you get told unexplained infertility, that's not really what you want to hear and that's not an answer I can accept," Malik said.She spent years researching, advocating for herself and searching for answers before ultimately learning she had a blood-clotting condition that contributed to her losses.Despite the heartbreak, Malik said the experience eventually led her to a larger purpose."Welcomed our rainbow baby on Nov. 8 of 2024, my husband's birthday, and I just felt this calling of don't let others walk alone," she said.That mission became the foundation of Hope Rising.Malik says one of the most difficult parts of infertility and pregnancy loss is the isolation many families experience.The Hope Rising event is designed to change that.Organizers are bringing together local businesses, wellness providers and community partners to create a Support Village where attendees can connect with resources and others who understand the journey firsthand."We can have those that unfortunately are on a fertility journey feel seen and supported," Malik said.Among those helping organize the event is Jenny Frattaruolo, owner of Jupiter Fit Club, who became part of Malik's support system during her fertility journey."Just having resources and having someone along the journey with you is everything," Malik said during an earlier interview.While the event centers around a 5K and fun walk, organizers say the focus extends far beyond race day.Participants will be able to leave messages of encouragement on wooden hearts, honor loved ones through remembrance activities and celebrate children born after pregnancy loss on a Rainbow Baby Wall.The event will also raise money for the Hope Rising Grant, which aims to help Florida families facing the financial challenges often associated with infertility treatment."Fitness is a great way to bring people together, so this race is going to bring a lot of women together and hopefully we can help them find resources," Frattaruolo said.Pregnancy loss remains a topic many families struggle to discuss openly, even though countless people are affected by it.Frattaruolo believes connection can make a meaningful difference."It's one of those, if you know, you know," she said. "I think we will all experience death and grief in our lifetime, but miscarriage is the only death you will experience inside your own body."For Malik, that understanding is exactly why Hope Rising exists.What began as a search for answers has evolved into a movement focused on support, community and hope.The Hope Rising 5K and Fun Walk will take place Oct. 17 at Carlin Park in Jupiter.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm & Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman “Sulli” Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. No arrests have been made, and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense. The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room.As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm & Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life.Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. “He touched everybody’s heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room,” Rodriguez said.Bah's close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him.Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. “He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future,” Cortez said.Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. “Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul,” Espinosa said.The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff's office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense. No arrests have been made.Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. She said she wants investigators to consider all the facts as they determine what happened.“I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right,” Godfrey said. “I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail.”During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the impact he had on their lives.Angela Sanders, one of Bah's former sixth grade teachers, remembered his personality and smile. “His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room,” Sanders said.Myan Agosto said Bah was the type of friend who regularly checked on the people around him. “He never failed to make sure everybody was okay,” Agosto said. “He was just a really good friend.”Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person.The memories shared Wednesday showed how many people Bah touched during his 17 years.“He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth — look at this room,” another speaker said during the celebration.Bah's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

A $43 million expansion project to level up the Port of Palm Beach is moving forward, with port leaders saying the improvements could attract new cruise opportunities, boost tourism and generate more economic activity in Palm Beach County.But some residents are urging local leaders to slow down and take a closer look at what those changes could mean for the waters around Peanut Island and the Inlet.WATCH BELOW: $43M Port of Palm Beach expansion raises concernsLast month, the Port Commission voted to seek proposals for a project that would expand cruise facilities, a plan identified as a priority in the port's 2023 master plan. The project includes a parking garage, a new passenger loading bridge, expanded screening and baggage areas and the addition of mooring dolphins that would allow the port to accommodate longer ships."Our goal is to bring more cruise passengers to Palm Beach County and the City of Riviera Beach, creating greater economic benefits to our community," said Blair Ciklin, chair of the Port Commission.According to the port, there is currently one cruise ship homeported in Palm Beach County, the Margaritaville at Sea Paradise, which began operating from the port in 2022.For Bradford Gary, a longtime mariner and Palm Beach resident, the concern is not cruise ships themselves."I don't want to stop the port from development, but I don't want them to put a big boat in here that's going to hazard small boats and swimmers and mariners," Gary said.Gary emailed WPTV reporter Joel Lopez, worried that larger vessels could create conflicts with the recreational users who frequent Peanut Island and surrounding waters.He appeared before the Town of Palm Beach council on Tuesday urging local leaders to support federal restrictions that would cap ships entering the Port of Palm Beach at roughly 700 feet in length, about the size of the Margaritaville at Sea Paradise currently operating from the port."We don't think those big 700-foot, 1,000-foot boats mix with small boats or swimmers or traffic, particularly on Peanut Island," he said.Lopez took Gary's concerns straight to Port of Palm Beach officials for answers on safety and impacts to the waterways."So right now we fit our ship, which is 730 (feet), but it's really not about the size of the vessel. It's about the controls of the vessel," said Michael Meekins, executive director of the Port of Palm Beach.Meekins said newer ships can come equipped with advanced propulsion systems that make them easier to maneuver than traditional vessels.The debate also centers on proposed mooring dolphins, offshore structures that allow ships to tie up beyond the existing dock.Meekins described the structures as a common maritime tool that can accommodate different vessel configurations without constructing an entirely new dock."You have the normal pier and then out from the pier you just have a catwalk, and then there's a concrete anchorage system with some moorings on it, and that allows the ship to tie up out there without having to build an entire dock," Meekins said.He said no final approval has been made on how many mooring dolphins will be installed or how far out from the port they will be.I addressed Gary's concerns about larger ships with boaters, swimmers and snorkelers near Peanut Island, and Meekins pushed back."The cruise line really has zero impact on the local tourists who are going out to Peanut Island or anything else," Meekins said. "All it does is open up and vary the different options that the port has to offer."According to Meekins, cruise ships typically arrive before most beachgoers and snorkelers head out for the day and depart around dusk. He also noted the port currently has only one cruise berth, limiting the amount of cruise traffic moving through the inlet.Beyond cruise operations, Meekins says the project is intended to improve the passenger experience and create opportunities for future growth."It's a magnificent job producer, and it creates a lot of economic impact to the local community," he said.The port says cruise activity currently accounts for about 30% of its revenue and supports jobs ranging from vessel services and maintenance to hotels, restaurants and transportation providers throughout the region.Meekins said the Port of Palm Beach District has not levied property taxes since 1975.Design and permitting work is expected to begin following the solicitation process. According to Meekins, renderings could become available in the coming months, while construction is likely still several years away.Meanwhile, Gary says he hopes the discussion continues before final decisions are made.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A 54-year-old man suspected of robbing a pizza delivery driver was fatally shot by a Palm Beach County sheriff's deputy Tuesday after a pursuit ended near Jog and Woolbright roads, Sheriff Ric Bradshaw said.Bradshaw said the investigation began after a pizza delivery driver was robbed around 10 p.m. The suspect allegedly ordered a pizza to a location and told the driver he only had a $100 bill. When the driver pulled out money to make change, the suspect allegedly grabbed him, and the two struggled over the cash.BREAKING NEWS: Deputy fatally shoots robbery suspect after chaseThe delivery driver provided investigators with a description of the suspect's vehicle and a license plate number, Bradshaw said.Investigators entered that information into license plate readers and received an alert Tuesday that the vehicle was in the Lake Park area.PBSO tactical units located the vehicle and conducted surveillance to confirm the registered owner was driving, according to Bradshaw. When deputies attempted a traffic stop, the driver fled, Bradshaw said.The pursuit traveled south on Interstate 95, with the Florida Highway Patrol becoming involved, before ending near Jog and Woolbright roads. Bradshaw said the driver crossed a median, apparently blew multiple tires and crashed into a fence.A PBSO helicopter was overhead as the man got out of the vehicle and began running along Jog Road, Bradshaw said. Something was wrapped around his right hand, and deputies in the helicopter believed he might have been holding a firearm.Bradshaw said the man attempted to take cover behind concrete light poles as deputies tried to stop him using two types of less-lethal weapons. Three less-lethal rounds struck him but had no effect, according to the sheriff.Bradshaw said the man repeatedly yelled at deputies, "You're gonna have to kill me."When the man reached a second pole, Bradshaw said he got into a kneeling position and raised his hands in what appeared to be a shooting position.A deputy then opened fire, striking the man. He died at the scene.Bradshaw later confirmed investigators did not find a firearm on the man.The sheriff said the 54-year-old was a convicted felon whose criminal history included carjacking, robbery, kidnapping, assault and drug offenses.The man's identity has not been released pending notification of his next of kin.Jog Road was shut down in both directions between Woolbright Road and Grand Isle Drive during the investigation.Bradshaw said additional information, including a more detailed timeline and information about the suspect, will be released as the investigation continues.This is a developing story.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Tuesday that 25 people have been charged in connection with what authorities describe as a large-scale drug trafficking organization responsible for distributing cocaine, fentanyl and methamphetamine across multiple Florida counties.According to investigators, 19 suspects are already in custody and six remain outstanding following a months-long investigation dubbed Operation Ice Breaker.WATCH BELOW: 25 charged in major drug trafficking investigationOfficials said the investigation targeted a drug trafficking network operating mainly in Palm Beach, Broward and St. Lucie counties, as well as communities in Miami-Dade and Florida's west coast."These were not users. These were wholesalers," Uthmeier said during a news conference in Boynton Beach "These were large-scale traffickers pushing massive amounts of drugs through our communities."The investigation began in March 2026 and involved the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, the Drug Enforcement Administration and the Office of Statewide Prosecution.Authorities identified Ariel Fernandez Alonso as the primary target of the investigation. Through undercover work and other investigative efforts, agents established probable cause to charge 25 individuals and obtained 21 search warrants, which were served over the past several days.As a result of the operation, investigators said they seized:Approximately 45.5 kilograms of cocaine84 grams of fentanylAbout 2.5 pounds of methamphetaminePrescription pills14 pounds of marijuanaFive rifles11 handguns, including one reported stolenOfficials said several of the suspects face charges including conspiracy to commit racketeering, drug trafficking and unlawful use of a two-way communications device. Uthmeier said some defendants face mandatory minimum prison sentences of 15 years if convicted.Investigators found evidence that large quantities of cocaine were being shipped into Florida from California, with some loads arriving weekly before being distributed throughout South Florida."When you've got investigators finding 20, 30, 40 kilos coming in every single week of cocaine, this is not just a small quantity hand-off," Uthmeier said. "This is a large-scale coordinated network that's passing through massive amounts of drugs."Major Lawrence Poston of the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said the arrests demonstrate the impact of coordinated law enforcement efforts."When we all combine our efforts together, we can take dangerous, violent individuals like this off the streets," Poston said.FDLE Special Agent in Charge Michael Stein highlighted the role of Florida's State Assistance for Fentanyl Eradication, or SAFE, program, which provides funding and resources for narcotics investigations.According to Stein, since the program was established in 2023, Florida law enforcement agencies have seized nearly 300 kilograms of fentanyl, more than 400 kilograms of cocaine and more than 200 kilograms of methamphetamine. Authorities have also confiscated more than $6 million in cash and over 1,000 firearms while making more than 3,000 arrests.Representatives from the Health Care District of Palm Beach County said local treatment and recovery programs have helped connect thousands of overdose patients with long-term care and support services.Uthmeier said the investigation remains active and additional charges could be filed as authorities continue to follow leads connected to the trafficking network."Our belief is that we've taken down the hub of the operation here in Florida," Uthmeier said. "We'll continue to follow the breadcrumbs and make additional arrests as needed."

South Florida utility crews and first responders are aiding recovery efforts in Florida's Panhandle following Hurricane Isaias. On Saturday, the Fort Pierce Utilities Authority sent seven crew members and five trucks to the area to help restore power. The crew is working with Choctawhatchee Electric Cooperative, also known as CHELCO, alongside other utility companies from across Florida. They are rebuilding power lines, removing damaged equipment, and installing new transformers and distribution lines. The American Public Power Association said nearly 67,000 CHELCO customers lost power during the storm, affecting about 90% of its system. Fort Pierce Utilities said a statewide mutual-aid agreement allows utilities to quickly send crews to areas where they are most needed. This agreement has also brought outside crews to South Florida following previous hurricanes. "Because of the collaboration and the help provided by the mutual aid agreements, we're able to help each other out. And we couldn't do it on our own. It's too much damage, and it gets our customers back up in a shorter amount of time when there's power loss," said Keith Stephens, director of gas and electric for Fort Pierce Utilities Authority. The Fort Pierce crew is expected to remain in the Panhandle throughout this week or as long as the crew's assistance is required. Florida Power Light has also sent thousands of lineworkers to the Gulf Coast to help restore power. Palm Beach County Fire Rescue and Delray Beach Fire Rescue have deployed crews as well, and they are expected to assist with recovery efforts for the next two weeks.

Lucie family is turning unimaginable loss into hope after choosing organ donation following the death of their 14-year-old son , who was struck by a vehicle while walking to school, according to police. Lucie police said the teen was walking along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near Squirrel Avenue on Oct. 7 when he was struck from behind. He died from his injuries two days later. Now, the family’s decision to donate his organs could help multiple people waiting for lifesaving transplants while creating a lasting legacy in his memory. Organ donation advocates say the family’s choice highlights an ongoing need for registered donors. According to transplant advocates, more than 100,000 people nationwide are currently waiting for an organ transplant, and 15 lives are lost each day while patients remain on waiting lists. The teen’s family chose organ donation in the days following his death, a decision supporters say can have a profound impact on recipients and their families. “It’s a courageous thing for them to do, and I think it’s the right thing,” said St. Lucie County Tax Collector Chris Craft. Craft has worked with Donate Life Florida through the tax collector’s office to encourage organ donor registration and raise awareness about the need for donors. For Tyre Gray, a kidney transplant recipient and the chief administrative and legal officer for South Florida Donor Network, the family’s decision carries special meaning. “Organ donation is one of the few places where grief and gratitude exist in the same place,” Gray told WPTV. Gray said he spent five years waiting for a kidney transplant before receiving the life-saving organ he needed. “I know for a fact that I wouldn’t be here without a family making that election in their deepest moment of despair,” he said. Gray described years of uncertainty while waiting for a match. “That’s five years of uncertainty, five years of being paralyzed, five years of not being able to grow,” he said. Organ donation advocates say the need for donors continues across Florida and the United States. Gray noted that a single donor has the potential to save multiple lives and help many more patients through tissue donation. “One donor is to save upwards of nine lives and to be able to heal another 75 lives,” Gray said. Behind those numbers are people awaiting a second chance, he said. “Let’s all be heroes and save lives,” Gray added. Advocates say organ donation often allows families to find meaning during some of life’s most difficult moments. “I would hope that they could see the lasting impact that a selfless act can make on others,” Craft said. “If you can help somebody else, it’s an amazing thing.” For transplant recipients, organ donation can mean more time with family, additional milestones and opportunities. In the midst of tragedy, one Port St. Lucie family’s decision could now help save lives and ensure their son’s legacy continues through the people he may help. Lynora's Italian restaurant, a South Florida staple that started as an 800-square-foot pizzeria in Lake Worth in 1976, is marking 50 years in business — and the family behind it is planning to grow beyond Palm Beach County.Angelo Abbenante, son of founders Raffaele and Maria Abbenante, now leads the restaurant brand, which currently has 6 locations spanning Palm Beach County from Jupiter to Boca Raton."From a little hole in the wall in Lake Worth to now we've gotten to the point where we have six locations we have about five more in the pipeline," he said.The expansion will reach beyond Palm Beach County, with Melbourne set to be next."Our next location is going to be Melbourne, Florida and then from there we're going to hit Fort Lauderdale, and then we have Wellington, Royal Palm Beach coming and then Delray," Abbenante said.The Lynora's story begins with Abbenante's parents, who emigrated from Italy and chose South Florida after his mother found the cold weather in New York unbearable."They came to Italy first and stopped in New York and my mom didn't like the cold weather so she decided to go back to Italy or move to a warmer area, so they had the opportunity to come to South Florida and they landed in Lake Worth," he said.Growing up in the family business meant no traditional weekends off."We didn't have the luxury of the typical American weekends off, this was 7 days a week, 24 hours a day, it was really just putting their feet in the ground. Working 7 days a week and really trying to build a great life for the family," Abbenante said.He worked his way through every job in the restaurant."Dishwashing, washing tables, bartending, making pizzas, working with my mom in the line, just doing whatever had to be done," Abbenante said.I reviewed an original menu, a reminder of how it all began. A large pizza was priced at $3.65 to $4.70. Many of those early dishes are still on the menu today."Yeah, we have all the same dishes from our hoagies where we use the same bread to our eggplant parmesan to our chicken and veal parmesan," Abbenante said.Reflecting on 50 years, Abbenante said family unity and commitment to quality are what have set Lynora's apart."We didn't go out on weekends you know me and my brother it was like we were working and helping mom and helping Dad and when you get to that point you think about the business a little differently - we are really united and I think that is what has made Lynora's so special for the last 50 years. Is when you walk into these restaurants…you get that energy and you get that homemade food. And everything is made with love so it's been a great run and we're looking forward to the next 50 years," Abbenante said.The recipes have remained true to their origins, with bread, pasta, and sauces still made in-house."It really brings us back to how it all started right and the food has been the same, we still make our own bread we still make our own pasta and all the dishes we have created have really been from our mom the sauces," Abbenante said.Among Lynora's most distinctive preparations is its signature sauce."One of the things that is really true to us is how our sauces are made our sauces still take 8 hours to make," Abbenante said.The restaurant's famous meatballs carry the same recipes as when Lynora's first opened."These are actually the same recipes that my mom started 50 years ago, you can kind of see our sauce is a little different than most restaurants... our flavors are basically built into the sauce and our meatballs you know they really speak for themselves," Abbenante said.Quality and consistency, Abbenante says, are the foundation of the restaurant's longevity."It's about making sure that we have the quality ingredients, highest quality, and when you make the food - you have to make sure it's done consistent year in and year out, day in and day out, and when you do that, that's the secret sauce," Abbenante said.Each Lynora's location is designed to reflect the personality of its community."So, when you're Jupiter you get that little feel of Jupiter and when you're in Boca you get that feel of Boca," Abbenante said.Lynora's pizza is made in a wood-burning oven using a hybrid style that blends New York and classic Italian techniques."So we do a mixture of New York style and classic Napoletano pizza and so it's a hybrid and the reason we do that is, because of our oven - our oven is not a gas oven it's a wood burning oven," Abbenante said. "We cook our pizzas typically between 700 to 800 degrees."During a demonstration, Abbenante chose his personal favorite to make."So, we're going to make my favorite which is a classic it's Margherita," he said.Community support, Abbenante says, has been a key ingredient in the restaurant's success."Without the community giving us the support we have we wouldn't be where we're at," he said.As Lynora's enters its next chapter, Abbenante says what it takes has never changed."At the end of the day it's a lot of work a lot of sacrifice it's all the little things it's very meticulous and you have to love it.
