For many working families in Palm Beach County, having a job is no longer enough to guarantee they can afford a place to live.That was the message from faith leaders and community members with People Engaged in Active Community Efforts (PEACE), who gathered Monday at St. Ann Catholic Church to call attention to the county’s housing affordability crisis and urge local leaders to take action.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:“We are gathered today because across our congregations and our community, we continue to hear the same concern,” said the Rev. Latifah Griffin, a PEACE board of trustees member. “People who are working here are struggling to live here.”PEACE is a coalition of 31 congregations across Palm Beach County. Members say conversations within their congregations reveal a growing number of residents struggling with rising rents, stagnant wages and the possibility of being priced out of the communities where they work and raise their families.Palm Beach County data underscores those concerns. According to the county’s January 2025 affordable housing report, the average rent for a two-bedroom apartment increased from $1,899 in 2021 to $2,833 in 2024 — a 49.2% increase in three years. The cost of buying a home has also risen. The county report found the median price of a single-family home climbed from $425,000 in late 2020 to $600,000 in late 2024, an increase of 41.2%. Nationally, Redfin reported in August 2026 that households needed an annual income of nearly $110,000 to afford a typical U.S. For residents working in service and other modest-wage jobs, those costs can make independent living difficult even when they work consistently.Harry Wolin shared his family's experience at Monday’s gathering. He said he and his wife, who are retired and living on a fixed income, help support their adult daughter, a waitress who lives in Lake Worth.Woolen said his daughter has worked in the restaurant industry for more than 20 years, but her income is not enough to afford housing without help from her parents.“She’s doing everything that we’ve told people they’re supposed to do: get a job, work hard, help support your family,” Wolin said. “And it just doesn’t work given the price of housing.”He said he worries about workers in similar circumstances who do not have relatives able to help them financially.“What do they do if they don’t have a family who can help them?” Wolin asked.Wolin said his family is willing to make sacrifices to ensure his daughter has a safe place to live, but he worries about what will happen when he and his wife are no longer able to provide that support.Mamie Kisner, who represents Tabernacle Missionary Baptist Church, said the experiences Wolin described reflect what PEACE members hear from families across the county.She said residents have reported increasing rents, adult children unable to afford homes of their own and families doubling up in crowded living conditions. Some workers are moving farther away in search of more affordable housing, she said, while businesses struggle to retain employees who cannot afford to live nearby.“These aren’t just numbers; these are people that we know and love,” Kisner said. Faith leaders urged elected officials to listen to residents experiencing housing insecurity and consider solutions that help working people remain in Palm Beach County.PEACE members said raising awareness is only one part of their effort. The organization is also encouraging residents to hear directly from county commission candidates about their understanding of the housing crisis and the steps they would take to address it.The group announced a community kickoff and Palm Beach County Commission candidate forum focused on affordable housing.The event is scheduled for Monday, Oct. Juliana Catholic Church.For PEACE members, the issue comes down to whether people who contribute to the county every day can afford to remain part of the communities they help sustain.

A recent change to a flight out of Vero Beach is sparking a bigger conversation about travel options on the Treasure Coast. Travelers tell WFLX that limited flight schedules and a lack of convenient transportation alternatives can make getting in and out of the area difficult, sometimes forcing them to drive to larger airports or rearrange their plans. At the Vero Beach Regional Airport, travelers shared their frustrations with WFLX reporter Brooke Chau about the challenges of getting where they need to go. “In the Treasure Coast area, Vero Beach specifically, it is difficult to get around,” said Peter Masella. He pointed to the lack of a Brightline station in Vero Beach, saying people often have to travel to other cities to access additional transportation options. A recent schedule change to Breeze Airways’ route between the New York area and Vero Beach has added to those concerns. The flight, which previously departed from Westchester, New York in the evening, now leaves in the morning. A New York City physician told WFLX the change has affected his work schedule. “I’m a physician working in New York City, and because of the change of flight for Vero Beach, I have had to rearrange my patients’ schedules two days in a row,” he said. Another traveler from Westchester, New York said the change can mean a longer trip. “Then I have to take a taxi all the way down and around to Vero Beach. It’s very inconvenient,” she said. However, Breeze Airways has also been adding destinations from Vero Beach. Last month, the airline introduced nonstop service to Trenton, Baltimore, Pittsburgh and Atlantic City, expanding the airport’s commercial flight options. Vero Beach Airport Director Brandon Dambeck says airlines regularly evaluate the performance of their routes, which can lead to new destinations as well as schedule or route changes. “All of these airlines are monitoring the routes and their gauge of success,” Dambeck said. For travelers, more destinations are welcome, but they say flight times that fit their schedules are just as important.

A legal battle has erupted in Martin County as the developer behind a massive data center project files a sprawling lawsuit against the Village of Indiantown, its village council, planning board, and local residents. Silver Fox 606 LLC filed the complaint and verified petition for a writ of prohibition, claiming local officials are illegally derailing its $25 million project. Silver Fox purchased the over 600-acre property at 13820 SW Silver Fox Lane in 2025 following zoning verifications confirming that computer and data processing facilities were permitted as an as-of-right use in Heavy Industrial districts. Following the 2026 municipal elections, a newly sworn-in village council attempted to stall or ban data center developments despite what the lawsuit alleges were prior municipal marketing efforts that actively recruited similar tech infrastructure. See also: ICU nurse accused of taking fentanyl from critically ill patient at PSL hospital Indiantown's Community and Economic Development Director administratively approved the Silver Fox plat on September 17. The lawsuit highlights a turbulent political climate, pointing to a September 1 emergency council meeting where the village manager and long-serving village attorney were ousted. Shortly after, an administrative appeal was filed by a local resident seeking to overturn the director's approvals. Silver Fox's legal team argues that the planning, zoning, and appeals board lacks the legal jurisdiction to review the plat approval, citing state statutes rendering recorded plats unassailable without landowner consent. Furthermore, the suit alleges that the Village Council violated Florida's Sunshine Law during the abrupt personnel changes. The developer is seeking emergency injunctive relief, a preliminary injunction halting any stop-work orders or retroactive reviews, and declaratory judgments affirming its vested development rights.

The county received the application Monday, one day before commissioners considered the moratorium.Because the application was submitted before the proposed moratorium, it would not be affected by the measure.The proposal comes amid concerns from residents about the future of data center development in Martin County.WPTV is continuing to hear from residents about those concerns as commissioners consider what restrictions, if any, should be placed on future data center development.Stay with WPTV.com and WPTV News for updates on this development story.

Martin County commissioners are moving forward with a proposed one-year moratorium on large-scale data centers, giving the county more time to study their potential impact before allowing new projects to move forward. The Board of County Commissioners unanimously approved the proposal on its first reading Tuesday, Oct. A second public hearing is scheduled for Oct. 27 before the moratorium can receive final approval. The proposed ordinance would temporarily stop the county from accepting new applications for large-scale data centers in unincorporated areas of Martin County. It would not apply to municipalities. Under the proposal, large-scale data centers are defined as facilities with an anticipated peak electrical demand of 50 megawatts or more. County officials say the pause would give them time to study concerns surrounding data centers, including noise, water usage, electricity consumption, wastewater disposal and potential environmental impacts. During Tuesday's meeting, officials also revealed that the county received an application for a data center on Monday, just one day before the hearing. See also: Florida drug trafficking bust leads to 19 arrests, 6 more suspects sought Applications deemed complete before the moratorium takes effect would be allowed to move forward under existing regulations. Commissioner Sarah Heard questioned whether 365 days would be enough time for the county to complete the necessary research. She also asked whether the moratorium could apply to smaller facilities using 20 megawatts or more of electricity. County staff explained that the 50-megawatt threshold comes from state law defining large-scale data centers. Commissioner Edward Campi said the county needs to hear from experts on both sides of the issue before making long-term decisions. Campi referenced a recent visit to Virginia, where he toured an area with approximately 120 data centers and observed their appearance and noise levels. He said the proposed moratorium would provide an opportunity for supporters and opponents to share their perspectives. Blake Capps also supported the proposal, saying the county needs to carefully consider where data centers could be located, including areas within its urban services boundaries. Commissioner Heatherington was absent from Tuesday's meeting. The county first directed its attorney to draft the moratorium in August as concerns grew over the potential impact of large-scale data centers. The proposal will return to commissioners for a second public hearing on Tuesday, Oct. If approved, the moratorium would give Martin County up to a year to review its regulations before accepting new applications for large-scale data centers.

A Florida prisoner who claimed he killed his cellmate so he could be moved to death row is set to be executed Tuesday, nearly 18 years after the fatal attack.James Robertson, 63, pleaded guilty to first-degree murder and waived all appeals in the 2008 strangling of Frank Hart. Robertson is set to receive a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke starting at noon.Robertson was supposed to be one of two executions carried out by Florida on Tuesday, but Gov. Ron DeSantis withdrew a death warrant last week for William Lee Thompson. The Republican governor did not provide a reason for withdrawing Thompson’s death warrant but had temporarily stayed his execution last month pending a psychiatric evaluation.Records show that this is the first time DeSantis has withdrawn a death warrant, which does not technically change Thompson’s sentence. He will remain on death row, and a new death warrant could be signed for him in the future.Robertson's execution comes at a time of escalating attention on the death penalty in the U.S. In Tennessee, Christa Pike survived an execution attempt two weeks ago despite receiving two lethal doses of pentobarbital. And last week, the Pentagon announced that the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan would be livestreamed.According to court records, Robertson was incarcerated at Charlotte Correctional Institution, north of Fort Myers, in December 2008 when he tied several socks together and strangled Hart while the other man slept. Robertson told investigators that the attack was unprovoked and that he killed his cellmate so that he would be sentenced to death, rather than having to live out his days in prison.Robertson was 17 years old when he went to prison in 1980 for burglary and assault. Years of convictions for escape, battery and weapons while in prison kept adding time to his total sentence. Hart was sent to prison in 2003 following a sexual battery conviction.Robertson pleaded guilty and waived a penalty phase, where a jury would recommend the death penalty or life in prison. A judge sentenced Robertson to death, and he later waived all post-conviction proceedings. Robertson reiterated his position during a hearing earlier this month, telling a judge that he understood his execution had been scheduled and that he didn't want to make any final appeals to the Florida Supreme Court or U.S. Supreme Court.While proponents of the death penalty have long claimed that it is a deterrent, Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty released a statement saying that this case demonstrates the opposite."Frank Hart deserved to be safe in state custody, and his loved ones deserve our compassion," the group's legal and policy director, Maria DeLiberato, said in the statement. "When someone commits murder to try to secure his own execution, we have to confront the conditions that contributed to that decision and the reality that the existence of the death penalty may have caused the very violence it purportedly prevents."Meanwhile, DeSantis is the third Florida governor to sign a death warrant for Thompson. Bob Graham and Bob Martinez both scheduled executions for Thompson in the 1980s, but years of appeals and stays allowed him to avoid the electric chair, the state's method of execution at the time. The 74-year-old death row inmate was convicted of first-degree murder, kidnapping and sexual battery in the 1976 killing of 23-year-old Sally Ivester.Thompson will remain on Florida’s death row, and a new death warrant could be signed for him in the future. His attorneys have said he suffers from dementia, and his health is failing. They said he should be relocated to an adequate medical facility to get the care he needs.Only one other Florida inmate remains alive following a death warrant signed by DeSantis. James Dailey, 80, was scheduled to die in late 2019 for the murder of a 14-year-old girl, but a federal judge halted the execution as attorneys argued against his guilt. The stay was eventually lifted, but DeSantis didn't sign a new death warrant. The state halted all executions during the COVID-19 pandemic and didn't restart until 2023.DeSantis, who leaves office in January, oversaw 19 executions in 2025, more than any other Florida governor in a single year since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Robertson would be the state's 17th execution of 2026, with two more already scheduled, not counting Thompson.William Reaves, 77, is scheduled to be executed on Oct. 20, followed by Jesse Guardado, 64, on Nov. Reaves was convicted of fatally shooting a deputy after dropping a gun in front of the law enforcement officer in 1986. Guardado was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.If Robertson, Reaves and Guardado are all executed as planned, that would match the state's 2025 total, with eight weeks remaining in 2026.DeSantis has made few public comments about the unprecedented number of executions but explained previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out."I felt I owed it to them to make sure this ran very smoothly. If I honestly thought someone was innocent, I would not pull the trigger," the governor said last year.A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 30 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.

There have been moments during the first five games of the season when Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis has shown the arm talent and athleticism that made new GM Jon-Eric Sullivan and coach Jeff Hafley bring him over from Green Bay to usher in a new era in Miami.There have also been challenges — such as issues with accuracy and decision-making that were evident in Sunday's 31-24 loss to Cincinnati. Willis began the game 0-for-4 and didn’t complete a pass until the second quarter, finishing 15 of 27 for 137 yards and a touchdown passing and rushing. He threw two interceptions. And he lost a fumble for the third game in a row.Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley said he's not considering any quarterback changes, but stressed the need for improvement from Willis and the Dolphins' passing game.Hafley also cautioned against placing the sole blame on Willis, who started just the 11th game of his career and is leading a young offense with mostly inexperienced receivers who are still developing chemistry."We need to be better. Malik needs to be better, OK?" Hafley said. The headline is we all need to be better, and I mean that."Willis has completed just 56.2% of his passes this season and has more interceptions (four) than passing touchdowns (two). He appeared unsettled to begin Sunday's game, missing open receivers on a couple of instances and throwing picks to Bengals safety Jordan Battle on back-to-back drives in the second quarter.Still, Willis has shown his ability to elevate Miami's rushing attack with his legs. His 74 yards rushing on Sunday were the most ever by a Dolphins quarterback in a single game. He had a 39-yard run in the fourth that was the longest rush by a quarterback this season, and the longest by a Dolphins QB since Ryan Tannehill had a 40-yard scamper during a game in 2014."So there’s times it’s great,” Hafley said. "And then there’s times when it needs to be better. It needs to be better from him, we need to get the right route run at the right depth. It needs to be better for sure, but there are signs of it. There was flashes yesterday in that game."Willis said he was encouraged by Miami's ability to pull within a touchdown late but added at some point, the young Dolphins will need the results to match their effort."It is too much and too hard to keep saying, ‘We’re just young’ or ‘We’re trying to build this and build that,’” Willis said. "At the same time, we've got to hold each other accountable because we can’t keep doing this to ourselves. If we’re going to be in games versus good teams, we've got to be able to take advantage of it and go and win those games, because there’s no point to be in the game if you can’t go and win it."The Dolphins have stuck with their run-first identity despite losing star running back De'Von Achane for the season a couple of weeks ago. Third-year running back Ollie Gordon has led a solid rushing attack the past two games, and Miami's run blocking has improved.The Dolphins' pass rush was not able to replicate the success it had when it had four sacks against Kyler Murray in Week 4. Miami didn't generate much pressure against Joe Burrow, failing to get a sack in a game for the fourth time this season.Gordon. One week after rushing for a career-high 100 yards against Minnesota, he had 18 carries for 88 yards against Cincinnati, including a 22-yard rush and a 1-yard rushing touchdown. He has three TDs in his past three games, matching his total from last season.Special teams. Chris Tabor's unit has had a rough start to the season and began Sunday's game by giving up an 81-yard kickoff return. Jaylen Wright also fumbled a kick return — before recovering it — and kicker Riley Patterson missed an extra point and had a kickoff fall short of the landing zone.RG Jonah Savaiinaea injured his ankle in the second quarter Sunday, and cornerback JuJu Brents left with a stinger.68.4% — Willis' passer rating through the first five games, which is the worst among the 20 quarterbacks who have started all five of their teams' games this season.The Dolphins have a bye during Week 6, which Hafley said the team will use to get healthy and evaluate the performance of both players and coaches.

The Miami Dolphins are not treating their bye week as a throwaway. The team hit the practice field Tuesday at Baptist Health Training Complex in Miami Gardens to regroup after an 0-5 start to the season.After the break, the Dolphins will head north to take on divisional rival New York Jets (2-3) on Oct. Players say the focus right now is on health and coming back locked in.Running back Ollie Gordon III said the team is using the time to get right and come together."Everybody is getting their legs back and everybody getting everything back together and everybody getting 100 percent and us getting out there and getting healthy while we get back and work together,"Gordon said.Offensive lineman Kadyn Proctor said the message from the coaching staff has been clear about what the team needs heading out of the bye."We have to have that fire in us. A recent change to a flight out of Vero Beach is sparking a bigger conversation about travel options on the Treasure Coast.Travelers tell WPTV that limited flight schedules and a lack of convenient transportation alternatives can make getting in and out of the area difficult, sometimes forcing them to drive to larger airports or rearrange their plans.WATCH: At the Vero Beach Regional Airport, travelers shared their frustrations with WPTV reporter Brooke Chau about the challenges of getting where they need to go."In the Treasure Coast area, Vero Beach specifically, it is difficult to get around," said Peter Masella. He pointed to the lack of a Brightline station in Vero Beach, saying people often have to travel to other cities to access additional transportation options.A recent schedule change to Breeze Airways' route between the New York area and Vero Beach has added to those concerns. The flight, which previously departed from Westchester, New York in the evening, now leaves in the morning.A New York City physician told WPTV the change has affected his work schedule."I'm a physician working in New York City, and because of the change of flight for Vero Beach, I have had to rearrange my patients' schedules two days in a row,” he said.Another traveler from Westchester, New York said the change can mean a longer trip."Then I have to take a taxi all the way down and around to Vero Beach. It’s very inconvenient," she said.However, Breeze Airways has also been adding destinations from Vero Beach. Last month, the airline introduced nonstop service to Trenton, Baltimore, Pittsburgh and Atlantic City, expanding the airport's commercial flight options.Vero Beach Airport Director Brandon Dambeck says airlines regularly evaluate the performance of their routes, which can lead to new destinations as well as schedule or route changes.“All of these airlines are monitoring the routes and their gauge of success," Dambeck said. For travelers, more destinations are welcome, but they say flight times that fit their schedules are just as important.

Lucie family is turning unimaginable loss into hope after choosing organ donation following the death of their 14-year-old son, who was struck by a vehicle while walking to school, according to police.Port St. Lucie police said the teen was walking along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near Squirrel Avenue on Oct. 7 when he was struck from behind. He died from his injuries two days later.WATCH: Port St. Lucie Teen's Legacy Lives On Through DonationNow, the family's decision to donate his organs could help multiple people waiting for lifesaving transplants while creating a lasting legacy in his memory.Organ donation advocates say the family's choice highlights an ongoing need for registered donors. According to transplant advocates, more than 100,000 people nationwide are currently waiting for an organ transplant, and 15 lives are lost each day while patients remain on waiting lists.The teen's family chose organ donation in the days following his death, a decision supporters say can have a profound impact on recipients and their families."It's a courageous thing for them to do, and I think it's the right thing," said St. Lucie County Tax Collector Chris Craft.Craft has worked with Donate Life Florida through the tax collector's office to encourage organ donor registration and raise awareness about the need for donors.For Tyre Gray, a kidney transplant recipient and the chief administrative and legal officer for South Florida Donor Network, the family's decision carries special meaning."Organ donation is one of the few places where grief and gratitude exist in the same place," Gray told WPTV.Gray said he spent five years waiting for a kidney transplant before receiving the life-saving organ he needed."I know for a fact that I wouldn't be here without a family making that election in their deepest moment of despair," he said.Gray described years of uncertainty while waiting for a match."That's five years of uncertainty, five years of being paralyzed, five years of not being able to grow," he said.Organ donation advocates say the need for donors continues across Florida and the United States.Gray noted that a single donor has the potential to save multiple lives and help many more patients through tissue donation."One donor is to save upwards of nine lives and to be able to heal another 75 lives," Gray said.Behind those numbers are people awaiting a second chance, he said."Let's all be heroes and save lives," Gray added.Advocates say organ donation often allows families to find meaning during some of life's most difficult moments."I would hope that they could see the lasting impact that a selfless act can make on others," Craft said. "If you can help somebody else, it's an amazing thing."For transplant recipients, organ donation can mean more time with family, additional milestones and opportunities.In the midst of tragedy, one Port St. Lucie family's decision could now help save lives and ensure their son's legacy continues through the people he may help.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Lucie City Council approved three major site plans for projects along the Southern Grove, a developing jobs corridor in the city.One of those plans: the long-awaited Costco retail store.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie City Council approves site plan for Costco"This is something that we have been looking forward to for a long time,” Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said.Samples and Wes McCurry, president and CEO of the St. Lucie County Economic Development Council, said the 163,000-square-foot store is just the beginning for a new phase of growth in western Port St. Lucie."This is getting closer to the finish line," Samples said.The Costco will join other companies like Amazon, Tamco and Cheney Brothers, calling the Southern Grove area home.McCurry said since the jobs are now here, new commercial development will follow."They see all the development that's occurring here, along with the demographics that they like to see,” said McCurry. "It only makes sense that Costco opens a retail store here."City council approved two other major site plans for the area, including a 5.5-acre site making up the first phase of the Tradition Entertainment District set to bring restaurants and retail."This area has historically been largely underserved by restaurants and retail, and especially entertainment facilities,” McCurry said. "It's kind of catching up to the rooftops that are happening. You know, rooftops always drive that demand, but there's more to come."The other plan is space for an acute care rehabilitation hospital, featuring inpatient and outpatient services with 42 beds in a more than 55,000-square-foot building."A growing area needs services, and that's just another component of services that are coming into the area is expanded healthcare access," McCurry said.McCurry said the plans for retail, healthcare and entertainment are fulfilling the city’s master plan for what Southern Grove was destined to become."The plan is coming together. The vision is coming together. What everyone saw 20 years ago is now starting to happen," McCurry said.Samples said Costco still must close on the land, move on to construction design planning and permitting before any shovels hit the ground.

Some residents in Boca Raton's Spanish Village neighborhood say new construction is changing their community's character, and they're seeking answers after a decades-old oak tree was cut down at a development site.Neighbors reached out to WPTV Boca Raton reporter Victor Jorges with concerns about the growing number of new homes being built in the area. They say the large, modern houses don't reflect the Spanish-style architecture and older homes that have long defined the neighborhood.WATCH BELOW: Neighbors raise concerns over development, removal of decades-old treeFor some residents, the changes have left them feeling stuck. They say the offers they're receiving from developers for their properties aren’t enough to afford another home elsewhere.The recent removal of a large oak tree is what prompted neighbors to speak out."A friend of mine planted it. Probably 25, 30 years ago; and it was a big, beautiful oak tree," said Jan Bassett, who lives next door to the construction site. "In the beginning they said they weren't gonna tear it down. And all of a sudden they came in last week and cut it down."Karolina Michniewicz, another Boca Raton resident, contacted WPTV expressing frustration with the development taking place in her neighborhood."Our beautiful neighborhood is getting pummeled by a developer called Alpha Premium Development," Michniewicz wrote in an email.She criticized the design of the new homes and said neighbors were particularly upset about the loss of mature trees."We are furious as neighbors, and we don't know how to stop it," she wrote.Getting answers from the developerJorges reached out to Alpha Premium Development to find out why the tree was removed despite neighbors saying they were initially told it would be preserved.Jared Niles, a real estate broker for Alpha Premium Development, responded on behalf of the company, clarifying that he is not the builder and does not directly oversee construction operations.Niles said preserving the tree had been part of the original construction plan."From the outset, every effort was made to preserve the existing tree. It was specifically tagged and retained during demolition, and the home's shell was intentionally built around it," Niles said.However, he said crews later discovered termites and several major branches with structural damage.According to Niles, the company was advised that the termite infestation could not be treated and posed a potential risk to nearby homes.He said Alpha Premium Development intends to fully landscape the property once construction is complete and strives to preserve existing landscaping whenever possible.If you have a similar story, or any story you'd like to share in Boca Raton, reach out to Victor via email: victor.jorges@wptv.com

During the COVID-19 pandemic, the program shifted from dine-in meals to a grab-and-go format, which continues today.WPTV reporter Christy Waite connected with neighbors like Agatha Bythwood and her daughter. She says the meals provide help before the school day begins."It's very helpful," Bythwood said. "It's great that they do all of this and feed the kids before they go off to school."Miller said the ministry is about more than serving food. The church also wants to provide a welcoming place for people who may be struggling."Trinity United Methodist doors are wide open as a welcoming refuge for seniors navigating isolation and students carrying quiet morning burdens," Miller said."You will feel seen, welcomed, valued by the community and our church," Miller said.

Organizers say the event continues to grow as it enters its 17th year.In a region with a large Hispanic population, organizers say the festival provides an opportunity for students and community members to engage with artists and musicians while learning more about the diversity of Hispanic cultures.The festival began Thursday with an art exhibition featuring artists representing more than 10 countries.Visitors viewed a wide range of artistic styles and mediums, including oil paintings, photography and metalwork.Among the featured artists was Franco Sotillo, a visual artist originally from Lima, Peru, who said his work combines mixed media and reflects both his heritage and personal experiences."I'm a visual artist and came from Lima, Peru," Sotillo said. "I moved to this country 12 years ago."Sotillo said his work incorporates materials including oils, paper and other raw elements. He said sharing his art allows him to introduce audiences to Peruvian artistic expression."I'm an immigrant, but also bringing my culture to the states to show people how Peruvian art is expressed," Sotillo said.Festival Director Michael O'Connor said the event continues to evolve each year."We're expanding every year," O'Connor said.O'Connor said this year's festival marked the first time organizers expanded programming beyond art and classical music to also include popular music from Hispanic cultures."What we want to do is we want to celebrate the Hispanic artistic heritage, because here in South Florida, especially, we have a very, very large Hispanic population," O'Connor said.Organizers said they hope attendees leave with a deeper appreciation for Hispanic artistic traditions and the people behind them."We hope they'll be inspired too to see the artworks here at the exhibition and to see how the Hispanic world makes itself known through visual arts," O'Connor said. "Not just the art is Hispanic, but also the artists are Hispanic."The festival concluded Saturday with performances featuring both classical and popular Hispanic music.Organizers say they hope the festival continues for many years to come as it celebrates the art, music and cultural heritage that help shape South Florida's diverse communities.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. At a Let’s Hear It event in Okeechobee last month,, WPTV anchor and Navy veteran Mike Trim spoke with a local veteran dedicated to serving fellow vets.Gregg Maynard, an Army veteran and founder of the nonprofit Thank You For Your Service, helps disabled veterans through projects such as building wheelchair ramps and providing other assistance.WATCH:Now, Maynard is working to bring the Traveling Vietnam Memorial Wall to Okeechobee. He hopes the display will give local Vietnam veterans, especially those unable to travel to Washington, D.C., the opportunity to experience the memorial and reflect on their service.“Not only does it help those veterans who may never make the trip to D.C., but I think these stories and what these guys went through can also be an educational experience for kids,” Maynard told Trim. “It gives them a chance to learn.”Maynard said it costs thousands of dollars to bring the wall to the area and is raising funds through his nonprofit. Those interested in supporting the effort can contact him at thankyouforyourservice34972@gmail.com .Ultimately, Maynard hopes the memorial will have a meaningful impact on the local Vietnam veteran community.“I want them to feel appreciated,” Maynard said. “But most importantly, if it helps just one Vietnam veteran, then all the work and effort that goes into making this happen will be worth it.”

A recent change to a flight out of Vero Beach is sparking a bigger conversation about travel options on the Treasure Coast.Travelers tell WPTV limited flight schedules and a lack of convenient transportation alternatives can make getting in and out of the area difficult, sometimes forcing them to drive to larger airports or rearrange their plans.WATCH: At the Vero Beach Regional Airport, travelers shared their frustrations with WPTV reporter Brooke Chau about the challenges of getting where they need to go.“In the Treasure Coast area, Vero Beach specifically, it is difficult to get around,” said Peter Masella. He pointed to the lack of a Brightline station in Vero Beach, saying people often have to travel to other cities to access additional transportation options.A recent schedule change to Breeze Airways' route between the New York area and Vero Beach has added to those concerns. The flight, which previously departed from Westchester, New York in the evening, now leaves in the morning.A New York City physician told WPTV the change has affected his work schedule.“I’m a physician working in New York City and because of the change of flight for Vero Beach, I have had to rearrange my patients schedule two days in a row,” he said.Another traveler from Westchester, New York said the change can mean a longer trip.“Then I have to take a taxi all the way down and around to Vero Beach. It’s very inconvenient,” she said.However, Breeze Airways has also been adding destinations from Vero Beach. Last month, the airline introduced nonstop service to Trenton, Baltimore, Pittsburgh and Atlantic City, expanding the airport's commercial flight options.Vero Beach Airport Director, Brandon Dambeck, says airlines regularly evaluate the performance of their routes, which can lead to new destinations as well as schedule or route changes.“All of these airlines are monitoring the routes and their gauge of success," Dambeck said. For travelers, more destinations are welcome, but they say flight times that fit their schedules are just as important.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Tuesday that 25 people have been charged in connection with what authorities describe as a large-scale drug trafficking organization responsible for distributing cocaine, fentanyl and methamphetamine across multiple Florida counties.According to investigators, 19 suspects are already in custody and six remain outstanding following a months-long investigation dubbed Operation Ice Breaker.Officials said the investigation targeted a drug trafficking network operating mainly in Palm Beach, Broward and St. Lucie counties, as well as communities in Miami-Dade and Florida's west coast."These was not a users. These were wholesalers," Uthmeier said during a news conference in Boynton Beach "These were large-scale traffickers pushing massive amounts of drugs through our communities."The investigation began in March 2026 and involved the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, the Drug Enforcement Administration and the Office of Statewide Prosecution.Authorities identified Ariel Fernandez Alonso as the primary target of the investigation. Through undercover work and other investigative efforts, agents established probable cause to charge 25 individuals and obtained 21 search warrants, which were served over the past several days.As a result of the operation, investigators said they seized:Approximately 45.5 kilograms of cocaine84 grams of fentanylAbout 2.5 pounds of methamphetaminePrescription pills14 pounds of marijuanaFive rifles11 handguns, including one reported stolenOfficials said several of the suspects face charges including conspiracy to commit racketeering, drug trafficking and unlawful use of a two-way communications device. Uthmeier said some defendants face mandatory minimum prison sentences of 15 years if convicted.Investigators found evidence that large quantities of cocaine were being shipped into Florida from California, with some loads arriving weekly before being distributed throughout South Florida."When you've got investigators finding 20, 30, 40 kilos coming in every single week of cocaine, this is not just a small quantity hand-off," Uthmeier said. "This is a large-scale coordinated network that's passing through massive amounts of drugs."Major Lawrence Poston of the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said the arrests demonstrate the impact of coordinated law enforcement efforts."When we all combine our efforts together, we can take dangerous, violent individuals like this off the streets," Poston said.FDLE Special Agent in Charge Michael Stein highlighted the role of Florida's State Assistance for Fentanyl Eradication, or SAFE, program, which provides funding and resources for narcotics investigations.According to Stein, since the program was established in 2023, Florida law enforcement agencies have seized nearly 300 kilograms of fentanyl, more than 400 kilograms of cocaine and more than 200 kilograms of methamphetamine. Authorities have also confiscated more than $6 million in cash and over 1,000 firearms while making more than 3,000 arrests.Representatives from the Health Care District of Palm Beach County said local treatment and recovery programs have helped connect thousands of overdose patients with long-term care and support services.Uthmeier said the investigation remains active and additional charges could be filed as authorities continue to follow leads connected to the trafficking network."Our belief is that we've taken down the hub of the operation here in Florida," Uthmeier said. "We'll continue to follow the breadcrumbs and make additional arrests as needed."

A former surgeon turned Wall Street analyst is taking on his city, its mayor and surveillance technology company Flock Safety in federal court. He has no lawyer and wants the city's license plate cameras gone for good. Steven Greer filed the lawsuit in August against Port St. Lucie, Mayor Shannon Martin and Flock Safety, arguing the technology police use to track criminals also threatens Americans' constitutional rights from privacy to gun ownership. "I was appalled at what I learned," Greer told the CBS12 News I-Team. Greer said he spent much of August researching Flock's technology and preparing the federal lawsuit himself. While he has no formal legal training, he says his years working as a surgeon and later on Wall Street prepared him for the technical research and writing involved in representing himself. Flock's automated license plate readers photograph passing vehicles, recording identifying information along with the time and location. Police can search those records to help identify vehicles connected to crimes, but Greer argues the technology also allows officers to reconstruct someone's movements without obtaining a warrant. His amended complaint alleges Port St. Lucie operated 53 Flock cameras and another 73 Axon license plate readers, for a combined network of 126 devices. See also: Brevard County sheriff’s agent killed in wrong-way crash while responding to shooting Greer argues the collection and sharing of that information violates the Fourth Amendment, which protects against unreasonable searches and seizures. The CBS12 News I-Team has been reporting on Flock cameras since last year, examining how the technology is used by law enforcement and more recently, allegations of misuse. In Fort Pierce, Officer Josepher Crutchfield was arrested after investigators accused him of searching his ex-girlfriend's vehicle 382 times. In another case, a woman was arrested and jailed after investigators mistakenly linked her vehicle to a deadly hit-and-run crash. The charges against her were later dropped. Greer cites both cases in his complaint, but argues the larger problem is the surveillance system itself. During their interview, CBS12 I-Team reporter Katie Bente asked Greer about people who aren't concerned about surveillance because they have nothing to hide. "A lot of people say, you know, 'I'm not doing anything wrong. So what does it really matter?'" Bente asked. "Those are the people who don't deserve freedoms. It's just sheer ignorance. They don't even understand why we have a Fourth Amendment," Greer responded. Law enforcement agencies, however, defend license plate readers as valuable investigative tools, crediting the technology with helping identify suspects, recover stolen vehicles and solve crimes. "I know that police have always argued these Flock cameras really help solve crimes. What would be your response to that?" Bente asked. "That's their number one defense. It's not true," Greer said. His assertion is disputed by law enforcement agencies that have documented cases in which license plate reader information helped investigators. Whether the technology is useful in solving crimes is a separate question from whether particular searches are constitutional. Greer's lawsuit also raises an argument not typically associated with traffic cameras: the right to bear arms. He points to Flock cameras reportedly installed at the entrance to the Ocala Shooting Range, a public gun range in Marion County. Greer argues that recording who visits a shooting range could discourage people from exercising their Second Amendment rights. "When I saw that case where they have Flock cameras in gun ranges, I said, 'Whoa, that's a Second Amendment violation,'" Greer told the I-Team. The key buzzword is chilling. You know, if they scare you away from using your gun rights that's a violation." The complaint also challenges the city's handling of public records requests, alleging officials withheld information about camera locations and system audit logs. It includes claims under Florida's constitutional privacy protections and questions the legality of public spending on the network. Greer has also raised First Amendment concerns following a Sept. Lucie City Council meeting. He told the I-Team that the number of police officers present made him feel intimidated and could discourage residents from speaking out. I'm looking around, I see police officers all over the place," Greer said. Meanwhile, the legal debate over Flock is playing out across the country. In Oklahoma, a federal judge ruled Oct. 1 that a warrantless search of approximately a month of license plate location records violated the Fourth Amendment, suppressing evidence obtained following the search. The ruling concerned the specific circumstances of that case and did not establish that all Flock searches are unconstitutional. Law enforcement agencies have continued to defend the technology, while privacy advocates argue that large networks of searchable cameras allow police to monitor ordinary drivers on a scale that wasn't previously possible. Florida is already seeing changes. The Florida Department of Transportation revoked permits for automated license plate readers on state highway rights-of-way, requiring their removal from those locations. Lucie also voted to remove 18 of its 53 Flock cameras. But for Greer, taking down some cameras isn't enough. When Bente pointed out that Port St. Lucie was already removing cameras, Greer argued that voluntary decisions can be reversed by future administrations. "The end result is to get a consent decree, where the city and Flock agrees to pull the cameras forever," he said. His amended lawsuit seeks a declaration that the city's surveillance program violates constitutional protections and an injunction restricting operation of the network or national data sharing without a warrant supported by probable cause. It also seeks disputed public records, statutory damages under federal privacy law and litigation costs. Greer told the I-Team that his primary goal is a binding court order, not a financial payout. "I'm not running for office. I'm not seeking attention," he said. "It's my way of doing something." The lawsuit still faces significant legal hurdles, including potential motions to dismiss. A federal judge has not ruled that Port St. Lucie's camera program violates the Constitution. Greer says he's willing to accept help from an attorney, but for now, he's prepared to continue the fight himself. "You cannot have this technology and not violate the Fourth Amendment. There's no way around it," he said. "You've got to get rid of it.

Lucie Boulevard say more needs to be done to protect pedestrians as construction continues on the busy road. Their concerns come after a 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student died from injuries he suffered when he was hit by an SUV while walking to school. Police say the freshman was walking along the edge of Southwest Port St. Lucie Boulevard near Squirrel Avenue on the morning of Oct. 7 when he was struck from behind. He was pronounced clinically deceased two days later. His family chose to donate his organs . Much of the roadway remains under construction, and there are no sidewalks along large sections of the corridor. Recent heavy rain also left portions of the shoulder flooded, further limiting space for pedestrians. "He was just going to school," said neighbor Irene Ange. "He was just starting his high school year. He had the right to be safe." Irene Ange, who has lived near the boulevard for more than two decades, says students often walk or bike close to traffic, sometimes before sunrise. The stretch of road is dangerous, Ange said. It’s very dark, and drivers are not following the speed limits. Ange said she saw first responders rushing to the crash site and was heartbroken for the student and his family. See also: Suspect booked into Martin County Jail after undercover drug sting, sheriff says The teen’s mother told CBS12 by phone that her son was a people person who made friends easily. She said the family does not want this to happen to another child. The Florida Department of Transportation is widening the southern portion of Port St. Lucie Boulevard from two lanes to four and adding sidewalks on both sides of the road. FDOT says the sidewalks will be eight to 10 feet wide. The project is expected to be completed in winter 2028, with an estimated cost of about $25.6 million. CBS 12 saw crews building sidewalks several blocks from where the crash happened. FDOT did not respond to questions about what pedestrian safety measures are in place while construction continues. "No accountability with that response because now there's another death," Ange said. Ange says more needs to be done now to keep children safe on their way to school. "This did not have to happen to this family," Ange said. The family now have to mourn him." The driver initially told officers he believed he had struck a construction barrel and has been cooperating with investigators. It remains unclear whether any charges will be filed.

Lucie City Council approved three major site plans for projects along the Southern Grove, a developing jobs corridor in the city.One of those plans: the long-awaited Costco retail store."This is something that we have been looking forward to for a long time,” Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said.Samples and Wes McCurry, president and CEO of St. Lucie County Economic Development Council said the 163,000-square-foot store is just the beginning for a new phase of growth in western Port St. Lucie."This is getting closer to the finish line,” Samples said.The Costco will join other companies like Amazon, Tamco and Cheney Brothers, calling the Southern Grove area home.McCurry said since the jobs are now here, new commercial development will follow."They see all the all the development that's occurring here, along with the demographics that they like to see,” said McCurry. “It only makes sense that Costco opens a retail store here."City council approved two other major site plans for the area, including a 5.5-acre site making up the first phase of the Tradition Entertainment District set to bring restaurants and retail.“This area has historically been largely under-served by restaurants and retail, and especially entertainment facilities,” McCurry said. “It's kind of catching up to the rooftops that are happening. You know, rooftops always drive that demand, but there's more to come.”The other plan is space for an acute care rehabilitation hospital, featuring inpatient and outpatient services with 42 beds in a more than 55 thousand square foot building."Growing area needs services, and that's just another component of services that are coming into the area is expanded healthcare access,” McCurry said.McCurry said the plans for retail, healthcare and entertainment is fulfilling the city’s master plan for what Southern Grove was destined to become."The plan is coming together. The vision is coming together. What everyone saw 20 years ago is now starting to happen,” McCurry said.Samples said Costco still must close on the land, move on to construction design planning and permitting before any shovels hit the ground.

Police are searching for a hit-and-run cargo van driver accused of fatally striking a man riding a gas scooter before he crashed into a nearby business and ran away in Fort Pierce. Police officers received multiple 911 calls just before 9 p.m. Sunday about a vehicle crash involving a motorcycle, which later was identified as a gas scooter, close to the intersection of Okeechobee Road and 25th Street, near HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. A white cargo van was behind the scooter, traveling east on Okeechobee Road, Maj. Michael Santiago told WPBF's Angela Rozier at a briefing Monday afternoon. The van driver fled the scene and made a U-turn to drive in the wrong direction across the median on Okeechobee Road, but he crashed into the side of a building, the Kings Queens Unisex Salon. The man then ran from the scene. Salon owner Sheila Hampton showed the damage, and is thankful no one was inside at the time. Hampton said she feels for the victim and his family. "His family told me he was just leaving from one of his friend's houses and just going home," she said. A second vehicle, a Toyota pickup truck, was also struck, but no one was injured. Lucie County Sheriff's Office K-9 Unit and Aviation Unit assisted Fort Pierce police and the K-9 Unit in efforts to locate the driver. They are in possession of the van. Police described the driver as a Hispanic man wearing a dark-colored top with light-colored pants or shorts. "So, that in itself proves intent that that person knew exactly what they were doing at the time and was just trying to simply get away," Santiago said. Anyone with information should call the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-8477. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

A 17-year-old was killed in a Fellsmere shooting Friday night after a meetup of more than 100 teens turned violent, according to the sheriff. The shooting happened around 11:24 p.m. at Garcia’s Boat Ramp , where a large crowd had gathered. Sheriff Eric Flowers said the group included teens ages 14 to 19, with drinking and fighting reported. These have been happening since before I was in high school, since before many of you were in high school. This has been going on for a long time. But now we're adding guns into the mix, and we're adding social media into the mix. CBS12 confirmed with the family that the slain 17-year-old was Sulliman Bah, a senior at Sebastian River High School. He and a group of friends approached a pickup truck with two 18-year-olds inside. Detectives say Bah opened the door and attempted to punch someone inside when the passenger fired a single shot at Bah. See also: What Florida voters need to know about the 3 constitutional amendments on the Nov. ballot Bah was taken by friends toward Fellsmere. Deputies and EMS met them at Fellsmere City Hall and performed CPR before he was taken to Sebastian River Medical Center and later transported to Holmes Regional Medical Center in Melbourne, where he succumbed to his injuries. No arrests have been made. Flowers said the driver and passenger inside the truck have cooperated with investigators and turned over the truck and firearm. The sheriff said the preliminary investigation indicates a self-defense claim may apply. We will be submitting a warrant in the case, but at this time it looks as though there will be a self-defense claim as a result, Flowers said. The sheriff said the state will ultimately decide whether charges are filed. Investigators used Flock technology to identify people connected to the truck and shooting. Deputies also recovered additional guns and multiple shell casings. Flowers said investigators believe the meetup was part of a growing trend of teens gathering at remote locations arranged through Snapchat , where fights are recorded and shared online. "We got kids out here losing their lives chasing likes and shares on social media," he said. "We've got kids out here losing their lives trying to go viral on social media." He said there may have been as many as four fights at the boat ramp that night, and investigators are still working to identify people who were there. "They had a history of fighting," Flowers said. "This has been an ongoing thing." The sheriff urged parents to ask their children whether they attended the meetup and encouraged anyone who witnessed the shooting or recorded it to contact investigators. "It's not safe," Flowers said. There's guns, and those two just don't mix. And now add in the fuel of the fire of social media, and now we have a 17-year-old dead." In a statement, the Indian River School District gave its condolences to the teen's family: The School District of Indian River County is heartbroken by this young person’s death. Our hearts are with his family, friends, and the students and staff who knew and cared about him. Grief support was in place over the weekend, including counselors at Sebastian River High School’s Homecoming Dance, and continues today as students and staff return to school. Our teams will remain available in the days ahead, offering care and responding to the needs of those affected. A spokesperson for SDIRC said the student had recently withdrawn from Sebastian River High School to be home schooled.

Brandee Anthony, known as the Vero Beach Mermaid, is an elite level PADI dive instructor, who teaches people of all ages to become mermaids — offering experiences that range from glamorous mermaid makeovers and beach photoshoots to poolside swimming lessons."I was a professional live streamer a long time ago, so I thought it would be really cool to take all my viewers underwater, but how can I make that interesting and magical?" Anthony said.That curiosity grew into a deep and lasting passion."That was 10 years ago and I'm a little in love with mermaiding for sure," Anthony said.The experience begins with a mermaid makeover, starting inside Anthony's custom fantasy closet — brimming with tropical-inspired tails, tops and accessories created just for mermaid gear."We're going to start with a mermaid makeover, which is one of my favorite parts," Anthony said. "Kate, so this is your magical closet."The closet features silicone tails that each weigh about 30 to 35 pounds. Accessories are on hand to complete every look."Mermaid crowns and armbands and embellishments, kind of the final touches to help people really feel like they have a full ensemble," Anthony said.Armbands come in a variety of styles, including options with a vibrant teal accent."We have a few options if you want to go with armbands. We have these, these are super cute and they have that nice teal," Anthony said.Anthony even offered a personalized recommendation while I was browsing through the options."I think with what you are wearing I would probably wear this one," she said.Browsing the closet felt like being a kid in a candy store — wanting more of everything. Anthony said that reaction is exactly the goal."That is exactly what you should feel like," she said. "So, we'll pick out a tail, a top, some accessories, and a crown, and then we'll head over to the beach."After settling on a look — including a tail Anthony called a "wind trader" and a stunning leafy sea dragon design — I was feeling the mermaid vibe and ready for the beach.Anthony, a professional photographer for 15 years, combines breathtaking backdrops and elaborate costumes to create magic where whimsy meets the water. Once suited up, I made my way toward the water, making my mermaid marks in the sand along the way."Like a sea turtle you are going to migrate towards the ocean," she said. "And then your going to turn toward me put your fin over here — we call it a fluke."Anthony walked me through the first poses on the shoreline."The seated is the easiest first pose — you can kind of just look at the ocean and relax and let the wind take your hair," she said. "Look out towards the beach — a little water love."Next, I headed poolside for a basic mermaiding class.Anthony caters to every client's ability, even those who are a little cautious about the experience."Once people get in a tail and they find their groove, it turns into a bunch of people just playing in a pool," she said.People come to the experience for all kinds of reasons."I've had people come to me for fun and some for deeper reasons," Anthony said."Coming on a retreat or take a course really did change their lives — or changed the trajectory of their lives. I've turned a few people into pro mermaids," Anthony said.In the pool, Anthony was ready to teach me how to mermaid — stripping back the glam and focusing on the fundamentals."So now you've had the photoshoot and the glam and now we are going to strip it back and just have some fun swimming as a mermaid," Anthony said.She walked me through every step of the movement."So you can flex your foot up towards the top of the water and then push it down…and just do that a few times….you can feel the resistance of the water and that's what propels you," Anthony said. "I'm going to have you back float in the tail — I'll kind of help you float there."The lesson even included a dive completely underwater."3.2.1. breathe out — we dive down and then pop up," Anthony said. "That was so good — that was fun — and that's how we shoot video underwater."For Anthony, the joy of mermaiding as an adult goes far beyond the water itself. "I think that's what mermaiding as an adult feels like is you don't have to act like a kid but you can be an adult that plays," she said. "And that's where it can be fun or it can be more — some people just want to feel empowered. Or good in their skin and they do a photo shoot or a bucket list thing."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

A Hobe Sound woman is facing multiple animal cruelty charges after deputies say she killed and buried several kittens because she believed they were possessed by demons.The Martin County Sheriff's Office (MCSO) arrested 36-year-old Alba Chavez on Thursday after responding to reports of animal cruelty at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park.WATCH BELOW: Woman buried cats alive, thought they were demons, deputies sayAccording to MCSO Sheriff John Budensiek, three youths living in the home called 911 after they discovered several of their kittens had disappeared. The children told deputies they believed Chavez had killed two kittens earlier in the week and were worried about the remaining animals.Budensiek said the children had attempted to protect three kittens by locking them inside a bedroom before going out to dinner Thursday evening. When they returned, they found the door had been forced open, and the kittens were gone."When deputies arrived, she admitted she thought the kittens had demons and said she didn't want black cats or brown cats in her residence," Budensiek said during a Friday news conference.Investigators said Chavez told deputies she had killed two kittens on Monday, thrown them into the trash, later removed them and buried them in the backyard.Deputies said she then led them to a burial site behind the home and told them to bring gloves, shovels and bags if they wanted to find the missing kittens.Despite heavy rain and lightning, deputies began digging in the backyard."As they were digging, they could hear cries from the kittens," Budensiek said.Deputies rescued two kittens that were buried alive inside a plastic Publix bag. The two kittens killed earlier in the week were also recovered deceased from the burial site.A fifth kitten remains missing. Budensiek said deputies and investigators extensively searched the backyard and mobile home but have not located the animal.The two surviving kittens were rushed to a veterinary emergency clinic, where they are being treated for dehydration and monitored for potential long-term effects from being buried underground."If they survive, they'll eventually be taken to the Humane Society and go through the adoption process," Budensiek said.Chavez was arrested on four counts of animal cruelty involving torture, inflicting pain, serious injury or death to an animal. Authorities said additional charges could follow if the missing kitten is found dead.The arrest marks at least the third animal cruelty or neglect case in Martin County since late July. Asked whether the trend surprised him, Budensiek said reports of violence against animals often mirror broader societal problems."We've seen society kind of going downward and we see more violence with interactions with humans, and then that translates into animals," Budensiek said. "In fact, a lot of times it starts with animals and then moves over to humans. So unfortunately, based on the trends and societal trends that we're seeing, it does not surprise me, but when we see it, it's extremely alarming.Budensiek said Chavez is being held without bond at the Martin County Jail and is also subject to an immigration hold. The sheriff identified her as a Venezuelan national who he said is in the United States illegally.According to the sheriff, deputies had previously responded to the home for incidents involving Chavez's mental health but had never received complaints related to animal cruelty.When asked about Chavez's motive, Budensiek said investigators still aren't certain whether mental health issues played a role."She said they were demonic. She said she didn't want those cats in her house," Budensiek said. "I don't know whether it was a mental health issue or she just didn't like the cats."Budensiek said the three youths who reported the incident were emotional but showed courage by contacting law enforcement."I applaud them for reaching out, calling 911 and letting us save the two kittens," he said.The children were taken into the custody of the Florida Department of Children and Families before being turned over to their father, who lives locally, according to investigators.Other adult cats found at the home were examined by animal services and determined to be healthy.Budensiek called the case "extremely alarming" and praised the responding deputies for their efforts to rescue the buried animals."We're going to aggressively pursue criminal charges on her to make sure she pays for the damage that she did to these animals," he said.

The WPTV Town Hall on Amendment 3 has led to more questions about the referendum facing voters on raising the homestead exemption to lower property taxes and reduce revenue for cities and counties.One question attendees posed was: Why are our property taxes increasing every year?WATCH BELOW: Florida property tax increases explained ahead of Amendment 3 votePalm Beach County Administrator Joe Abruzzo talked about it at the town hall, saying inflation is a big factor."This is a national problem, not even a Florida problem; it's not a Palm Beach County problem," Abruzzo said. "What it cost for traffic arms where our lights go: $700,000 five years ago. Now, they're at 1.5 million. The cost of labor, asphalt, concrete, the things we actually use in government is just skyrocketing, so we have to budget appropriately to be able to afford the things we need to buy." Another email asked why municipal workers get raises every three years."They're not coming in and saying we want to take a pay cut," said West Palm Beach Mayor Keith James, talking about negotiating with police, fire and labor unions. "Every three years we're looking at increases, and we also want to pay our employees so they’re competitive with the market; otherwise we lose them to the private sector and other cities, and they're living in a city where affordability is an issue."Another question asked about the impact on apartment living."Over 50% of the occupied housing units in West Palm Beach are renters," James said. "There is no dispute that the rents are going to increase, because those are not homesteaders and so the taxes will go up on those units and the landlords will pass those expenses on to the renters."

WPTV is continuing to follow flooding issues at the intersection of California and Savona boulevards in Port St. The water has receded, but earlier this week, the intersection looked like a lake.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie flooding hits pizza shop hard as city works on fixWPTV is pressing city leaders about any solution to keep the water levels down.Neighbors shared video of the roadways, looking like a river."We were actually calling it the California River, as a joke," said Joe Dascoli, who works at Estella Pizzaria right of the intersection. "It becomes like an island around here."That island is a shopping plaza where the pizza shop is located. Due to the flooding on Thursday, Dascoli said they had to close early."It's an ongoing thing that you know should be resolved," said Dascoli.Dascoli told WPTV customers couldn't go in and orders couldn't go out during this week’s flooding."We've lost thousands of dollars just in revenue and people not being able to come in," said Dascoli. "Some of our drivers, their cars aren't capable of going through the floods, so we have to stop deliveries."WPTV pressed the city of Port St. Lucie about any solutions to the flooding.Scott Samples with the city said it's starting a pilot program for water level sensors at flood-prone areas in the city."There'll be alerts that'll be able to go to Public Works and the police to say, 'Hey, this area is seeing rapid flooding,' so they might be able to respond quicker," said Samples.Samples said long-term solutions include a large-scale drainage project for the Oak Hammock neighborhood.The project includes two new retention ponds, baffle boxes to collect runoff, and even raising sections of the roadway at California and Savona boulevards.Right now, Samples said the project is in the data collection phase before moving on to design."This is one of the highest priorities that we have in terms of capital investment projects, and so it's going to take time," said Samples.

A 54-year-old Jupiter woman is facing felony charges after she allegedly removed fentanyl from a critically ill patient's IV infusion while working at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital, the Port St. Lucie Police Department said Monday. On Thursday, Leslie Pope was arrested in Jupiter in conjunction with the Palm Beach Marshals Task Force and faces three felonies: grand theft of a controlled substance, possession of a controlled substance without a prescription and fraudulently obtaining a controlled substance. Pope was booked into the Palm Beach County Jail on Thursday morning on an out-of-county warrant. She was released on Saturday morning after posting an original bond of $150,000. Pope is not an inmate at the St. "We take these allegations very seriously," Cleveland Clinic spokeswoman Rebecca Astorga told WPBF in a statement. "She individual no longer works with us, and we are fully cooperating with law enforcement. Because this is an active investigation, we are unable to comment further at this time." https://www.facebook.com/PortStLuciePolice/posts/pfbid02W5HqPQihHo4JSGqHsePU1wjBMmTubGN5HyptojT8wtSJU5Pft8YBVYsKgckEN7mDl Port St. Lucie police arrested Pope after an investigation into the allegations. Investigators learned a family member reported witnessing Pope use a syringe to withdraw fluid from the patient's fentanyl infusion, place the syringe in her pocket and leave the room. Pope was not assigned to the patient's care. The next evening, Pope allegedly returned to the patient's room and again approached the IV equipment, police said. The family member intervened. Detectives later reviewed video footage that shows Pope manipulating protective caps on the equipment. No additional medication was removed during the second incident, according to investigators. A 15-page arrest affidavit includes witness interviews, hospital video footage, medical and administrative records, medication transaction reviews and coordination with the Drug Enforcement Administration. "PSLPD takes allegations of criminal misconduct seriously, particularly when they involve individuals entrusted with the safety and well-being of others," the police agency said in a news release.
