New details reveal more problems in the failed execution of Christa Pike. Now we're learning about a major delay in getting an ambulance to the prison.WPTV's partners at NewsChannel5 Investigates discovered there was a lot of confusion about whether to even send first responders to Riverbend after the state failed to put Pike to death.It all began with a 911 call for an ambulance from the prison.NewsChannel5 Investigates does not have the actual first 911 call from the prison because the Department of Correction argues that hearing the caller's voice would reveal his identity and state law makes the names of everyone involved in the execution process confidential.But through a public records request, NewsChannel5 Investigates was able to get a transcript of that call and other crucial audio that reveals how efforts to get Christa Pike emergency help got off to a really rough start.It began at 8:40 p.m. that night with a 911 call from Riverbend Prison.The state had tried and failed to execute death row inmate Christa Pike.But there was a problem.Metro's Emergency Communications Center requires callers from the state prison in northwest Nashville to follow a certain security protocol to prevent prank or fake calls or prison escapes.In the 911 call, after the dispatcher asked the location of the emergency and the caller said Riverbend, the dispatcher asked, "What's your code?"The caller appeared confused and said, "I'm sorry?"Again, the dispatcher asked, "What's your code?"The caller, whom NewsChannel5 Investigates says is an official with the Tennessee Department of Correction, not only didn't have the required code, but didn't even seem to know about it.He asked, "My code? For reporting an emergency or do you (want to) know what the emergency is?"Again, the dispatcher asked, "What's, what's the code? For the location?"The caller, "I, I don't have a code."The dispatcher responded, "Ok. You don't have a verification code?"The caller replied. "I don't."Again, this call came in at 8:40 p.m. Keep in mind, this was more than half an hour after media witnesses said they watched Pike gasp for air and it was clear they said there'd been a problem with the execution.What's not clear is why the Department of Correction waited more than 30 minutes to make that 911 call or why the TDOC official had no idea about the required code.What then followed was a series of calls where 911 employees tried to figure out what to do next.We hear them call a Metro Police supervisor, then Nashville Fire and the THP, seeking guidance.No one was sure if this was a real call and no one could believe the 911 caller didn't know about the required code.In one call between one of the dispatchers and a Nashville Fire employee, the dispatcher explained, "They said they don't have a code and it's for the woman that's supposed to be executed. But they said they don't have a code."The Fire employee's reaction? "How do they not have a code? Is it at Riverbend?"The dispatcher confirmed, "Yes, at Riverbend."The NFD employee replied, "That's the one place you definitely need a code."Dispatchers even repeatedly called the prison, trying to verify the call.One prison employee replied, "We didn't call anybody. I would have been the one to call you guys."And that prompted an announcement from dispatch over the radio, alerting crews that it was, in fact, "a false call" and emergency crews were not needed.But moments later, at 9:06 p.m., nearly half an hour after the original request for an ambulance, there was another call from the prison asking dispatchers to send help. Only this time, the caller said, "Let me know when you're ready for the code."And it was about this same time, another call came into 911. This one from one of Christa Pike's lawyers.Attorney Kelly Gleason can be heard saying, "She is still alive and breathing and needs immediate life-saving care."A firetruck and ambulance had actually been dispatched to the prison shortly after the initial call, but waited just outside the gate until someone could produce the security code. But even then, they still waited, as dispatchers tried to find someone to escort the fire crew into the prison, first calling the THP and being turned away.Finally, reporters covering the execution spotted the emergency crews pulling onto the prison grounds. And then the fire truck and ambulance stopped just outside the gate, waiting another a minute and a half, apparently for their security escort to show up.Pike was finally loaded onto an ambulance nearly an hour after the initial 911 call and at 9:28 p.m., the ambulance can be seen, with flashing lights, pulling out of the prison property.There was even more confusion in the emergency radio traffic. The fire crew waiting outside the prison was being told at one point, by dispatch, that it was a false call. Then, they reported that someone had come running up to them from the prison, insisting it was real and demanding they go in. This person apparently identified themselves as a state official. But again, that person did not have the code.There was also confusion about where to take Pike. According to the radio traffic, they were on their way to one hospital when the staff there diverted them elsewhere and they ended up at Vanderbilt.NewsChannel5 Investigates did reach out to the Tennessee Department of Correction to ask why the caller, a TDOC official, didn't have the code or even seem to know about it. NewsChannel5 Investigates believed this person would at least be aware of the security protocol at the prison or at least when informed that they needed a code would be able to get it rather quickly since they were there at the prison.The TDOC spokesperson told NewsChannel5 Investigates she was unable to comment right now.

Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico returned to the campaign trail over the weekend after a 9-day absence that fueled speculation about his whereabouts.His opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, and other Republicans questioned Talarico's explanation that he had been home with the flu.At one point, Paxton called for "proof of life" in a social media post questioning Talarico's whereabouts.The speculation included unsubstantiated claims circulating online that Talarico had been receiving treatment at a mental health facility in Ohio.“I had the flu," Talarico insisted in an interview with MS Now on Sunday. "This is the craziest thing I’ve ever heard. It’s wild that someone can just post something on the internet and then the media just runs with it."The rumors prompted the Lindner Center of HOPE to publicly deny that Talarico had been a patient."Representative James Talarico has never received treatment from Lindner Center of Hope," Lindner Center HOPE posted on X. Talarico responded to the post by saying, "I’ve never even been to Ohio 😂"Over the weekend, Talarico was seen meeting with potential voters at the Austin City Limits Music Festival. He also attended a Kacey Musgraves concert in Dallas on Saturday, where he met with the country singer.The Texas Senate contest is among the most closely watched races in the country as Democrats seek their first statewide election victory in more than 30 years.

Lucie family is turning unimaginable loss into hope after choosing organ donation following the death of their 14-year-old son, who was struck by a vehicle while walking to school, according to police.Port St. Lucie police said the teen was walking along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near Squirrel Avenue on Oct. 7 when he was struck from behind. He died from his injuries two days later.WATCH: Port St. Lucie Teen's Legacy Lives On Through DonationNow, the family's decision to donate his organs could help multiple people waiting for lifesaving transplants while creating a lasting legacy in his memory.Organ donation advocates say the family's choice highlights an ongoing need for registered donors. According to transplant advocates, more than 100,000 people nationwide are currently waiting for an organ transplant, and 15 lives are lost each day while patients remain on waiting lists.The teen's family chose organ donation in the days following his death, a decision supporters say can have a profound impact on recipients and their families."It's a courageous thing for them to do, and I think it's the right thing," said St. Lucie County Tax Collector Chris Craft.Craft has worked with Donate Life Florida through the tax collector's office to encourage organ donor registration and raise awareness about the need for donors.For Tyre Gray, a kidney transplant recipient and the chief administrative and legal officer for South Florida Donor Network, the family's decision carries special meaning."Organ donation is one of the few places where grief and gratitude exist in the same place," Gray told WPTV.Gray said he spent five years waiting for a kidney transplant before receiving the life-saving organ he needed."I know for a fact that I wouldn't be here without a family making that election in their deepest moment of despair," he said.Gray described years of uncertainty while waiting for a match."That's five years of uncertainty, five years of being paralyzed, five years of not being able to grow," he said.Organ donation advocates say the need for donors continues across Florida and the United States.Gray noted that a single donor has the potential to save multiple lives and help many more patients through tissue donation."One donor is to save upwards to nine lives and to be able to heal another 75 lives," Gray said.Behind those numbers are people awaiting a second chance, he said."Let's all be heroes and save lives," Gray added.Advocates say organ donation often allows families to find meaning during some of life's most difficult moments."I would hope that they could see the lasting impact that a selfless act can make on others," Craft said. "If you can help somebody else, it's an amazing thing."For transplant recipients, organ donation can mean more time with family, additional milestones and opportunities.In the midst of tragedy, one Port St. Lucie family's decision could now help save lives and ensure their son's legacy continues through the people he may help.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Fort Pierce police are searching for a driver who they say hit and killed a man riding a scooter before fleeing the scene, crashing into a salon and running away on foot Sunday night. The deadly crash happened shortly before 9 p.m. on October 11 along Okeechobee Road, just west of South 25th Street. According to Major Michael Santiago with the Fort Pierce Police Department , a man riding a scooter was stopped at a red light behind a Toyota pickup truck when a white van traveling eastbound failed to stop and struck him from behind. "That in turn led to a domino effect where the motorcyclist was ejected from the scooter itself and was thrown into the vehicle in front of the scooter," Santiago said. Lucie County Fire District officials said crews were dispatched at 8:51 p.m. and arrived four minutes later. The scooter rider was pronounced dead at the scene. No other patients were transported. But investigators say the van driver did not remain at the scene. See also: No lawyer, no law degree: Port St. Lucie man takes on Flock cameras in federal court Instead, Santiago said the driver reversed, made a U-turn, briefly traveled westbound in the eastbound lanes of Okeechobee Road, crossed the median and lost control before crashing into Kings & Queens Unisex Salon. "After he crashed into the business, he fled on foot," Santiago said. Police responded to multiple 911 calls reporting the crash around 8:42 p.m. and immediately established a perimeter, searching for the driver using K-9 units and assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office aviation unit. Despite their efforts, they were unable to locate him. Two additional vehicles involved in the crash remained at the scene, according to police. The department's Traffic Homicide Unit, Crime Scene Investigations and other personnel processed the scene as part of the ongoing investigation. By Monday afternoon, the van had been removed, but significant damage remained. Broken concrete and debris were piled outside the entrance, which was boarded up and surrounded by caution tape. Salon owner Sheila Hampton said she received a phone call about the crash and arrived to find extensive damage to her business. "They just called me at the last minute and I just seen a hole in my wall. Hampton said she was unable to open the salon Monday and was concerned about when she would be allowed to resume business. And I'm just hoping tomorrow will be a better day," she said. Despite the damage to her business, Hampton also expressed sympathy for the family of the man who died. "My condolences from King and Queen Salon. We give out our condolences to the family," she said. "This shouldn't have ever happened." Police searching for driver Santiago said witnesses described the driver as a Hispanic man wearing a dark top and light-colored pants or shorts. Investigators believe he may have been injured in the crash, based on evidence recovered at the scene. Police have recovered the van and identified its registered owner, but have not confirmed who was driving. Santiago said the registered owner lives approximately one to one-and-a-half miles from the crash scene. He also said the owner stopped communicating with investigators after officers began asking who had access to the vehicle. Police have not ruled anyone out as they continue pursuing leads. Investigators are also searching for surveillance footage that could help identify the driver. As of Monday afternoon, Santiago said they had not obtained video showing the suspect himself. "We are desperately needing the public's help in identifying who was behind the wheel of this box van," Santiago said. He urged anyone who saw the white van in the area Sunday night, recognized someone who may have been driving it or captured video of the incident to come forward. The victim's identity has not been released as police work through the family notification process. No arrest had been announced as of Monday afternoon. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department.

An explosion inside a Port St. Lucie home destroyed almost everything owned by a family of four. Lucie County Fire District, the initial call came in at 1:24 p.m. for a fire at a home in the 100 block of Carmelite Street Friday afternoon. Neighbors called 911 after noticing the home was on fire. "I looked, and there was all kinds of smoke going through the yard," said neighbor Rob Roadman. "I was outside in the backyard, and then I see very heavy smoke," said Marina Cheong, who lives a few doors down. Cheong said she ran toward the home to help but was stopped by the explosion. "And then there was explosion, very loud, loud explosion, and debris started flying everywhere," she said. "I heard a huge explosion. At first, I thought maybe it's a transformer or something, but it was much, much, much louder than that," Roadman said. Neighbors said the man who lives in the home told them he had been cooking when a grease fire started in the garage, where the propane tank was located. The explosion sent the propane tank flying out of the garage, across the street, and into the garage of a neighbor's home. "I thought it was an air raid. It was not a casual thing. My house shook," Roadman said. "I thought that the whole house had exploded. It was very loud," Cheong added. Roadman said he spoke to the man shortly after the explosion. "I asked the dad if he was OK, and he goes, 'Yeah.' But you could tell he wasn't. Who wouldn't be?" Roadman said. The man was briefly hospitalized but returned to the house a few hours later to join family and friends in going through the debris to see what could be salvaged. They said there wasn’t much left. However, a family member told WPBF 25 News that they consider themselves lucky that nobody was seriously injured. She said the family has a strong community and a strong church to help them persevere. The family has set up a GoFundMe account for donations. The West Palm Beach GreenMarket is more than a weekend destination. It’s also serving as a launching pad for local entrepreneurs, including several new vendors making their debut this season.For this week’s Saturday Small Business, WPTV’s Christy Waite visited Truffle Smiles, one of five new vendors joining the GreenMarket this year.Owner Robert Hurbanek specializes in artisan truffle products imported from Italy.“We import artisan truffle products from Italy. If you love to cook, this is the place to stop,” Hurbanek said.Visitors to the Truffle Smiles booth can find a variety of products, including oils, pasta, sauces, and truffle chips.Hurbanek recommends the truffle mayonnaise.“The mayonnaise! Oh my gosh, if you put that on a burger or a BLT sandwich, it changes everything,” he said.With so many options, Hurbanek said one product customers keep coming back for: Parmesan Reggiano.“People come back for the Parmesan Reggiano,” Hurbanek said. “You can put it on mashed potatoes, a burger. I have even made decadent grilled cheese sandwiches.”The business also fits into this year’s GreenMarket theme, “The World Right Here,” which celebrates the food traditions, people and cultures that make the community unique.Hurbanek said choosing the West Palm Beach GreenMarket was an easy decision because farmers markets give him the opportunity to connect directly with customers and hear how they use his products.“I mostly sell at farmers markets. I like interacting with people and listening to people’s recipes, and just being here at the GreenMarket, which is a nice place to be,” he said.Truffle Smiles is one of the new businesses shoppers can check out this season at the West Palm Beach GreenMarket in downtown West Palm Beach.

A busy stretch of Haverhill Road across from Greenacres Elementary School will become a designated school zone after parents raised concerns about children crossing the road.WPTV reporter Christy Waite has been pressing the county, city and the Palm Beach County School District for answers. WATCH BELOW: School zone, crosswalk coming to Greenacres ElementaryBrandon and Lynn Pote reached out to Waite after growing increasingly concerned about student safety. The couple lives across from Greenacres Elementary School, where the speed limit along Haverhill Road is 40 mph, and there is currently no designated school zone or crosswalk."Right here on Haverhill Road there is no crosswalk and no school zone, and cars are going 40 mph," Brandon Pote said.The nearest guarded crosswalks are near Greenacres Christian Academy and another near 10th Avenue and Swain Boulevard.While reporting in the area, Waite witnessed some of the safety concerns families described, including children and families navigating traffic and students riding e-bikes and scooters. She also witnessed a crash along the roadway. Neighbors like Omar Trevino have lived in the area for about 20 years, and he says something needs to be done before someone gets hurt."Cars can't cross, much less kids," Trevino said.After WPTV began asking questions, Engineering and Public Works said a pedestrian safety study determined an additional crosswalk is needed along Haverhill Road to serve Greenacres Elementary School. EPW also says they are considering placing the crosswalk on Haverhill at the intersection of either Carver Street or Fourth Street. The new crosswalk will also be guarded.The City of Greenacres told WPTV it will allocate funding for the crossing guard(s) but the city will not be financially responsible for the rest of the project.But the guarded crosswalk is not the only safety change coming to the area.After Waite continued pressing the county about the lack of a designated school zone along Haverhill Road, EPW says the road will become a designated school zone.Greenacres Elementary already has a school zone along Jackson Avenue, where traffic speeds are limited to 20 mph during arrival and dismissal. However, the stretch of Haverhill Road bordering the school is not currently a designated school zone.The city also requested flashing signals or beacons to help improve visibility for students and crossing guards.For parents like Pote, the plans are welcome news after his family reached out to Waite asking for help."I watch you guys, and I see you guys do reports where you sit down and listen to the community," Pote said. "Thank you guys so much."Engineering and Public Works say they are now working to determine the location for the crosswalk and designated school zone. Once the location is determined, both are expected to be ready by early next year.The county has not said how much the project will cost.

Fort Pierce police are searching for a driver who they say hit and killed a man riding a scooter before fleeing the scene, crashing into a salon and running away on foot Sunday night. The deadly crash happened shortly before 9 p.m. on October 11 along Okeechobee Road, just west of South 25th Street. According to Major Michael Santiago with the Fort Pierce Police Department , a man riding a scooter was stopped at a red light behind a Toyota pickup truck when a white van traveling eastbound failed to stop and struck him from behind. "That in turn led to a domino effect where the motorcyclist was ejected from the scooter itself and was thrown into the vehicle in front of the scooter," Santiago said. Lucie County Fire District officials said crews were dispatched at 8:51 p.m. and arrived four minutes later. The scooter rider was pronounced dead at the scene. No other patients were transported. But investigators say the van driver did not remain at the scene. See also: No lawyer, no law degree: Port St. Lucie man takes on Flock cameras in federal court Instead, Santiago said the driver reversed, made a U-turn, briefly traveled westbound in the eastbound lanes of Okeechobee Road, crossed the median and lost control before crashing into Kings & Queens Unisex Salon. "After he crashed into the business, he fled on foot," Santiago said. Police immediately established a perimeter and searched for the driver using K-9 units and assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office aviation unit, but were unable to locate him. By Monday afternoon, the van had been removed, but significant damage remained. Broken concrete and debris were piled outside the entrance, which was boarded up and surrounded by caution tape. Salon owner Sheila Hampton said she received a phone call about the crash and arrived to find extensive damage to her business. "They just called me at the last minute and I just seen a hole in my wall. Hampton said she was unable to open the salon Monday and was concerned about when she would be allowed to resume business. And I'm just hoping tomorrow will be a better day," she said. Despite the damage to her business, Hampton also expressed sympathy for the family of the man who died. "My condolences from King and Queen Salon. We give out our condolences to the family," she said. "This shouldn't have ever happened." Police searching for driver Santiago said witnesses described the driver as a Hispanic man wearing a dark top and light-colored pants or shorts. Investigators believe he may have been injured in the crash, based on evidence recovered at the scene. Police have recovered the van and identified its registered owner, but have not confirmed who was driving. Santiago said the registered owner lives approximately one to one-and-a-half miles from the crash scene. He also said the owner stopped communicating with investigators after officers began asking who had access to the vehicle. Police have not ruled anyone out as they continue pursuing leads. Investigators are also searching for surveillance footage that could help identify the driver. As of Monday afternoon, Santiago said they had not obtained video showing the suspect himself. "We are desperately needing the public's help in identifying who was behind the wheel of this box van," Santiago said. He urged anyone who saw the white van in the area Sunday night, recognized someone who may have been driving it or captured video of the incident to come forward. The victim's identity has not been released as police work through the family notification process. No arrest had been announced as of Monday afternoon. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department.

Police are searching for a hit-and-run cargo van driver accused of fatally striking a man riding a gas scooter before he crashed into a nearby business and ran away in Fort Pierce. Police officers received multiple 911 calls just before 9 p.m. Sunday about a vehicle crash involving a motorcycle, which later was identified as a gas scooter, close to the intersection of Okeechobee Road and 25th Street, near HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. A white cargo van was behind the scooter, traveling east on Okeechobee Road, Maj. Michael Santiago told WPBF's Angela Rozier at a briefing Monday afternoon. The van driver fled the scene and made a U-turn to drive in the wrong direction across the median on Okeechobee Road, but he crashed into the side of a building, the Kings Queens Unisex Salon. The man then ran from the scene. A second vehicle, a Toyota pickup truck, was also struck, but no one was injured. Police were unable to locate the suspect despite aerial and K-9 units. They are in possession of the van. Anyone with information should call the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 800-273-8477. The award for funniest player on the Miami Dolphins goes to Ollie Gordon. Gordon is in his second year as a Dolphin, and the running back says the key to the team's potential this season comes down to what is happening inside the locker room.WATCH BELOW: Ollie Gordon sits down with WPTV sports reporter Eleanor SheahanGordon sat down with WPTV to talk about team chemistry, the competitive culture within the Dolphins' roster, his role as the locker room's self-proclaimed class clown — and why he believes this group is built to surprise people."I feel like it's going well. You know, it's getting to the basics, you know, the basics of football. I feel like we've built a good bond here. We got a new team, we got new coaches, and I feel like we're getting that brotherhood and that familyhood," Gordon said.When asked who the most competitive player in the locker room is, Gordon rattled off several names before making sure to include himself."I feel like we got a couple of people. I'm gonna say, Jordyn Brooks. He's one of the most competitive. Jacob (Rodriguez) also, Jordan Phillips, DJ Campbell. I'm gonna throw myself in there. I feel like I'm competitive too." Gordon said.Gordon said Aaron Brewer and Patrick Paul also raise the bar for the team's competitive attitude."I mean, everyone really. I feel like we just got a competitive locker room. You know, I feel like that's what makes the team. That's what makes us a good team and able to play for each other just because of stuff like that," Gordon said.Off the field, Gordon wears another title with equal pride — funniest guy on the team."I think you're looking at him. I think I can go with that. I think I can agree with that one." Gordon said.Asked why he deserves to wear that crown, Gordon was direct."Because I think that's just me. I feel like I'm always goofing around with everybody. I feel like no matter who it is, offense, defense, best teams, we're just here to have a good time," Gordon said.During practice, Gordon is uplifting his teammates and even dialing up a few handshakes with the Dolphins staff."You got to mix it up with everybody. You know, you got to get everybody ready to get everybody juice for work," Gordon said.That upbeat energy, Gordon explained, does not conflict with his competitive side; it is all about knowing when to flip the switch."I really just got to have that switch. You know, when you're in between those white lines, I feel like it's game mode. It's us versus them, you know? And then when we get outside of that, we can play around. But you know, I feel like once we're in between those white lines, those 100 yards, you know, I feel like it's go mode. We got to be ready for whatever, honestly," Gordon said.Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley said Gordon is upbeat and has grown in practice and maturity on the field."I appreciate that, Coach Hafley," Gordon said. "This is a young team, and I feel like some of us all got to lead by example, even if it's not being the oldest on the team, but it's still just showing the young guys how to go. I feel like Coach Hafley has instilled that in us. Like he doesn't just talk to the vets; he talks to all of us. He tells all of us we're leaders in some way. So I feel like with him being like that, I feel like that's turned me that way."Hafley has preached all season long about growth and development. When he was asked to finish the sentence: "The Dolphins team is going to surprise people this year because...," Gordon kept the focus on unity."We stick together, and we play for each other. You know, we come out here every day. I feel like we spend so much time together that we are willing to do anything for each other. You know, and I just feel like when you go back and look, we took a bunch of games down to the wire, and in the NFL, everybody's good. Some teams get in that they hit a wall, but I feel like that's not going to be us. I feel like we're going to push through this moment and stick together as we do," Gordon said.Fans should keep an eye on the No. 0 jersey; that's Ollie Gordon.

A 54-year-old Jupiter woman is facing felony charges after she allegedly removed fentanyl from a critically ill patient's IV infusion while working at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital, the Port St. Lucie Police Department said Monday. On Thursday, Leslie Pope was arrested in Jupiter in conjunction with the Palm Beach Marshals Task Force and faces three felonies: grand theft of a controlled substance, possession of a controlled substance without a prescription and fraudulently obtaining a controlled substance. Pope was booked into the Palm Beach County Jail on Thursday morning on an out-of-county warrant. She was released on Saturday morning after posting an original bond of $150,000. Pope is not an inmate at the St. "We take these allegations very seriously," Cleveland Clinic spokeswoman Rebecca Astorga told WPBF in a statement. "She individual no longer works with us, and we are fully cooperating with law enforcement. Because this is an active investigation, we are unable to comment further at this time." https://www.facebook.com/PortStLuciePolice/posts/pfbid02W5HqPQihHo4JSGqHsePU1wjBMmTubGN5HyptojT8wtSJU5Pft8YBVYsKgckEN7mDl Port St. Lucie police arrested Pope after an investigation into the allegations. Investigators learned a family member reported witnessing Pope use a syringe to withdraw fluid from the patient's fentanyl infusion, place the syringe in her pocket and leave the room. Pope was not assigned to the patient's care. The next evening, Pope allegedly returned to the patient's room and again approached the IV equipment, police said. The family member intervened. Detectives later reviewed video footage that shows Pope manipulating protective caps on the equipment. No additional medication was removed during the second incident, according to investigators. A 15-page arrest affidavit includes witness interviews, hospital video footage, medical and administrative records, medication transaction reviews and coordination with the Drug Enforcement Administration. "PSLPD takes allegations of criminal misconduct seriously, particularly when they involve individuals entrusted with the safety and well-being of others," the agency said in a news release. "We remain committed to thorough, evidence-based investigations and pursuing accountability when the evidence supports criminal charges." This remains an active criminal case. "Cleveland Clinic doesn’t comment on caregivers," spokeswoman Rebecca Astorga told WPBF. A federal judge on Sunday evening ordered the Trump administration to cancel any further airings of the controversial taxpayer-funded ads that promote President Donald Trump’s agenda.Judge Jennifer Rochon granted a temporary restraining order requested by a coalition led by the nonprofit government watchdog group Common Cause, which had challenged the ad buys in a New York federal court.RELATED STORY | Taxpayers have funded nearly $1.5M in pro-Trump ads. Criticism is mounting, including from the GOPThe Justice Department told Rochon, an appointee of Joe Biden, late Saturday that the ad push was set to end Sunday night. But Rochon said that timing didn’t render the lawsuit moot and ordered the government to halt any further airings as of 6:45 p.m. ET.Earlier, the government said in a filing to the court that it has already spent $19 million in taxpayer money on the ads.The administration allocated $20 million for the ads, which were classified as “public service announcements,” from US Customs and Border Protection, CNN previously reported. An advertising company, LMD Agency Inc., “purchased media buys under the terms of the Order through Sunday, October 11, 2026, at an approximate cost of $19,000,000,” senior Department of Homeland Security official Holly Mehringer said in a sworn declaration in the case.The Department of Homeland Security, which includes CBP, directed LMD “to not make any additional media buys past October 11,” she added. Mehringer noted there are “no plans” to purchase any additional ads.Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle expressed concerns about the unprecedented ad campaign when it began late last month.On October 5, Trump acknowledged the backlash and said “I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.,” his super PAC.But six days later, the taxpayer-funded ads were still airing.The Trump administration created at least 13 campaign-style ads, some of which have aired on TV networks including CBS, CNN, MS NOW, Fox News and Fox. Watchdog groups, including the nonprofit, nonpartisan Common Cause, said the ads mark a clear violation of appropriations law restricting the use of federal funding for propaganda or partisan communications. Common Cause and the Democratic National Committee separately sued the Trump administration over the ads.In a response to the Common Cause lawsuit, the Justice Department said in a filing late Saturday that an effort to halt the spending should be denied because the ads “will not continue past tomorrow.”The judge’s order Sunday would block any further ad buys for two weeks, so if the administration does consider resuming the ad campaign at taxpayer expense, DOJ lawyers would need to get the court order lifted.The coalition that brought the suit praised the judge’s order, writing, “We are pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda.”CNN previously reported that Trump has personally driven the video ads, including helping select the imagery and videos used, according to a source familiar with the matter. Two Trump advisers familiar with the ads said they were being created in-house by the White House video team — which is part of the communications team, responsible for the administration’s public messaging — though at least one of them was produced by a pro-Trump meme group.RELATED STORY | Trump defends ad, says MAGA Inc. will cover cost instead of taxpayersMehringer, in the court filing, described the ads as “depicting the President of the United States and his administration’s various efforts related to protecting America’s borders, including enhancements of border security by combating drug trafficking,” though that is not the exact substance of many of the ads obtained by CNN.And while the Justice Department conceded the ads “(attack) a generic list of ‘villains,’” it emphasized they did not “address any specific race, electoral candidate, or party.”A White House spokesperson said Monday that Trump did not plan to reimburse the government for the money already spent on the ad buys, and Mehringer and other officials did not indicate any plans for a refund.The White House Office of Management and Budget last month allocated $20 million in taxpayer money from CBP for what it called “OBBBA commemorative events.” (OBBBA is an abbreviation for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Trump signed into law in 2025.)Mehringer emphasized in her declaration that that money “did not fund the creation or production of any videos or media” and “only funded the airing of preexisting media.”Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was pressed during an appearance Sunday on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on whether the taxpayer dollars would be refunded.“Anytime we can do a public service announcement and brag about America, I’m all about it,” Mullin said, taking aim at negative coverage of the Trump administration as he pointed to success in securing the border and lowering fentanyl-related deaths.“We should be bragging about what’s happening inside America,” he said, adding, “I commend the opportunity of President Trump to give us the opportunity to brag about America.”The-CNN-Wire™ & © 2026 Cable News Network, Inc., a Warner Bros.

Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico returned to the campaign trail over the weekend after a 9-day absence that fueled speculation about his whereabouts.His opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, and other Republicans questioned Talarico's explanation that he had been home with the flu.At one point, Paxton called for "proof of life" in a social media post questioning Talarico's whereabouts.The speculation included unsubstantiated claims circulating online that Talarico had been receiving treatment at a mental health facility in Ohio.“I had the flu," Talarico insisted in an interview with MS Now on Sunday. "This is the craziest thing I’ve ever heard. It’s wild that someone can just post something on the internet and then the media just runs with it."The rumors prompted the Lindner Center of HOPE to publicly deny that Talarico had been a patient."Representative James Talarico has never received treatment from Lindner Center of Hope," Lindner Center HOPE posted on X. Talarico responded to the post by saying, "I’ve never even been to Ohio 😂"Over the weekend, Talarico was seen meeting with potential voters at the Austin City Limits Music Festival. He also attended a Kacey Musgraves concert in Dallas on Saturday, where he met with the country singer.The Texas Senate contest is among the most closely watched races in the country as Democrats seek their first statewide election victory in more than 30 years.

A fire that spread through the garage of a Port St. Lucie home Friday afternoon left a father injured and displaced a family, while neighbors and church members rallied to help them begin the cleanup process. The fire happened on Carmelite Street in the Northport Village neighborhood near St. According to the family, the fire started in the kitchen before spreading through the garage. They say a propane tank later exploded, causing additional damage and impacting a neighbor's garage doors across the street. Lucie County Fire District responded to the home around 1:30 p.m. Crews arrived to find heavy fire coming from the garage. When firefighters extinguished the flames, significant damage was left behind, including a charred garage door, blackened walls and belongings covered in soot. Renter Nigel Laidlow was inside the home when the fire broke out. He suffered burns to his legs and was transported for medical treatment. "I don't even know how to describe it. It was really surreal," Laidlow said. "I would've never thought a little fire would turn into this." By Saturday, family photos, furniture and other belongings were spread across the front yard as loved ones worked to salvage what they could. Members of the Fort Pierce Seventh-day Adventist Church spent the day helping move and sort through damaged items. "We have a really strong support system, especially from my church," Laidlow said. Despite the loss, Laidlow said he is grateful his family survived. "This right here is something not anybody would like to deal with. Not in a lifetime," he said. See also: MCSO warns scam emails may trick development applicants into wiring money The family is now focused on recovering and determining its next steps. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

For the first time, the family of a man set to be executed for the 1986 murder of an Indian River County sheriff's deputy is speaking publicly about their effort to save his life.William Reaves has spent nearly four decades on death row for shooting and killing 29-year-old Deputy Richard Raczkowski. Reaves' execution is scheduled for Oct. 20.WATCH BELOW: As execution nears, Reaves' family asks DeSantis to spare his lifeNow, with less than two weeks remaining, Reaves' family is asking Gov. Ron DeSantis to grant him clemency and commute his death sentence to life in prison."I mean, he's my uncle, and I love him," Reaves' nephew, Meredith Farrington, told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey.Farrington said his family does not dispute the gravity of Reaves' crime or the pain Raczkowski's family has endured."I can't be upset. I can't be mad at the governor or the decision," Farrington said. "I mean, my uncle did take a life."But Farrington added, "I just want the governor to look at the whole picture."That story stretches back to Sept. 23, 1986.According to court records, Reaves called 911 from a convenience store in Indian River County after he was unable to get a taxi.Raczkowski responded and was attempting to help Reaves call a cab when a gun fell from Reaves' pants. A struggle followed.Reaves shot Raczkowski four times in the back, killing him.For nearly 40 years, Raczkowski's brother, Marc Raczkowski, has lived with the loss."Why? Why?" he said while speaking with WPTV near his brother's gravesite. "It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody." A stretch of road near where the deputy was killed now bears Raczkowski's name — a memorial to a life taken and a crime that continues to reverberate through two families four decades later."The pain will still always be there," Marc Raczkowski said.DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant Sept. 22, scheduling his execution for Oct. 20.Farrington is not asking the governor to pardon his uncle or release him from prison. Instead, he wants DeSantis to commute Reaves' death sentence so the now-77-year-old can spend the rest of his life behind bars.Central to his plea is Reaves' history as a decorated Vietnam War veteran and questions raised during decades of appeals about his mental health, substance abuse and legal representation.Court records show Reaves repeatedly challenged his conviction and death sentence, including claims that his trial attorney failed to adequately investigate and present evidence concerning his drug use and mental health."The attorney wasn't an effective attorney for that type of case," Farrington said. "That was his first death row case."At Reaves' sentencing, testimony described him as suffering from what was then called "Vietnam syndrome," rather than post-traumatic stress disorder.Years later, other experts testified that Reaves suffered from PTSD, substance abuse and other impairments.Farrington said none of that excuses the murder."I'm not going to say that his PTSD, his drug use, his being on cocaine and all the other stuff excuses what he did," Farrington said. "I mean, he's being punished by being in prison, and he's 77. The governor can let him stay in prison for the rest of his life, and still he's being punished without killing him and taking another life."Farrington also acknowledges that his family is not the only one carrying grief into Oct. 20.On the other side is Raczkowski's family, which has spent four decades living with the consequences of Reaves' actions."I mean, trying to understand what he feels — there's no way I could do that," Farrington said of Raczkowski's brother.He said he understands why the deputy's family may want the execution to proceed."I know that the family, the officer ... I would probably want the same thing, and I can't even imagine," Farrington said.For the Raczkowski family, the case is about a life taken nearly 40 years ago.For Reaves' family, it is now about whether another life should end."But we're praying," Farrington said.Reaves has already lost his latest attempt to stop the execution in Indian River County court. He has appealed that decision to the Florida Supreme Court.For now, his execution remains scheduled for Oct. 20 unless a court intervenes or DeSantis grants clemency.If carried out, Reaves' execution will mark the 18th in Florida in 2026.

A Martin County woman is facing multiple animal cruelty charges after deputies say she buried several cats alive in her yard at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office arrested 37-year-old Alba Luz Chavez on four counts of aggravated animal cruelty after investigators said they discovered two live kittens and two dead kittens buried on a property in Hobe Sound. Deputies were called to the home Thursday night for what family members described as a mental health crisis. Family members told deputies Chavez believed the cats were demons and had killed several animals earlier in the week. According to the affidavit, deputies learned that Chavez had allegedly told residents of the home she killed two kittens on Monday, Oct. Three juveniles living at the residence told deputies Chavez had appeared to be experiencing a mental health episode for most of the week. The juveniles said they locked three surviving kittens inside a bedroom before leaving for dinner Thursday evening. When they returned around 6 p.m., they discovered Chavez had forced her way into the room and the kittens were gone. Investigators said Chavez initially refused to tell family members where the animals were. However, while speaking with deputies, Chavez allegedly said, “If you want the cats, you will need gloves, a red bag and a shovel,” and directed them to an area on the property. Deputies began digging and found two live kittens buried underground inside plastic Publix bags, according to the affidavit. Investigators later uncovered two deceased kittens that appeared to be in the early stages of decomposition. Detectives searched for a third missing kitten but were unable to locate it. During an interview, Chavez told investigators she had been cleaning her house and referred to the cats as “very ugly,” according to the affidavit. Investigators wrote that Chavez also made statements indicating she did not want black cats and suggested kittens of different colors “had different fates.” The affidavit states Chavez later began singing instead of answering additional questions. The two surviving kittens were taken to a pet emergency center for treatment. A veterinarian told investigators the kittens were about three weeks old and very weak. The veterinarian said it was too early to determine whether a lack of oxygen while confined inside the plastic bags had caused brain damage or other medical complications. The two deceased kittens are expected to undergo necropsies to determine their exact causes of death. Chavez was arrested and booked into the Martin County Jail on four felony counts of aggravated animal cruelty and is being held without bond.

A recent change to a flight out of Vero Beach is sparking a bigger conversation about travel options on the Treasure Coast.Travelers tell WPTV limited flight schedules and a lack of convenient transportation alternatives can make getting in and out of the area difficult, sometimes forcing them to drive to larger airports or rearrange their plans.WATCH: At the Vero Beach Regional Airport, travelers shared their frustrations with WPTV reporter Brooke Chau about the challenges of getting where they need to go.“In the Treasure Coast area, Vero Beach specifically, it is difficult to get around,” said Peter Masella. He pointed to the lack of a Brightline station in Vero Beach, saying people often have to travel to other cities to access additional transportation options.A recent schedule change to Breeze Airways' route between Vero Beach and the New York area has added to those concerns. The flight, which previously departed Vero Beach in the evening, now leaves in the morning.A New York City physician told WPTV the change has affected his work schedule.“I’m a physician working in New York City and because of the change of flight for Vero Beach, I have had to rearrange my patients schedule two days in a row,” he said.Another traveler from Westchester, New York said the change can mean a longer trip.“Then I have to take a taxi all the way down and around to Vero Beach. It’s very inconvenient,” she said.However, Breeze Airways has also been adding destinations from Vero Beach. Last month, the airline introduced nonstop service to Trenton, Baltimore, Pittsburgh and Atlantic City, expanding the airport's commercial flight options.Vero Beach Airport Director, Brandon Dambeck, says airlines regularly evaluate the performance of their routes, which can lead to new destinations as well as schedule or route changes.“All of these airlines are monitoring the routes and their gauge of success," Dambeck said. For travelers, more destinations are welcome, but they say flight times that fit their schedules are just as important.

A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student who was hit by a vehicle while walking to school last week has died from his injuries, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.Police said the crash happened the morning of Oct. 7 near the intersection of Southwest Port St. Lucie Boulevard and Southwest Squirrel Avenue.According to police, the freshman was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near the edge of the roadway when he was struck from behind by a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man.The teen suffered critical injuries and was transported to a local hospital. Police said he was pronounced clinically deceased on Oct. 9 shortly after 4 p.m.Investigators said the crash remains under investigation as detectives continue to examine the circumstances surrounding what happened.Amid the tragedy, the student's family made the decision to donate his organs in hopes of helping others and honoring their son's memory."In the midst of their grief, their decision offers the possibility of hope and healing for other families and individuals whose lives may be changed through this extraordinary gift," police said in a statement.Treasure Coast High School will provide grief counseling services for students and staff as the school community copes with the loss.The Port St. Lucie Police Department extended its condolences to the student's family, friends, classmates and the entire Treasure Coast High School community."We recognize that no words can ease the pain of losing a child, and our thoughts remain with everyone affected by this heartbreaking tragedy," the department said.

Yes, the Florida Panthers are already seeing injuries piling up.And yes, the Panthers know things could be much, much worse.Florida forward Brad Marchand will need six weeks to recover from his left leg injury and should be able to resume play with the Panthers sometime in November, coach Paul Maurice confirmed Friday. That comes on the heels of forward Aleksander Barkov, who is expected to need a similar timetable before he can play again, also because of a left leg injury.Losing two stars isn't good. But Maurice sees the silver lining."Nobody said 'months' yet," Maurice said.That's the difference between the injuries this season and what was happening to Florida at this point last season. By then, Barkov was already expected to be sidelined at least seven months with torn ligaments in his right knee and Matthew Tkachuk was also going to be out for multiple months while recovering from surgery to repair a sports hernia and torn adductor.Barkov wound up missing the entire season. Tkachuk didn't start his season until mid-January. The Panthers saw players miss a combined 544 games with injuries last season and missed the playoffs, an unceremonious end to their run as back-to-back Stanley Cup champions.So, yes, losing Barkov (who could be back by the end of November) and Marchand (who'll be back on the ice in three weeks, then is expected to need three more weeks to rehab and condition) for a few weeks now isn't ideal. But Florida has been there before."We're no stranger to guys going down the last few years and guys have done a great job of stepping up," Tkachuk said. "Worst case, you just got to win 1-0, 2-1."There have been clear sighs of relief with the knowledge that Barkov and Marchand will both return in a few weeks. Florida was short-handed in all four games of its season-opening road trip — Marchand missed the first two, Barkov missed the next two, and defenseman Aaron Ekblad also missed two because he and his wife were welcoming a baby — and the Panthers went 2-0-2 anyway.Ekblad is expected to be in the lineup when Florida plays its home opener Saturday against Minnesota."There's a threshold to this," Maurice said. "You can only survive so many (injuries) and we proved that. But you get two or three guys out, it's standard operating procedure in the National Hockey League. You prefer it's not your No. 1 at any one position because those guys hurt to lose. Everybody's got two or three. And then, you know, you get to five, it starts to get a little tight. Anything over five, you start to really feel it."

A Martin County employee helped rescue three girls who were struggling in a rip current Thursday afternoon at Bob Graham Beach near Jensen Beach.Amy Offenbach said she arrived at the beach around 2 p.m. to surf when she noticed three girls about 25 yards offshore holding onto the same surfboard. Watch report: Offenbach, who works in Martin County's Growth and Development Department and is an avid surfer, said something about the situation immediately caught her attention."The ocean could be very gentle and calm, but it can also be very heavy and crash very hard," Offenbach said.Offenbach said she became concerned when one of the girls appeared distressed."That kind of struck me as strange," she said. "The other one seemed a little agitated."Moments later, a girl on the beach told Offenbach she believed her friends needed help."By that time the girls were waving in the water like they needed help, so immediately I just went into rescue mode," Offenbach said.Offenbach and a friend went into the water and paddled toward the girls.When Offenbach reached the group, she said one of the girls appeared to be in serious distress."I looked at her, and she seemed kind of dazed and confused," Offenbach said. "I said, 'Get up on the board.'"Offenbach said she gave the surfboard she was riding to two of the girls and instructed them to hold on and kick toward shore. She then placed the third girl on her soft-top surfboard and paddled her back to the beach.Offenbach said she has some lifeguard training and quickly recognized the girl needed medical attention after they returned to shore."The girl that I rescued said that she blacked out under the water," Offenbach said. "She inhaled water, and she had a severe headache."Because Bob Graham Beach is unguarded, Offenbach said she drove the girl to a nearby lifeguard station, where an ambulance was called.Offenbach hopes the rescue serves as a reminder for beachgoers to understand ocean conditions before entering the water.She encourages people to swim at guarded beaches when possible, check rip current forecasts and use flotation devices or boards when appropriate."I'm just really happy that I was in the right place at the right time," Offenbach said.Offenbach said she has not been able to reconnect with the girl she rescued or learn more about her condition.While she enjoys spending time in the ocean, Offenbach said it is important to remember the dangers it can present."It can be very treacherous. Treacherous," she said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Martin County's contracted transit provider walked away from its agreement Thursday, halting all MARTY bus service and laying off 29 employees with no warning to riders or county leaders.Martin County issued an official statement acknowledging the disruption and pledging to work toward a solution."Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders," Martin County officials said in the statement.Martin County Transit, the company contracted to operate the MARTY system, blamed rising operating costs for the decision. In a statement, CEO Karen Deigl said, "we entered this contract in good faith and made every effort to find a path forward. We understand how important MARTY is to its riders and the community, and this decision was not made lightly.”Martin County Transit also acknowledged the abruptness of the shutdown."We understand that this news may feel sudden to riders and residents. As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system," Martin County Transit said.In an afternoon press conference, county leaders explained they were in negotiations after the vendor asked for a significant increase in the cost of the contract. Two weeks ago, the company gave notice it planned to leave in 180 days and instead, it walked away Thursday, according to the county.Jim Gordon, Martin County's Public Works Director, said the county had no warning the cancellation was coming."We were not given advanced notice that they were going to cancel service today," Gordon said.For Joe, a 67-year-old veteran and Martin County resident, losing MARTY service means losing his lifeline. Joe sat at the bus stop Thursday expecting his regular pickup, but no buses came. He relies on the transit system daily."[I use it] to go to work sometimes and to go down to the homeless place, the church that feeds us food," Joe said.Joe said he received no notice before service was cut."No warning at all, nothing, zero." Joe said.Physical limitations make alternative transportation all but impossible for Joe."I've had two broken necks, three broken backs, I can't feel my feet, so I'm not getting anywhere," Joe said.Tony Argudo, a Martin County resident, said the transit company's handling of the shutdown lacked transparency."I don't think letting people go first thing this morning was a good idea. There should have been more transparency and the people should have had some kind of notice so they could have made other plans," Argudo said.George Stokus, Martin County's Assistant County Administrator, said county officials are working urgently to restore service."We're doing everything we can humanly due to restore service as soon as we can," George Stokus said.In the meantime, the United Way of Martin County is stepping in through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents for trips to work, grocery stores, medical appointments and other essential services.The organization said it was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption and is now anticipating even greater need.Carol G. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County, emphasized the critical importance of transportation access for those who depend on it."Transportation isn't a luxury for the people who depend on it. It's how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table. When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn't disappear with it," Houwaart-Diez said.Houwaart-Diez said the United Way is committed to being there for riders during the disruption."This is important for people to be able to get to the doctor's, to get to wherever they need to go so we want to be there," Houwaart-Diez said.Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support the Ride United program's response, alongside a contribution from another donor. Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. However, United Way emphasized that the program cannot fully replace MARTY's fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its response is only a temporary solution dependent on available funding.Martin County said it will continue providing updates as it works to restore public transit service. Information about MARTY can be found on the county's transit website.Residents seeking transportation assistance can call the United Way of Martin County at 772-283-4800 or click here to visit their website.Residents seeking paratransit transportation assistance can call 772-463-2822.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

A fire that spread through the garage of a Port St. Lucie home Friday afternoon left a father injured and displaced a family, while neighbors and church members rallied to help them begin the cleanup process. The fire happened on Carmelite Street in the Northport Village neighborhood near St. According to the family, the fire started in the kitchen before spreading through the garage. They say a propane tank later exploded, causing additional damage and impacting a neighbor's garage doors across the street. Lucie County Fire District responded to the home around 1:30 p.m. Crews arrived to find heavy fire coming from the garage. When firefighters extinguished the flames, significant damage was left behind, including a charred garage door, blackened walls and belongings covered in soot. Renter Nigel Laidlow was inside the home when the fire broke out. He suffered burns to his legs and was transported for medical treatment. "I don't even know how to describe it. It was really surreal," Laidlow said. "I would've never thought a little fire would turn into this." By Saturday, family photos, furniture and other belongings were spread across the front yard as loved ones worked to salvage what they could. Members of the Fort Pierce Seventh-day Adventist Church spent the day helping move and sort through damaged items. "We have a really strong support system, especially from my church," Laidlow said. Despite the loss, Laidlow said he is grateful his family survived. "This right here is something not anybody would like to deal with. Not in a lifetime," he said. See also: MCSO warns scam emails may trick development applicants into wiring money The family is now focused on recovering and determining its next steps. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

Crews are making "steady" progress power restoration, and 24 parks have reopened after Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday, Gov. Hundreds of thousands of people lost power in the wake of the storm, and 430,000 customers remained without power Saturday morning. As of Sunday afternoon, more than 200,000 customers had power restored, DeSantis said. FLP is expected to be largely finished with power restoration efforts by Monday. CHELCO, which had about 46,000 customers without power as of the press conference, is targeting to have power restored by Tuesday, DeSantis said. "I know it’s frustrating to lose power and some of you have been without it for a couple of days now... Be assured we’re working around the clock to recover from this devastating hurricane," CHELCO CEO Steve Rhodes said. DeSantis held the press conference Sunday evening from Grayton Beach State Park in Santa Rosa Beach. The state park was closed after a bridge washout, but DeSantis said the park was expected to reopen Sunday night after substantial recovery efforts. WATCH HERE The bridge was "totally washed out" after the storm, and FDOT reported the 50-foot-long and 15-foot-deep washout was cutting off access and could "potentially cause harm to the to the beloved Western Lake here in Grayton Beach," DeSantis said. Recovery efforts at the Walton County park involved crews working overnight and bringing in 600 cubic yards of sand to restore the bridge in less than 18 hours, DeSantis said. DeSantis said the storm caused widespread damage across Northwest Florida. That damage came primarily from falling trees, debris and other wind damage, as opposed to storm surge, he said. The state plans to submit a major disaster declaration to the federal government, DeSantis said. "There's a certain damage threshold that has to be reached," he said. "I think clearly, just given the amount of trees that fell down on different things, there's going to be more than enough."The disaster declaration, which must be approved by the president, "provides a wide range of federal assistance programs for individuals and public infrastructure, including funds for both emergency and permanent work," according to FEMA. Isaias made landfall in the panhandle Friday night as a Category 2 hurricane. DeSantis has confirmed there were two storm-related deaths in Escambia County.Some of the hardest-hit counties included Santa Rosa County, where about 90% of customers were without power, Holmes County at 89%, Washington County at 86%, Walton County at 85%, Escambia County at 75% and Okaloosa County at 53%, according to the governor.Despite the storm's impacts, state emergency officials said Saturday they had not received any requests for large-scale search and rescue deployments.RELATED LINKS:Who to contact during power outagesLeon County deputies deploy to Santa Rosa Co.Firefighters battle house fire amid Hurricane IsaiasWakulla County escapes major damage

The man accused of crossing state lines and traveling to Indian River County to kill his ex-girlfriend was booked into the Indian River County Jail on Monday. According to Indian River County Jail records, Matthew Waggle, 33, was booked into the Indian River County Jail at around 5:20 a.m. He faces a charge of first-degree murder. CBS12 reported on the August shooting after authorities found the victim's body, identified as Dawn Kriskewic , in a roadway in the southern part of the county. Investigators say Waggle traveled to Vero Beach by bus and Uber before allegedly killing Kriskewic outside her home Sunday morning. See also: FHP: Wrong-way driver caused deadly I-95 crash Sunday near PB Lakes Boulevard Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said surveillance video captured Waggle walking through Kriskewic's neighborhood shortly after an Uber dropped him off. Investigators say Waggle then left the area, taking an Uber back to Orlando before boarding another Greyhound bus. He eventually made his way to West Virginia, where investigators say he hid at a motel. Flowers said at the time that Flock Safety cameras were instrumental in tracking down Waggle. Authorities had later tracked Waggle to a motel in West Virginia and taken him into custody. Authorities said Kriskewic had ended her relationship with Waggle before the shooting and had warned coworkers at the hair salon that she wanted no contact with him.

Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm & Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman “Sulli” Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. No arrests have been made, and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense. The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room.As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm & Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life.Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. “He touched everybody’s heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room,” Rodriguez said.Bah's close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him.Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. “He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future,” Cortez said.Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. “Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul,” Espinosa said.The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff's office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense. No arrests have been made.Bah's mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. She said she wants investigators to consider all the facts as they determine what happened.“I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right,” Godfrey said. “I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail.”During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the impact he had on their lives.Angela Sanders, one of Bah's former sixth grade teachers, remembered his personality and smile. “His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room,” Sanders said.Myan Agosto said Bah was the type of friend who regularly checked on the people around him. “He never failed to make sure everybody was okay,” Agosto said. “He was just a really good friend.”Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person.The memories shared Wednesday showed how many people Bah touched during his 17 years.“He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth — look at this room,” another speaker said during the celebration.Bah's funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

Lake Worth Beach is reducing fines for bulk and vegetation pickup violations and issuing partial refunds to residents after public backlash over 12-hundred citations issued since August.The city said more than 1,200 violations were issued after enforcement began Aug. 9 under its bulk trash and vegetation pickup rules. Residents complained they were unaware of the stricter enforcement and said they received costly citations without warning.The change comes after concerns raised by residents. Luis Carvajal, a Lake Worth Beach resident since 2009, contacted WPTV after receiving a bill that included a $335 violation charge.Carvajal said landscapers working on his property had trimmed palm fronds and placed them near the street for pickup."They're still continuing to work in the backyard or whatever. And there are trucks out here, and then the city solid waste comes by and they scoop it up and they leave. Okay, I didn't think nothing of it," Carvajal told WPTV's Michael Hoffman.Days later, he received a bill in the mail."Make it make sense to me. It didn't make sense," Carvajal said. "They're Palm Beach prices."Carvajal said he had never previously received a city violation notice.Concerns about the fines quickly spread among residents and eventually reached the Lake Worth Beach City Commission.According to city officials, though the changes went into effect in October 2025, more than 1,200 violations were issued after enforcement began in August, generating widespread criticism from residents who said they were not adequately informed about the rules.Vice Mayor Mimi May acknowledged residents frustrations during recent commission discussions."As somebody who's sitting here all the time, I'm like, how do you not know that?" May said. "But if I was just a non-informed resident, I would be upset about that."May is one of the officials who helped spearhead the changes when the ordinance took effect in October 2025.At the time, she recommended fines as high as $500 and opposed sending notification letters to residents before enforcement began.Now, she has changed her position."$300 is way too much money for people on a fixed income," May said.The vice mayor also issued a public apology on social media."I sincerely apologize for any confusion or frustration this situation has caused. I understand that a $335 fine can be a significant financial burden, especially when someone may not have fully understood the rules," May wrote.City leaders have now approved changes to the penalty structure.The city has reduced the violation fine from $335 to $135. Officials also plan to reimburse affected residents $200 for each violation issued under the previous rate.For residents like Carvajal, the city's decision comes as welcome news."That's great news, and I thank Channel 5 for looking into this matter," he told WPTV's Michael Hoffman.City officials say the reduced fines are now in effect, and eligible residents will receive reimbursements related to previous violations on their next bill.

Former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms was found guilty of a third-degree felony of official misconduct and not guilty of a second-degree felony of bid tampering on Thursday.Mimms was arrested in 2024 on charges of bid tampering and official misconduct.WATCH BELOW: Former Fort Pierce city manager found guilty of official misconductAccording to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Mimms was accused of rigging the bidding process for two vacant parcels of land along Avenue D, adjacent to the Lincoln Theater, in favor of a local nonprofit, Lincoln Park Young Professionals.Among that nonprofit's board was Caleta Scott, Mimms' niece, and also a city employee.The nonprofit had been awarded a $500,000 grant from Allegheny Franciscan Ministries for a community center project, but nothing was ever built.Johnathan Bridges, special assistant state attorney and Brandon White, major crimes attorney for the 19th Circuit, said there was a mountain of evidence, including emails and city documents that incriminated Mimms."What we learned is millions of dollars have been wasted by this city hall under the leadership of Nick Mimms, and for too long, it went unchecked,” said White. Pierce deserve better, and I think this verdict shows the corruption that was happening under Nick Mimms. Lucie County Courthouse.Prosecutors said he could face a maximum of five years in prison.
