As Hurricane Isaias heads toward the Florida Panhandle, homeowners across the state will see hurricane deductibles go into effect on their insurance policies."The trigger in this case for most policies is a (hurricane) watch or (hurricane) warning anywhere in the state of Florida," Robert Norberg of Arden Insurance in Lantana said.WATCH BELOW: Isaias triggers Florida insurance deductibles that could cost homeowners thousandsHurricane deductibles are common in Florida and are used for hurricane-related claims. They also have a much higher deductible than the usual deductibles on insurance policies."Typically, it's 2 to 3 percent of the property's insured value — not 2 to 3 percent of the claim — so it can be pretty extensive; some people even have 5 or 10 percent deductibles," Norberg said.A 2 percent deductible on a $300,000 home can run about $6,000.And that deductible applies anywhere in the state as long as a hurricane is posted somewhere in Florida."Any type of wind damage that causes a claim — say you're in Palm Beach County, those people will be subject to the wind deductible," Norberg saidThe hurricane deductible, according to state statute, expires 72 hours after the last hurricane warning is lifted.RELATED COVERAGE:

The detention center Florida dubbed "Alligator Alcatraz" may have shut down, but questions remain about who will ultimately pay for it.Last year, the federal government awarded Florida more than $600 million through FEMA to help fund operations at the immigration detention facility built in the Everglades. WATCH ALLIGATOR ALCATRAZ, IS FEDERAL FUNDING AT RISK?While state leaders touted the project and President Donald Trump praised it shortly after opening, only a portion of the promised funding has been distributed so far.Now, two federal reports are putting renewed attention on whether that money could be withheld and Florida could face additional scrutiny before receiving the rest of the funds."I think what these reports and the findings in them do is create a potential basis for scrutiny," said Stetson University law professor Anthony Palermo, who specializes in contracts.The questions stem from two separate federal reviews examining the facility's operations.A report from the Department of Homeland Security's Office of Inspector General found the detention center failed to meet several basic standards related to environmental health, safety, medical care, food service and hygiene.According to the report, some detainees reported lacking access to clean drinking water. Inspectors also documented detainees being confined in what were described as "small metal enclosures."A separate Government Accountability Office report highlighted concerns about spending and potential waste. The report found Immigration and Customs Enforcement had not finalized a contract or formal agreement with Florida before immigrants began arriving at the facility.Without pre-negotiated rates in place, the state sought reimbursement at significantly higher costs. The GAO found Florida's approved reimbursement rate was $249 per detainee per day, compared with ICE's reported median detention bed rate of $92 per day, a difference of 171%.So far, neither report concludes Florida violated the terms of its FEMA grant. That distinction could prove important.Palermo says federal agencies typically look first at whether grant recipients complied with the specific requirements attached to funding."Just because there is some sort of deviation from the anticipated standard doesn't necessarily mean that any funding will be withheld," Palermo explained.While the grant excludes typical termination language, it requires Florida to provide a detailed cost breakdown and justification for each reimbursement request.He noted that FEMA retains the authority to review spending, conduct audits and potentially challenge reimbursements if costs are deemed unreasonable. "There is always a chance that there could be an audit or even an investigation into reimbursement that was granted that could potentially lead to a reversal," Palermo said.Federal regulations also give agencies avenues to revisit previously issued payments."There is usually a chance under federal regulations for the government to potentially audit, investigate, review funds that have been paid out and make sure that they were reasonable and could potentially claw them back," he said.Gov. Ron DeSantis dismissed the findings in the federal reports and defended the state's handling of the facility.He also told us last month that additional federal funding continues to flow to the state. To date, just over $134 million has been dispersed from the grant according to USAspending.gov.Neither the Governor's office nor Florida's Department of Emergency Management responded to our inquiries about how the federal reports could impact funding for the facility.The detention center is closed. The federal money is still in question. And until federal officials determine whether all reimbursement requests meet grant requirements, Florida taxpayers have no guarantee they won't end up responsible for part of the final bill.

A Martin County employee helped rescue three girls who were struggling in a rip current Thursday afternoon at Bob Graham Beach near Jensen Beach. Amy Offenbach said she arrived at the beach around 2 p.m. to surf when she noticed three girls about 25 yards offshore holding onto the same surfboard. Watch report: Offenbach, who works in Martin County's Growth and Development Department and is an avid surfer, said something about the situation immediately caught her attention. "The ocean could be very gentle and calm, but it can also be very heavy and crash very hard," Offenbach said. Offenbach said she became concerned when one of the girls appeared distressed. "That kind of struck me as strange," she said. "The other one seemed a little agitated." Moments later, a girl on the beach told Offenbach she believed her friends needed help. "By that time the girls were waving in the water like they needed help, so immediately I just went into rescue mode," Offenbach said. Offenbach and a friend went into the water and paddled toward the girls. When Offenbach reached the group, she said one of the girls appeared to be in serious distress. "I looked at her, and she seemed kind of dazed and confused," Offenbach said. "I said, 'Get up on the board.'" Offenbach said she gave the surfboard she was riding to two of the girls and instructed them to hold on and kick toward shore. She then placed the third girl on her soft-top surfboard and paddled her back to the beach. Offenbach said she has some lifeguard training and quickly recognized the girl needed medical attention after they returned to shore. "The girl that I rescued said that she blacked out under the water," Offenbach said. "She inhaled water, and she had a severe headache." Because Bob Graham Beach is unguarded, Offenbach said she drove the girl to a nearby lifeguard station, where an ambulance was called. Offenbach hopes the rescue serves as a reminder for beachgoers to understand ocean conditions before entering the water. She encourages people to swim at guarded beaches when possible, check rip current forecasts and use flotation devices or boards when appropriate. "I'm just really happy that I was in the right place at the right time," Offenbach said. Offenbach said she has not been able to reconnect with the girl she rescued or learn more about her condition. While she enjoys spending time in the ocean, Offenbach said it is important to remember the dangers it can present. "It can be very treacherous. A proposed 150-unit assisted-living facility in Port St. Lucie is moving through the development process as nearby residents question whether enough is known about the environmental history of a neighboring property with petroleum contamination. The project, known as PSL Westmoreland ALF , is planned for 7.1 acres within the Rivella planned unit development, along Southeast Morningside Boulevard near Southeast Westmoreland Boulevard. The three-story facility would include assisted-living units and a memory care component. Lucie City Council approved the project’s major site plan on Sept. Construction has not begun, and the developer must still submit construction plans for technical review and additional agency reviews. A group of residents opposes the project, citing concerns about the neighboring property’s contamination history and the potential implications for people who could eventually live at the facility. See also: 'It's not safe': Treasure Coast neighbors raise concerns after teen hit walking to school It’s not about what is being built there, resident David Lipps said, arguing that nearby businesses and other facilities could also be affected by environmental concerns. Resident Charlie D’Agata said residents have raised objections at City Council meetings for about two years. He questioned why a developer would be allowed to build near a property he described as contaminated. Residents say they have contacted outside organizations, including the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Florida Department of Health , in an effort to get answers about the site. An engineering letter provides some context for their concerns. In a letter discussing a March 2026 meeting with environmental officials about the neighboring property, BTEX Engineering said the proposed remediation approach should be changed because of concerns about surrounding properties, including the planned assisted-living facility. The letter said vapors would need to be captured during remediation. The environmental history of the neighboring property and the extent of any potential impact on surrounding land remain central questions for residents seeking more information. The city has approved the major site plan, but the project must clear additional steps before construction can begin. The developer is expected to submit construction plans for technical review, followed by reviews involving the South Florida Water Management District and other agencies. Residents say they want clearer answers about the neighboring property’s environmental history and how any potential risks would be addressed as the project advances

Crews are making "steady" progress power restoration, and 24 parks have reopened after Hurricane Isaias made landfall Friday, Gov. Hundreds of thousands of people lost power in the wake of the storm, and 430,000 customers remained without power Saturday morning. As of Sunday afternoon, more than 200,000 customers had power restored, DeSantis said. FLP is expected to be largely finished with power restoration efforts by Monday. CHELCO, which had about 46,000 customers without power as of the press conference, is targeting to have power restored by Tuesday, DeSantis said. "I know it’s frustrating to lose power and some of you have been without it for a couple of days now... Be assured we’re working around the clock to recover from this devastating hurricane," CHELCO CEO Steve Rhodes said. DeSantis held the press conference Sunday evening from Grayton Beach State Park in Santa Rosa Beach. The state park was closed after a bridge washout, but DeSantis said the park was expected to reopen Sunday night after substantial recovery efforts. WATCH HERE The bridge was "totally washed out" after the storm, and FDOT reported the 50-foot-long and 15-foot-deep washout was cutting off access and could "potentially cause harm to the to the beloved Western Lake here in Grayton Beach," DeSantis said. Recovery efforts at the Walton County park involved crews working overnight and bringing in 600 cubic yards of sand to restore the bridge in less than 18 hours, DeSantis said. DeSantis said the storm caused widespread damage across Northwest Florida. That damage came primarily from falling trees, debris and other wind damage, as opposed to storm surge, he said. The state plans to submit a major disaster declaration to the federal government, DeSantis said. "There's a certain damage threshold that has to be reached," he said. "I think clearly, just given the amount of trees that fell down on different things, there's going to be more than enough."The disaster declaration, which must be approved by the president, "provides a wide range of federal assistance programs for individuals and public infrastructure, including funds for both emergency and permanent work," according to FEMA. Isaias made landfall in the panhandle Friday night as a Category 2 hurricane. DeSantis has confirmed there were two storm-related deaths in Escambia County.Some of the hardest-hit counties included Santa Rosa County, where about 90% of customers were without power, Holmes County at 89%, Washington County at 86%, Walton County at 85%, Escambia County at 75% and Okaloosa County at 53%, according to the governor.Despite the storm's impacts, state emergency officials said Saturday they had not received any requests for large-scale search and rescue deployments.RELATED LINKS:Who to contact during power outagesLeon County deputies deploy to Santa Rosa Co.Firefighters battle house fire amid Hurricane IsaiasWakulla County escapes major damageWant to see more local news?

Palm Beach Atlantic University wrapped up its three-day Hispanic Heritage Festival on Saturday, celebrating Hispanic art, culture and music during Hispanic Heritage Month in South Florida.The annual festival featured a contemporary art exhibition and a series of musical performances designed to showcase the cultural contributions and artistic traditions of the Hispanic world. Organizers say the event continues to grow as it enters its 17th year.In a region with a large Hispanic population, organizers say the festival provides an opportunity for students and community members to engage with artists and musicians while learning more about the diversity of Hispanic cultures.The festival began Thursday with an art exhibition featuring artists representing more than 10 countries.Visitors viewed a wide range of artistic styles and mediums, including oil paintings, photography and metalwork.Among the featured artists was Franco Sotillo, a visual artist originally from Lima, Peru, who said his work combines mixed media and reflects both his heritage and personal experiences."I'm a visual artist and came from Lima, Peru," Sotillo said. "I moved to this country 12 years ago."Sotillo said his work incorporates materials including oils, paper and other raw elements. He said sharing his art allows him to introduce audiences to Peruvian artistic expression."I'm an immigrant, but also bringing my culture to the states to show people how Peruvian art is expressed," Sotillo said.Festival Director Michael O'Connor said the event continues to evolve each year."We're expanding every year," O'Connor said.O'Connor said this year's festival marked the first time organizers expanded programming beyond art and classical music to also include popular music from Hispanic cultures."What we want to do is we want to celebrate the Hispanic artistic heritage, because here in South Florida, especially, we have a very, very large Hispanic population," O'Connor said.Organizers said they hope attendees leave with a deeper appreciation for Hispanic artistic traditions and the people behind them."We hope they'll be inspired too to see the artworks here at the exhibition and to see how the Hispanic world makes itself known through visual arts," O'Connor said. "Not just the art is Hispanic, but also the artists are Hispanic."The festival concluded Saturday with performances featuring both classical and popular Hispanic music.Organizers say they hope the festival continues for many years to come as it celebrates the art, music and cultural heritage that help shape South Florida's diverse communities.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Attendees can meet firefighters, learn about adoptable animals and help determine which firefighter-and-pet pairs will represent each month of the upcoming calendar.WPTV reporter Christy Waite will be emceeing the event and announcing which firefighter and animal duo were selected for which months.

Ron DeSantis said two people have died and more than 430,000 customers remain without power as state and local officials begin recovery efforts following Hurricane Isaias' landfall in the Florida Panhandle.Speaking Saturday in Okaloosa County, where the Category 2 hurricane came ashore Friday night, DeSantis said the storm caused widespread damage across Northwest Florida, primarily from falling trees and debris.WATCH BELOW: DeSantis confirms 2 storm-related deaths in Florida Speaking from Destin, Florida, the governor said both people died in Escambia County, highlighting ongoing safety concerns as residents cope with power outages.Escambia County Sheriff Chip Simmons said in a video posted to Facebook that one woman died after a tree fell on her home. In a second video, Simmons said the other victim, a man, died from a generator that was not properly ventilated. The sheriff said that four other people were inside the same home and had to be hospitalized. "What I saw was both from the structural perspective, I think our structures handled the storm very well," DeSantis said. "The problem is that the storm knocked over a lot of trees."State officials confirmed two storm-related deaths. One person in Escambia County was killed when a tree fell on a home. Another person died after operating a generator inside a garage, highlighting ongoing safety concerns as residents cope with power outages.Emergency crews have completed roughly 180 missions through the Florida Division of Emergency Management, according to the governor. State officials said nearly 10,000 power accounts have already been restored, but approximately 430,000 customers remained without electricity Saturday morning. About 325,000 of those outages are within Florida Power & Light's service area.Officials said debris removal remains one of the biggest challenges slowing restoration efforts."The folks have been out since daylight," DeSantis said. "Some of it is that you've got to get the debris out of the way before the linemen can connect it."The Florida Department of Transportation began clearing roads and bridges before sunrise, while the Florida Highway Patrol has completed dozens of debris-clearing missions. State officials said 85 traffic signals have been restored using generators.Northwest Florida Beaches International Airport has reopened to commercial air traffic, while airports in Pensacola and Fort Walton Beach remained closed Saturday but were expected to resume operations soon.Florida Division of Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said more than 16,000 utility workers have been mobilized to restore power throughout the region.Perdue also warned residents that flooding risks remain even after the storm's passage. Several rivers, including the Shoal River in Okaloosa County, are still rising and are not expected to crest for several days."We want to make sure we keep enough resources on hand in case search and rescue is needed," Perdue said.State leaders urged residents to avoid flooded roads and standing water, warning that even shallow water can quickly become dangerous.Meanwhile, Attorney General James Uthmeier said a small number of price-gouging complaints had already been reported. Residents who believe businesses are overcharging for essentials such as fuel, food or other emergency supplies are encouraged to file complaints through the attorney general's office.Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia also warned residents about post-storm scams, including unlicensed contractors and fraudulent roofers targeting homeowners.Officials urged residents not to sign contracts or provide deposits before verifying a contractor's credentials. The state also plans to establish insurance assistance hubs in impacted areas within the next 48 hours to help residents file claims and meet with insurance representatives.Businesses affected by the storm can report damage through the state's business damage assessment survey at FloridaDisaster.biz. State officials said the information will help expedite recovery assistance and assess losses.DeSantis said recovery efforts will continue across the Panhandle, where damage stretches from the Alabama state line to the eastern Panhandle.The governor cautioned that additional flooding could develop in the coming days as rivers continue rising but said Florida has water rescue teams and emergency assets positioned throughout the region."We're going to get through this," DeSantis said. "There's damage, and that's going to be difficult for people whose property was damaged, but I also feel like this is very surmountable for us if we all just work together and get the job done."

A first-of-its-kind program is coming to Boynton Beach High School. Martin County’s contracted transit provider walked away from its agreement Thursday, halting all MARTY bus service and laying off 29 employees with no warning to riders or county leaders. Martin County issued an official statement acknowledging the disruption and pledging to work toward a solution. “Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders,” Martin County officials said in the statement. Martin County Transit, the company contracted to operate the MARTY system, blamed rising operating costs for the decision. In a statement, CEO Karen Deigl said, “we entered this contract in good faith and made every effort to find a path forward. We understand how important MARTY is to its riders and the community, and this decision was not made lightly.” Martin County Transit also acknowledged the abruptness of the shutdown. “We understand that this news may feel sudden to riders and residents. As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system,” Martin County Transit said. In an afternoon press conference, county leaders explained they were in negotiations after the vendor asked for a significant increase in the cost of the contract. Two weeks ago, the company gave notice it planned to leave in 180 days and instead, it walked away Thursday, according to the county. Jim Gordon, Martin County’s Public Works Director, said the county had no warning the cancellation was coming. “We were not given advanced notice that they were going to cancel service today,” Gordon said. For Joe, a 67-year-old veteran and Martin County resident, losing MARTY service means losing his lifeline. Joe sat at the bus stop Thursday expecting his regular pickup, but no buses came. He relies on the transit system daily. “[I use it] to go to work sometimes and to go down to the homeless place, the church that feeds us food,” Joe said. Joe said he received no notice before service was cut. “No warning at all, nothing, zero.” Joe said. Physical limitations make alternative transportation all but impossible for Joe. “I’ve had two broken necks, three broken backs, I can’t feel my feet, so I’m not getting anywhere,” Joe said. Tony Argudo, a Martin County resident, said the transit company’s handling of the shutdown lacked transparency. “I don’t think letting people go first thing this morning was a good idea. There should have been more transparency and the people should have had some kind of notice so they could have made other plans,” Argudo said. George Stokus, Martin County’s Assistant County Administrator, said county officials are working urgently to restore service. “We’re doing everything we can humanly due to restore service as soon as we can,” George Stokus said. In the meantime, the United Way of Martin County is stepping in through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents for trips to work, grocery stores, medical appointments and other essential services. The organization said it was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption and is now anticipating even greater need. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County, emphasized the critical importance of transportation access for those who depend on it. “Transportation isn’t a luxury for the people who depend on it. It’s how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table. When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn’t disappear with it,” Houwaart-Diez said. Region Martin County Houwaart-Diez said the United Way is committed to being there for riders during the disruption. “This is important for people to be able to get to the doctor’s, to get to wherever they need to go so we want to be there,” Houwaart-Diez said. Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support the Ride United program’s response, alongside a contribution from another donor. Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. However, United Way emphasized that the program cannot fully replace MARTY’s fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its response is only a temporary solution dependent on available funding. Martin County said it will continue providing updates as it works to restore public transit service. Information about MARTY can be found on the county’s transit website . Residents seeking transportation assistance can call the United Way of Martin County at 772-283-4800 or click here to visit their website. A Martin County employee is being praised for her quick actions after rescuing a girl from drowning at Bob Graham Beach in Stuart on Thursday afternoon. Amy Offenbach, who came to the beach to surf, said the day took an unexpected turn. "It was just by chance that we were here and thank God that we were at the right time," Offenbach said. Offenbach, who has years of lifeguard training, said her instincts kicked in when she saw three girls struggling in the water. "I took off my clothes, grabbed the board, and started paddling," she said. "I immediately went into rescue mode." Authorities said one of the girls was choking on water, and the beach had no lifeguards on duty. Offenbach rushed in to help, using a surfboard to stabilize the girl. "Once she was on the board, she was kind of limp. Her body wasn't doing anything else," Offenbach said. Offenbach said the girl's forehead felt cold, prompting her to rush the child to the nearest lifeguard stand down the road. The girl was then taken to the hospital with minor drowning injuries. "I'm just really thankful that her parents have their child," Offenbach said. Offenbach, a Martin County employee, said she doesn’t feel the need for recognition. While some are calling her a hero, Offenbach said she was simply acting on her instincts as a mother. "I have a 14-year-old son myself, and I can't imagine him not coming back from hanging out at the beach with his friends," she said. The incident serves as a reminder to exercise caution at the beach, especially in areas without lifeguards. Deputies digging through a rain-soaked backyard in Martin County heard the cries of kittens buried up to 3 feet underground, leading to the rescue of two animals while two others were found dead, the sheriff revealed Friday. During a news conference, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek provided new details about the arrest of 36-year-old Alba Chavez, who is accused of killing two kittens and burying two others alive at a mobile home park in Hobe Sound. According to the sheriff's office, deputies responded to the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park on Thursday night after several minors inside the home called 911 to report that Chavez had allegedly killed two kittens Monday, placed them in the trash and later buried them in the backyard. The children, who feared for the safety of three remaining kittens, attempted to protect them by locking them inside a bedroom before leaving for dinner Thursday night. Budensiek said that when the children returned home, they discovered the bedroom door had been forced open and the kittens were missing. The children then called law enforcement to report the incident. When deputies arrived, Chavez was standing in the roadway and reportedly admitted to killing the two kittens. While speaking with deputies, Chavez said she believed the kittens had demons, described them as ugly and said she did not want black or brown cats inside the home. Chavez then led deputies to the backyard, where the kittens had allegedly been buried. "She took them to the backyard where our deputies started digging frantically trying to recover what they believed to be three live kittens and two dead kittens," Budensiek said. See also: Hurricane Isaias strengthens into major Category 3 storm near Florida Panhandle As deputies dug through the backyard, they heard cries coming from underground. Two kittens were recovered alive, while the two kittens Chavez allegedly killed Monday were found dead. A fifth kitten remains missing despite repeated searches of the property. Budensiek said the two surviving kittens were immediately taken to an emergency veterinary facility, where they were being treated for dehydration. The sheriff said veterinarians were also concerned about possible injuries caused by a lack of oxygen while the kittens were buried. Despite being rescued, the kittens could still die from their injuries. Chavez was arrested and charged with four counts of animal torture involving pain, serious injury or death, according to the sheriff's office. The four charges correspond to the two kittens found dead and the two rescued alive. The sheriff said Chavez was being held without bond at the Martin County Jail and also had an immigration hold. Investigators have not determined exactly how the first two kittens died. The sheriff said Chavez initially cooperated with deputies and led them to the burial site but later stopped answering questions about how the animals were killed. Authorities also have not determined her motive. Budensiek said deputies had previously responded to calls involving Chavez's mental health but had received no prior animal cruelty complaints at the residence. Additional charges could be filed if the fifth kitten is found dead, according to the sheriff. Following the incident, the Florida Department of Children and Families became involved, and the children were later released to their father, who lives locally. Officials said resources were available to help the children cope with what happened.

Dog lovers from across South Florida are heading to Fort Pierce this weekend for the Treasure Coast Kennel Club’s Pirate Cluster, a four-day event featuring dock diving, FastCAT racing, agility, frisbee competitions, and other canine sports. The event is taking place Oct. Lucie County Fairgrounds, where visitors can watch trained canine athletes compete or give their own dogs an opportunity to try several activities. According to Treasure Coast Kennel Club President Lisa Root, many of the events offer same-day participation. “It has to do with all kinds of sporting events that we do with our dogs, so dock diving, FastCAT, agility, UpDog (frisbee catching). The Pirate Cluster features activities for beginners and experienced competitors alike. Visitors can watch dogs leap into a pool during dock-diving competitions, sprint down a FastCAT course while chasing a lure, navigate agility obstacles, and participate in frisbee events. Root said the event is designed to be welcoming for both dog owners and spectators. “It’s a really family day. Admission and parking are free for spectators. Fees apply for participants entering dogs into individual events. One of the most popular attractions is dock diving, where dogs run down a platform and launch themselves into a pool in pursuit of a toy. Competitors say many dogs recognize the venue before they even leave the vehicle. “Once they start competing, they know what this dock means,” said dock-diving participant Janet. “You’ll see them when they start coming in. They just roll past the dock, and they’ll start barking in the cars and stuff because they know that they get to get up here and just jump.” Organizers say the excitement surrounding dock diving often becomes contagious for owners and spectators alike. In addition to the sporting events, the Pirate Cluster includes vendors, raffles and opportunities for families to spend time with fellow dog lovers. The event highlights the growing popularity of dog sports as a way for owners to stay active, build stronger relationships with their pets and connect with others in the community. Whether someone owns a highly trained competitor or simply wants to learn more about canine activities, organizers say the weekend provides an opportunity to see what these sports are all about. A new ammunition manufacturing facility in Indiantown is bringing additional manufacturing activity and planned job growth to Martin County as the Treasure Coast continues to contend with unemployment rates above the statewide average.Ikonick Energetics recently expanded its operations into Indiantown, opening a primer manufacturing facility that is part of the company’s broader ammunition production operation in Martin County.Richard Rhatigan, vice president of law enforcement and government sales at Ikonick USA, said the facility has significant production capacity.“At full capacity you're looking at a billion primers per year,” said Rhatigan.Primers are a small part of the larger puzzle in manufacturing ammunition. “It is one of the four components that go into building ammunition, so the primer actually ignites the powder which is incased within the brass,” said Rhatigan.While cameras were not permitted inside the primer manufacturing facility, Ikonick provided a look at its ammunition manufacturing operation in Stuart.At the Stuart facility, workers combine the primer, brass casing and projectile to produce finished ammunition.With the addition of the Indiantown facility, the company says about 75% of each piece of ammunition is now produced in Martin County.Ikonick also plans to hire over 100 additional employees across its two locations. The positions are expected to include both entry-level and more specialized manufacturing jobs.“When you talk about American manufacturing what that really means is, the people who work in our facilities, they live in our community,” said Rhatigan.The company says the expansion reflects the potential for additional manufacturing growth in the area.“The opportunity for expansion is here and it is part of supporting the community in Martin County,” said Rhatigan.The Indiantown Chamber of Commerce said the new facility represents a significant investment in advanced manufacturing for the region.The company also says its Martin County operations will help meet ammunition needs for law enforcement training.“We can support the state and local law enforcement training needs with our ammo with our facility in Stuart and here in Indiantown,” said Rhatigan.The expansion comes as Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties report unemployment rates above the statewide average, according to the latest unemployment data.For Indiantown, the facility represents another addition to the community’s manufacturing sector and could provide new employment opportunities as Ikonick continues to expand its operations.Portions of this story were assisted by artificial intelligence tools and reviewed by a WPTV journalists to ensure accuracy, clarity, and adherence to editorial standards.

A proposed 150-unit assisted-living facility in Port St. Lucie is moving through the development process as nearby residents question whether enough is known about the environmental history of a neighboring property with petroleum contamination. The project, known as PSL Westmoreland ALF , is planned for 7.1 acres within the Rivella planned unit development, along Southeast Morningside Boulevard near Southeast Westmoreland Boulevard. The three-story facility would include assisted-living units and a memory care component. Lucie City Council approved the project’s major site plan on Sept. Construction has not begun, and the developer must still submit construction plans for technical review and additional agency reviews. A group of residents opposes the project, citing concerns about the neighboring property’s contamination history and the potential implications for people who could eventually live at the facility. See also: 'It's not safe': Treasure Coast neighbors raise concerns after teen hit walking to school It’s not about what is being built there, resident David Lipps said, arguing that nearby businesses and other facilities could also be affected by environmental concerns. Resident Charlie D’Agata said residents have raised objections at City Council meetings for about two years. He questioned why a developer would be allowed to build near a property he described as contaminated. Residents say they have contacted outside organizations, including the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Florida Department of Health , in an effort to get answers about the site. An engineering letter provides some context for their concerns. In a letter discussing a March 2026 meeting with environmental officials about the neighboring property, BTEX Engineering said the proposed remediation approach should be changed because of concerns about surrounding properties, including the planned assisted-living facility. The letter said vapors would need to be captured during remediation. The environmental history of the neighboring property and the extent of any potential impact on surrounding land remain central questions for residents seeking more information. The city has approved the major site plan, but the project must clear additional steps before construction can begin. The developer is expected to submit construction plans for technical review, followed by reviews involving the South Florida Water Management District and other agencies. Residents say they want clearer answers about the neighboring property’s environmental history and how any potential risks would be addressed as the project advances

Martin County’s contracted transit provider walked away from its agreement Thursday, halting all MARTY bus service and laying off 29 employees with no warning to riders or county leaders. Martin County issued an official statement acknowledging the disruption and pledging to work toward a solution. “Martin County is actively working to identify solutions to restore transit service as quickly as possible and minimize the impact on our riders,” Martin County officials said in the statement. Martin County Transit, the company contracted to operate the MARTY system, blamed rising operating costs for the decision. In a statement, CEO Karen Deigl said, “we entered this contract in good faith and made every effort to find a path forward. We understand how important MARTY is to its riders and the community, and this decision was not made lightly.” Martin County Transit also acknowledged the abruptness of the shutdown. “We understand that this news may feel sudden to riders and residents. As strong advocates for reliable public transportation, we are disappointed that we are unable to continue to operate the MARTY system,” Martin County Transit said. In an afternoon press conference, county leaders explained they were in negotiations after the vendor asked for a significant increase in the cost of the contract. Two weeks ago, the company gave notice it planned to leave in 180 days and instead, it walked away Thursday, according to the county. Jim Gordon, Martin County’s Public Works Director, said the county had no warning the cancellation was coming. “We were not given advanced notice that they were going to cancel service today,” Gordon said. For Joe, a 67-year-old veteran and Martin County resident, losing MARTY service means losing his lifeline. Joe sat at the bus stop Thursday expecting his regular pickup, but no buses came. He relies on the transit system daily. “[I use it] to go to work sometimes and to go down to the homeless place, the church that feeds us food,” Joe said. Joe said he received no notice before service was cut. “No warning at all, nothing, zero.” Joe said. Physical limitations make alternative transportation all but impossible for Joe. “I’ve had two broken necks, three broken backs, I can’t feel my feet, so I’m not getting anywhere,” Joe said. Tony Argudo, a Martin County resident, said the transit company’s handling of the shutdown lacked transparency. “I don’t think letting people go first thing this morning was a good idea. There should have been more transparency and the people should have had some kind of notice so they could have made other plans,” Argudo said. George Stokus, Martin County’s Assistant County Administrator, said county officials are working urgently to restore service. “We’re doing everything we can humanly due to restore service as soon as we can,” George Stokus said. In the meantime, the United Way of Martin County is stepping in through its Ride United program, which provides free, pre-scheduled Lyft rides to eligible residents for trips to work, grocery stores, medical appointments and other essential services. The organization said it was already facing financial challenges due to increased demand and other funding reductions before the MARTY service interruption and is now anticipating even greater need. Houwaart-Diez, president and CEO of United Way of Martin County, emphasized the critical importance of transportation access for those who depend on it. “Transportation isn’t a luxury for the people who depend on it. It’s how they get to work, receive medical care and put food on the table. When a critical service like this disappears, the need doesn’t disappear with it,” Houwaart-Diez said. Region Martin County Houwaart-Diez said the United Way is committed to being there for riders during the disruption. “This is important for people to be able to get to the doctor’s, to get to wherever they need to go so we want to be there,” Houwaart-Diez said. Ashley Capital has committed an initial $2,500 donation to help support the Ride United program’s response, alongside a contribution from another donor. Since launching in September 2022, Ride United has provided thousands of rides for Martin County residents facing transportation barriers. However, United Way emphasized that the program cannot fully replace MARTY’s fixed-route bus and paratransit services and that its response is only a temporary solution dependent on available funding. Martin County said it will continue providing updates as it works to restore public transit service. Information about MARTY can be found on the county’s transit website . Residents seeking transportation assistance can call the United Way of Martin County at 772-283-4800 or click here to visit their website. Residents seeking paratransit transportation assistance can call 772-463-2822. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Lucie County Fire District has hit a snag in its effort to create a new policy for handling complaints against its own top leaders as fallout continues from a controversial hazing investigation. During a Fire District Board workshop Wednesday morning, board members had hoped to hear from outside law firms about helping draft a new complaint policy.WATCH BELOW: Fire district's new complaint policy effort stalls amid hazing falloutInstead, St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said one of the law firms contacted never returned her calls, while another disclosed a potential conflict of interest."I appreciated her honesty and forthrightness on that issue," Fowler said of the attorney during the meeting. "That being said, she did provide two references, both on the West Coast." The board discussed now reaching out to additional law firms in hopes of securing outside legal help ahead of its next meeting Oct. 21."I think we'd be doing ourselves an injustice if we at least we don't have a courtesy conversation with these other firms, so that we're at least prepared just in case these two firms aren't available, non-responsive," Board Member and Fort Pierce City Commissioner Curtis Johnson said. "I think we all have some sense of urgency of getting this thing closed, and and I don't want to delay any further." The effort follows a heated special board meeting Sept. 30, when members publicly acknowledged what they described as a significant gap in district policy: There is no clear process for independently handling complaints made against some of the district's own contract employees. "Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," Fowler said during that meeting. "They — being those positions — have essentially been able to investigate themselves."Those positions include the fire chief, district attorney, clerk treasurer and medical director.The issue came under increased scrutiny amid fallout from a hazing investigation involving three veteran firefighters.A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing.Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result.Hutchinson and Boudrias previously told WPTV they did not consider the conduct hazing and said there was no intent to hurt anyone."It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said."We're all still friends," Boudrias said. "Us and the victims, there was no ill intent."The controversy has also raised questions about how complaints involving district leadership have been handled.Months before the hazing incident came to light, Baldwin and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and then-District Attorney Kim Sabol in September 2025. District officials ultimately denied it. Baldwin and Hutchinson later filed additional complaints, including an amended complaint to investigators alleging the hazing investigation and their subsequent terminations were part of a broader pattern of retaliation. Lucie County Fire District told WPTV it is not currently in receipt of any official retaliation complaint from any party involved in this matter."That's not a good process," Fowler previously told WPTV.Sabol submitted her notice of retirement Sept. 30, just minutes after the special board meeting, effective 90 days from her notice. The District stated she will continue to provide services during that 90-day period. Lee previously acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process and told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey that he welcomed outside scrutiny."I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," Lee said, adding that he "welcomes any investigation from any agency."Lee also defended Sabol following her notice of retirement, calling it a "sad day" and saying she had been a "tremendous attorney for the district."Meanwhile, firefighters have been casting ballots in a union vote of no confidence in Lee."It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler previously said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message."Lee previously said he would wait for the results before commenting further on the vote."We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee said. "I came up on the labor side; I've always fought for our men and women on the line."The union is also continuing its legal fight to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin.During the Sept. 30 meeting, Fowler questioned whether the fire board itself may have the authority to bring the three firefighters back rather than waiting for the arbitration process to play out."I think we might actually," Fowler said at the time.Board members are expected to continue searching for an outside law firm to help develop the new policy before the Fire District Board meets again Oct.

Family, friends, teachers and classmates gathered at Farm Flame in Vero Beach on Wednesday to remember 17-year-old Sulliman “Sulli” Bah, who was fatally shot during a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp last week, according to the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office. No arrests have been made, and investigators are examining whether the shooting may have involved self-defense. The celebration of life was held at the Vero Beach restaurant where Bah worked. Through tears and memories, those who knew him described the Sebastian River High School student as kind, funny, hardworking and someone who could light up a room. As rain poured down Wednesday evening, flowers, candles and photographs filled Farm Flame while people who knew Bah stood together to honor his life. Isaac Rodriguez, who knew Bah, said Bah made an impact on everyone around him. “He touched everybody’s heart and he was just really kind and he always lit up the room,” Rodriguez said. Bah’s close friends told WPTV he was focused on his future and enjoyed spending time with the people closest to him. Alex Cortez said he and Bah boxed together, spent time together and shared many memories. “He was a very positive guy. He was always about working, he was intelligent, he had a big future,” Cortez said. Friend Xavi Espinosa remembered Bah as someone who could immediately make others feel welcome. “Even when I first met him, I felt he was such a good soul,” Espinosa said. The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office said Bah was at a meetup at Garcia Boat Ramp on Friday when shots were fired. The sheriff’s office said investigators are looking into whether the shooting was self-defense . No arrests have been made. Bah’s mother, Chelynn Godfrey, described her son as a loving and caring teenager who had his entire life ahead of him. She said she wants investigators to consider all the facts as they determine what happened. “I just ask that law enforcement truly looks at the big picture. I just want them to really look at the facts and I hope that they get this right,” Godfrey said. “I hope his shooter is arrested and I hope he goes to jail.” During the celebration, people took turns sharing memories of Bah and the impact he had on their lives. Angela Sanders, one of Bah’s former sixth grade teachers, remembered his personality and smile. “His personality is amazing, his smile lit up a room,” Sanders said. Myan Agosto said Bah was the type of friend who regularly checked on the people around him. “He never failed to make sure everybody was okay,” Agosto said. “He was just a really good friend.” Another friend, Zani Zoutten, remembered spending time with Bah during sixth period and described him as a happy person. The memories shared Wednesday showed how many people Bah touched during his 17 years. “He may not have lived so many years in this room, but the days he made on this earth — look at this room,” another speaker said during the celebration. Bah’s funeral is scheduled for Saturday.

A Hobe Sound woman is facing multiple animal cruelty charges after deputies say she killed and buried several kittens because she believed they were possessed by demons.The Martin County Sheriff's Office (MCSO) arrested 36-year-old Alba Chavez on Thursday after responding to reports of animal cruelty at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park.WATCH BELOW: Woman buried cats alive, thought they were demons, deputies sayAccording to MCSO Sheriff John Budensiek, three youths living in the home called 911 after they discovered several of their kittens had disappeared. The children told deputies they believed Chavez had killed two kittens earlier in the week and were worried about the remaining animals.Budensiek said the children had attempted to protect three kittens by locking them inside a bedroom before going out to dinner Thursday evening. When they returned, they found the door had been forced open, and the kittens were gone."When deputies arrived, she admitted she thought the kittens had demons and said she didn't want black cats or brown cats in her residence," Budensiek said during a Friday news conference.Investigators said Chavez told deputies she had killed two kittens on Monday, thrown them into the trash, later removed them and buried them in the backyard.Deputies said she then led them to a burial site behind the home and told them to bring gloves, shovels and bags if they wanted to find the missing kittens.Despite heavy rain and lightning, deputies began digging in the backyard."As they were digging, they could hear cries from the kittens," Budensiek said.Deputies rescued two kittens that were buried alive inside a plastic Publix bag. The two kittens killed earlier in the week were also recovered deceased from the burial site.A fifth kitten remains missing. Budensiek said deputies and investigators extensively searched the backyard and mobile home but have not located the animal.The two surviving kittens were rushed to a veterinary emergency clinic, where they are being treated for dehydration and monitored for potential long-term effects from being buried underground."If they survive, they'll eventually be taken to the Humane Society and go through the adoption process," Budensiek said.Chavez was arrested on four counts of animal cruelty involving torture, inflicting pain, serious injury or death to an animal. Authorities said additional charges could follow if the missing kitten is found dead.The arrest marks at least the third animal cruelty or neglect case in Martin County since late July. Lucie County jury convicted former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms of official misconduct Thursday, finding he improperly obstructed, delayed or prevented information about a possible felony involving the city from being communicated. Jurors found Mimms not guilty of bid tampering, the first count he faced. But they found him guilty on the official-misconduct count and specifically determined the misconduct involved obstructing, delaying or preventing communication of information related to a possible felony that directly involved or affected the government entity he served. The verdict followed a trial that began Sept. 29 and centered on allegations that Mimms improperly influenced the city’s bidding process for two vacant Lincoln Park-area lots. Prosecutors alleged Mimms steered the process toward Lincoln Park Young Professionals , a nonprofit whose board included his niece and another city employee. The organization sought a lease involving the properties, near the Lincoln Theater. During trial, FDLE Agent Derek Brisky testified about emails, city records and the request-for-proposals process. Prosecutors pointed to communications showing Mimms continued to discuss the RFP’s evaluation criteria and committee after the matter had been referred to the city’s purchasing department. The defense argued the purchasing department controlled the RFP’s publication and administration, and challenged the state’s claim that the process amounted to an improper sole-source arrangement. See also: 4 people arrested after drugs, 26 firearms found at North Palm Beach home Court records show Circuit Judge Michael James Linn denied the state’s request to have Mimms taken into custody pending sentencing. Mimms was allowed to remain free on bond. Sentencing is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Lucie County Circuit Court.

A Martin County employee helped rescue three girls who were struggling in a rip current Thursday afternoon at Bob Graham Beach near Jensen Beach. Amy Offenbach said she arrived at the beach around 2 p.m. to surf when she noticed three girls about 25 yards offshore holding onto the same surfboard. Watch report: Offenbach, who works in Martin County's Growth and Development Department and is an avid surfer, said something about the situation immediately caught her attention. "The ocean could be very gentle and calm, but it can also be very heavy and crash very hard," Offenbach said. Offenbach said she became concerned when one of the girls appeared distressed. "By that time the girls were waving in the water like they needed help, so immediately I just went into rescue mode," Offenbach said. Offenbach and a friend went into the water and paddled toward the girls. When Offenbach reached the group, she said one of the girls appeared to be in serious distress. "I looked at her, and she seemed kind of dazed and confused," Offenbach said. "I said, 'Get up on the board.'" Offenbach said she gave the surfboard she was riding to two of the girls and instructed them to hold on and kick toward shore. She then placed the third girl on her soft-top surfboard and paddled her back to the beach. Offenbach said she has some lifeguard training and quickly recognized the girl needed medical attention after they returned to shore. "The girl that I rescued said that she blacked out under the water," Offenbach said. "She inhaled water, and she had a severe headache." Because Bob Graham Beach is unguarded, Offenbach said she drove the girl to a nearby lifeguard station, where an ambulance was called. "I'm just really happy that I was in the right place at the right time," Offenbach said. Offenbach said she has not been able to reconnect with the girl she rescued or learn more about her condition. Hurricane Isaias became the first hurricane to make direct landfall in the United States in more than two years when it came ashore late Friday as a Category 2 storm.By Saturday morning, Isaias had weakened into a post-tropical cyclone as it moved across Alabama. While no longer a hurricane, its remnants were expected to bring heavy rain and gusty winds across parts of the South on Saturday before spreading into the Great Lakes and Northeast on Sunday.As of 2 p.m. CT Saturday, more than 700,000 customers were without power. More than 400,000 outages were reported in Florida's Panhandle, while Alabama reported more than 180,000 outages and Georgia reported about 40,000.At its peak, nearly 900,000 customers were without power. The storm also caused significant wind damage in the Pensacola area, where a hotel lost its roof as Isaias made landfall.RELATED STORY | Study: Super-sized El Niño could cause more than 450,000 heat deaths by FebruaryThe hurricane pushed storm surge onto coastal roadways across the Florida Panhandle.Escambia County Sheriff Chip W. Simmons confirmed one person died during the storm. He added that some roads were impassable due to downed trees and power lines. Away from the coast, a death was reported in Birmingham, Alabama, due to a fallen tree limb. Isaias marked a departure from what had been one of the quietest Atlantic hurricane seasons in recent years. It was also the first hurricane to form in the Atlantic basin in 2026.Forecasters had predicted a below-normal season because of a strong El Niño, which typically creates upper-level winds that can disrupt tropical cyclone development.Although Isaias was the ninth named storm of the season, all previous systems had peaked at tropical-storm strength.The same upper-level winds that limited hurricane activity this year also contributed to Isaias weakening before landfall. The storm maintained Category 3 strength for much of Friday before being downgraded to a Category 2 hurricane just hours before reaching the coast.RELATED STORY | El Nino keeps Atlantic hurricane season historically calmBehind Isaias, the National Hurricane Center said it was not tracking any additional systems. The Atlantic hurricane season typically peaks around Sept. 10 and begins to wind down by mid-October before ending Nov. 30.Since 2013, only two hurricanes have made U.S. The most recent was Hurricane Nicole in 2022.

Ron DeSantis said Saturday morning that nearly 450,000 utility customers remained without power across Northwest Florida after Hurricane Isaias made landfall in the Panhandle. Speaking from Destin later in the day, he confirmed there were two storm-related deaths in Escambia County.The governor said Isaias came ashore near Destin at 9:30 p.m. Friday as a Category 2 hurricane with sustained winds of about 105 mph. Wind gusts reached as high as 116 mph near Santa Rosa Sound, while storm surge pushed water levels approximately 5.5 feet above normal in some areas.WATCH BELOW: Santa Rosa County among hardest hit counties, DeSantis saysAlthough the storm has since weakened into a post-tropical cyclone and moved out of Florida, DeSantis warned that flooding remains a concern, particularly in parts of the Panhandle and Big Bend expected to receive 4 to 8 inches of rain through the weekend."As of now there have been no confirmed fatalities," DeSantis said, noting reports of a possible death in Escambia County linked to a fallen tree had not yet been confirmed by the state.State officials said more than 16,000 linemen were staged ahead of the storm and began restoration efforts as early as 3 a.m. Saturday.By 7 a.m., approximately 448,000 customer accounts were without electricity statewide, including about 323,000 Florida Power & Light customers and roughly 110,000 customers served by electric cooperatives.Some of the hardest-hit counties included Santa Rosa County, where about 90% of customers were without power, Holmes County at 89%, Washington County at 86%, Walton County at 85%, Escambia County at 75% and Okaloosa County at 53%, according to the governor.The Florida Department of Transportation and Florida Highway Patrol launched overnight "cut and toss" operations to clear roads of fallen trees and debris. Officials said all state-owned bridges had been inspected and reopened by 6 a.m. 98, two major transportation corridors in the region, were also reopened.Northwest Florida Beaches International Airport resumed commercial operations Saturday morning, while Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport and Pensacola International Airport remained closed.Despite the storm's impacts, state emergency officials said they had not received any requests for large-scale search and rescue deployments.Florida Division of Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said state teams remain on standby as flood risks continue."We are going to keep search and rescue teams ready to go," Perdue said. "There could be continued flooding from all of the rainfall."Officials urged residents to avoid driving through flooded roadways, stay clear of downed power lines and limit unnecessary travel while utility crews and emergency workers continue recovery efforts.Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier also warned residents to watch for scams in the aftermath of the storm, including reports of fraudulent text messages offering tree-removal services and unlicensed contractors seeking repair work.State officials said damage assessments are underway and will help determine whether Florida qualifies for additional federal disaster aid beyond the pre-landfall emergency declaration already approved by FEMA.DeSantis said he planned to visit storm-damaged areas in the Panhandle later Saturday, including parts of Okaloosa County, to assess conditions and meet with local officials."We were ready for the worst," DeSantis said. "We'll get everything back up and running and let people go on with their lives as soon as possible."

Julie Wallace Thomas of Delray Beach has been part of the WPTV First Alert Weather Spotters program since it began and a recent visit to the WPTV newsroom gave her a new appreciation for the role she plays.WATCH BELOW:I connected with Thomas and gave her a tour of the station to learn more about what brought her to the team.During the visit, Thomas learned that Weather Spotters have direct communication with the weather service and that their observations actively help the weather service do its job. She said finding that out was a turning point."I didn't know that," she said. "Knowing this now knows that helps me to understand that I can make a difference in other people's lives to confirm that there was a tornado in my neighborhood that it could make a difference means a lot to me." Her passion for weather stretches back to her childhood."I've always loved the weather ever since a kid in science class when they're teaching us about the different kinds of clouds," Thomas said. "More recently, to be able to see on the radar what the weather is coming up."As a spotter, Thomas has captured many memorable moments, from sunsets to stunning rainbow shots."The sunset shots, the rainbow shots. Our church goes out to Anchor Park in Delray for a beach baptism, and as my husband, the pastor of our church, took this man's wife out into the waters to baptize her, we were rewarded with this brilliant double rainbow," she said. "So, I got some great pictures."Weather Spotters play an important role in the community no matter what weather is headed our way.

Deputies digging through a rain-soaked backyard in Martin County heard the cries of kittens buried up to 3 feet underground, leading to the rescue of two animals while two others were found dead, the sheriff revealed Friday. During a news conference, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek provided new details about the arrest of 36-year-old Alba Chavez, who is accused of killing two kittens and burying two others alive at a mobile home park in Hobe Sound. According to the sheriff's office, deputies responded to the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park on Thursday night after several minors inside the home called 911 to report that Chavez had allegedly killed two kittens Monday, placed them in the trash and later buried them in the backyard. The children, who feared for the safety of three remaining kittens, attempted to protect them by locking them inside a bedroom before leaving for dinner Thursday night. Budensiek said that when the children returned home, they discovered the bedroom door had been forced open and the kittens were missing. The children then called law enforcement to report the incident. When deputies arrived, Chavez was standing in the roadway and reportedly admitted to killing the two kittens. While speaking with deputies, Chavez said she believed the kittens had demons, described them as ugly and said she did not want black or brown cats inside the home. Chavez then led deputies to the backyard, where the kittens had allegedly been buried. "She took them to the backyard where our deputies started digging frantically trying to recover what they believed to be three live kittens and two dead kittens," Budensiek said. See also: Hurricane Isaias strengthens into major Category 3 storm near Florida Panhandle As deputies dug through the backyard, they heard cries coming from underground. Two kittens were recovered alive, while the two kittens Chavez allegedly killed Monday were found dead. A fifth kitten remains missing despite repeated searches of the property. Budensiek said the two surviving kittens were immediately taken to an emergency veterinary facility, where they were being treated for dehydration. The sheriff said veterinarians were also concerned about possible injuries caused by a lack of oxygen while the kittens were buried. Despite being rescued, the kittens could still die from their injuries. Chavez was arrested and charged with four counts of animal torture involving pain, serious injury or death, according to the sheriff's office. The four charges correspond to the two kittens found dead and the two rescued alive. The sheriff said Chavez was being held without bond at the Martin County Jail and also had an immigration hold. Investigators have not determined exactly how the first two kittens died. The sheriff said Chavez initially cooperated with deputies and led them to the burial site but later stopped answering questions about how the animals were killed. Authorities also have not determined her motive. Budensiek said deputies had previously responded to calls involving Chavez's mental health but had received no prior animal cruelty complaints at the residence. Additional charges could be filed if the fifth kitten is found dead, according to the sheriff. Following the incident, the Florida Department of Children and Families became involved, and the children were later released to their father, who lives locally. Officials said resources were available to help the children cope with what happened.

The Soup Kitchen in Boynton Beach is seeing a surge in demand, with need up about 25% as residents struggle with rising gas prices, medical bills, and other monthly expenses.Marlene Mejia, CEO and executive director of The Soup Kitchen, said the need is increasing."I would say it's about 25% higher need," she said.People are telling the kitchen that tough times are getting tougher."They're telling us that the gas prices are killing them, that medication and the bills that they have to pay at the end of the month, it's not enough," Mejia said. "So, that's why we're coming in and filling in the gap." The Soup Kitchen is filling in the gap for every walk of life, including employed residents, who have homes and cars but are still not making ends meet at the end of the month."You can see people from all over and we call them the household person, which is asset limited income constrained," Mejia said. "But they're employed, so they have cars, they may have a house, they may have an apartment, and it's just not adding up at the end of the month." Yolanda Marcellus was among the dozens of people standing in a long line and walking through The Soup Kitchen for food."I just come here. They have good food every day. So, I'm thank God I'm here," Marcellus said.The kitchen is able to distribute hundreds of pounds of food every day through faithful volunteers, like Mary Webb."You just feel good helping out other people and it comes back to you," Webb said. "The goodness comes back to you." The Soup Kitchen is located at 8655 W. and they can be contacted at 561-732-7595.

James Talarico has been absent from the campaign trail over the past 12 days as the Texas Senate race enters a critical stretch, prompting Republicans to open a new line of attack on the Democratic nominee.At a campaign rally in San Antonio Wednesday, Texas attorney general and GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton led the crowd in a chant about his opponent’s whereabouts.“Where is James Talarico?” Paxton prompted the crowd to ask.Paxton’s campaign has also drawn attention to the topic in social media posts in recent days, and President Donald Trump has jumped into the debate on Truth Social, describing Talarico as “MISSING IN ACTION.”Talarico’s campaign said the Texas Democrat has been getting over being sick.“James looks forward to being back out this weekend after recovering from the flu,” said JT Ennis, a spokesperson for Talarico’s campaign, on Thursday. “It’s been 83 days since James challenged Ken Paxton to come out of hiding and answer Texans’ question in a debate, which even President Trump called on him to do last night. Ball is in Paxton’s court.”RELATED STORY | Trump faces hecklers while making high-profile Texas campaign pushTalarico revealed his flu diagnosis September 30 when he spoke virtually with the United States Hispanic Business Council, an event he was supposed to attend in person.“I was starting to feel kind of under the weather a few days ago and last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas, and I was diagnosed with the flu,” Talarico told the crowd gathered in Edinburg, Texas, over video conference. “I’m running a fever, and I’m at my most contagious right now, and I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail and so I want to keep everybody safe.”Talarico’s last public appearance in Texas took place on September 26 when he held a press conference on suspending the federal gas and diesel tax and ending the war with Iran.“This is the kind of immediate action we need to provide Texans some relief at the pump in the middle of this affordability crisis,” Talarico said at a gas station in Carrollton, Texas.After publication of this story, a Talarico campaign source noted the candidate attended a private fundraiser in New York City featuring actor Robert De Niro on September 28.During this time stretch, Paxton has made several campaign trail stops, including speaking at Trump’s rally in San Antonio on Wednesday. Paxton has spoken at four other campaign events, including a conversation with the USHBC, and was on hand at the president’s event in Denton. At that stop, Trump said he didn’t even know Paxton was there and jokingly called him a “pain in the ass.”In a Truth Social post Wednesday night, Trump questioned Talarico’s whereabouts and called for a debate between the two Senate candidates.“He should immediately report to a Debate Stage against Ken Paxton, who is ready, willing, and able,” Trump wrote.The Paxton campaign did not respond to a request for comment about Trump’s proposed debate between the two candidates. Talarico has challenged Paxton to several debates, including one on Fox News, but the window for debates is narrowing with Election Day less than four weeks away.Talarico will appear at a town hall hosted by CNN and Jubilee Media on Wednesday, October 14 in Fort Worth, Texas. The media outlets have also extended a town hall invitation to Paxton.The two candidates are locked in a tight battle for the US Senate seat currently occupied by GOP Sen. (CBS12) The American Red Cross assisted five people, including two children, following two house fires in Palm Beach and St. According to a news release issued Friday, Oct. 9, Red Cross Disaster Action Team volunteers responded to both fires within a 12-hour period. The fires occurred at two locations: ● Riviera Beach: A home on West 28th Street, where one adult received assistance. Lucie: A home on Northwest Carmelite Street, where four people, including two adults and two children, received assistance. Red Cross volunteers provided emergency financial assistance, health and mental health services, and recovery support to those affected. The organization’s Disaster Action Team consists of specially trained volunteers who respond to emergencies 24 hours a day, seven days a week, providing resources and support to families impacted by disasters. All Red Cross disaster assistance is provided free of charge through donations. The Red Cross did not release information about what caused either fire or the extent of the damage. Residents interested in supporting disaster relief efforts can donate at redcross.org/donate. Information about home fire safety and preparedness is available at redcross.org/homefires.

An explosion inside a Port St. Lucie home destroyed almost everything owned by a family of four. Lucie County Fire District, the initial call came in at 1:24 p.m. for a fire at a home in the 100 block of Carmelite Street Friday afternoon. Neighbors called 911 after noticing the home was on fire. "I looked, and there was all kinds of smoke going through the yard," said neighbor Rob Roadman. "I was outside in the backyard, and then I see very heavy smoke," said Marina Cheong, who lives a few doors down. Cheong said she ran toward the home to help but was stopped by the explosion. "And then there was explosion, very loud, loud explosion, and debris started flying everywhere," she said. "I heard a huge explosion. At first, I thought maybe it's a transformer or something, but it was much, much, much louder than that," Roadman said. Neighbors said the man who lives in the home told them he had been cooking when a grease fire started in the garage, where the propane tank was located. The explosion sent the propane tank flying out of the garage, across the street, and into the garage of a neighbor's home. "I thought it was an air raid. It was not a casual thing. My house shook," Roadman said. "I thought that the whole house had exploded. It was very loud," Cheong added. Roadman said he spoke to the man shortly after the explosion. "I asked the dad if he was OK, and he goes, 'Yeah.' But you could tell he wasn't. Who wouldn't be?" Roadman said. The man was briefly hospitalized but returned to the house a few hours later to join family and friends in going through the debris to see what could be salvaged. They said there wasn’t much left. However, a family member told WPBF 25 News that they consider themselves lucky that nobody was seriously injured. She said the family has a strong community and a strong church to help them persevere.
