France’s high-speed rail network was hit Friday with widespread and “criminal” acts of vandalism including arson attacks, paralyzing travel to Paris from across the rest of France and Europe only hours before the grand opening ceremony of the Olympics.French officials condemned the attacks as “criminal actions,” though they said there was no sign of a direct link to the Games, and prosecutors in Paris opened a national investigation saying the crimes could carry sentences of 15 to 20 years.As Paris authorities geared up for a spectacular parade on and along the Seine River, three fires were reported near the tracks on the high-speed lines of Atlantique, Nord and Est, causing disruptions that affected hundreds of thousands of travelers.Among them were two German athletes in showjumping who were on a train to Paris to take part in the opening ceremony but had to turn back in Belgium because of the closures, and will now miss the ceremony, German news agency dpa reported.“There was no longer a chance of making it on time,” rider Philipp Weishaupt, who was traveling with teammate Christian Kukuk, told dpa.French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal wrote on the social media platform X that France’s intelligence services have been mobilized to find the perpetrators.Attal characterized them as “acts of sabotage,” which were “prepared and coordinated.”There were no known reports of injuries.RELATED STORY | Previewing the Paris Summer Olympics: When does it start, how to watchTransport Minister Patrice Vergriete described people fleeing from the scene of fires and the discovery of incendiary devices. “Everything indicates that these are criminal fires,” he said.The incidents paralyzed several high-speed lines linking Paris to the rest of France and to neighboring countries, Vergriete said, speaking on BFM television.The French national rail company SNCF said that areas affecting rail track intersections were targeted to double the impact.“For one fire, two destinations were hit,” the company's CEO, Jean-Pierre Farandou.It was “a premeditated, calculated, coordinated attack" that indicates "a desire to seriously harm” the French people, Farandou said.The attack occurred against a backdrop of global tensions and heightened security measures as the city prepared for the 2024 Olympic Games. Many travelers were planning to converge on the capital for the opening ceremony, and many vacationers were also in transit.French authorities have foiled several plots to disrupt the Olympics, including arresting a Russian man on suspicion of planning to destabilize the games.The Paris police prefecture “concentrated its personnel in Parisian train stations” after the “massive attack” that paralyzed the TGV high-speed network, Laurent Nuñez, the Paris police chief, told France Info television.RELATED STORY | Olympic soccer gets off to violent and chaotic start as Morocco fans rush the field vs ArgentinaAlso Friday, the French airport of Basel-Mulhouse on the border with Germany and Switzerland was evacuated in the morning and remained temporarily closed “for safety reasons," the airport said. It wasn't clear whether there was a connection to the rail attacks.The disruptions hit Paris’ Montparnasse station particular hard.In the station's crowded hall, Maiwenn Labbé-Sorin said she spent hours stranded on a train before it doubled back to Paris.“We stayed two hours without water, without toilets, without electricity," she said. "Then we could go out on the track for a bit and then the train returned. Now I’m not sure what’s going to happen.”Many passengers at the Gare du Nord, one of Europe’s busiest train stations, were looking for answers and solutions on Friday morning. All eyes were on the central message boards as most services to northern France, Belgium and the United Kingdom were delayed.“It’s a hell of a way to start the Olympics,” said Sarah Moseley, 42, as she learned that her train to London was an hour late.“They should have more information for tourists, especially if it’s a malicious attack,” said Corey Grainger, a 37-year-old Australian sales manager on his way to London, as he rested on his two suitcases in the middle of the station.Sports Minister Amélie Oudéa-Castera said authorities were working to “evaluate the impact on travelers, athletes, and ensure the transport of all delegations to the competition sites” for the Olympics. Speaking on BFM television, she added, “Playing against the Games is playing against France, against your own camp, against your country.”SNCF said it did not know when traffic would resume and feared that disruptions would continue “at least all weekend.” SNCF teams “were already on site to carry out diagnostics and begin repairs,” but the “situation should last at least all weekend while the repairs are carried out,” the operator said. SNCF advised “all passengers to postpone their journey and not to go to the station,” specifying in its press release that all tickets were exchangeable and refundable.Valerie Pecresse, president of the regional council of the greater Paris region, speaking from Montparnasse station, said “250,000 travelers will be affected today on all these lines.” Substitution plans were underway, but Pecresse advised travelers “not to go to stations.”The troubles comes ahead of an opening ceremony has been planned for later Friday, in which 7,000 Olympic athletes are due to sail down the Seine past iconic Parisian monuments such as Notre-Dame Cathedral, the Louvre Museum, and the Musee d’Orsay.

Celebrating its reputation as a cradle of revolution, Paris kicked off its first Summer Olympics in a century on Friday with a rain-soaked, rule-breaking opening ceremony studded with stars and fantasy along the Seine River.On-and-off showers — the first rain at a Summer Olympics' opening ceremony in more than 70 years — did not seem to hamper the enthusiasm of the athletes. Some held umbrellas as they rode boats down the river in a showcase of the city’s resilience as authorities investigated suspected acts of sabotage targeting France's high-speed rail network.Widespread travel disruptions triggered by what French officials called coordinated arson attacks on high-speed rail lines as well as the weather had dampened the mood ahead of the ceremony.Still, crowds crammed the Seine's banks and bridges and watched from balconies, “oohing” and “aahing” as Olympic teams paraded in boats down the waterway that got increasingly choppy as the weather worsened.Undeterred from the festivities, many of the hundreds of thousands of spectators huddled under umbrellas, plastic ponchos or jackets as the rain intensified, others danced and sang, and some dashed from their seats for shelter.“The rain can't stop us,” said U.S. basketball star LeBron James, sporting a plastic poncho along with the other American flag bearer, tennis player Coco Gauff.The weather made for some bizarre scenes at the show combining prerecorded and live performances: a stiff upper-lipped pianist played on even as small puddles formed on his grand piano. A breakdancer flipped her moves on the sheen of a rain-drenched platform. Some athletes in Bermuda-style colorful shirts looked dressed for the beach, not a deluge.As global audiences tuned in, Paris put its best foot forward — quite literally, with a spectacular Olympic launch that lifted spirits and joyous French cancan dancers featured early on. A humorous short film featured soccer icon Zinedine Zidane. Plumes of French blue, white and red smoke followed.Lady Gaga sang in a prerecorded performance, in French, with dancers shaking pink plumed pompoms, injecting a cabaret feel. To close the show, Celine Dion, standing under the Eiffel Tower, belted out her first live performance since the French-Canadian singer was diagnosed with stiff person syndrome, a rare neurological disorder, at the end of 2022.French-Malian pop star Aya Nakamura, the most listened-to French-speaking artist in the world, emerged from a pyrotechnic display in an all-gold out to sing her hit “Djadja” accompanied by a Republican guard band of the French army.More than three hours into the show, French President Emmanuel Macron declared the Games open. In a gaffe shortly beforehand, the five-ring Olympic flag was raised upside down at the Trocadero across from the Eiffel Tower.The final torch relay spanned landmarks like the Louvre and included sports legends like tennis greats Serena Williams and Rafael Nadal before French judo champ Teddy Riner and three-time Olympic champion runner Marie-Jose Perec lit the Olympic cauldron attached to a giant balloon, which floated into the Paris night.The ceremony celebrated women, including 10 golden statues of female pioneers that rose from giant pedestals along the river. Among them was Olympe de Gouges, who drafted the Declaration of the Rights of Women and the Female Citizen in 1791 during the French Revolution. She campaigned for the abolition of slavery and was guillotined in 1793.The Paris Games aim to be the first with equal numbers of men and women competing.With the ambitious ceremony, the stakes for France were immense. Dozens of heads of state and government were in town, and the world was watching as Paris turned itself into a giant open-air theater. Along the Seine, iconic monuments became stages for dancers, singers and other artists.Sofia Cohen, 20, watching with her father, called the ceremony “electric.” The Nicaraguan-Americans said the roar of applause given to the Ukrainian team was their favorite part.“Every Olympics is different, and this one was very French. The ceremony started out very majestic and regal. And as the rain started pouring down and time went on, everything got a little more hectic and fun,” she said.The sprawling event gave organizers bigger crowds to transport, organize and safeguard than would have been the case if they’d followed the example of previous Olympic host cities that opened with stadium shows.Still, as the show got underway, optimism soared that Paris — true to its motto that speaks of being unsinkable — might just see its gambles pay off. That's despite the soggy weather — no other Summer Olympics opening ceremony has had rain since Helsinki in 1952.Paris organizers said 6,800 of the 10,500 athletes would attend before they embark on the next 16 days of competition.The boats carrying the Olympic teams started the parade by breaking through curtains of water that cascaded down from Austerlitz Bridge, the start of the 6-kilometer (nearly 4-mile) route. The jetting waters were a wink at the fountains of Versailles Palace, the venue for Olympic equestrian competitions.Per Olympic protocol, the first boat carried athletes from Greece, birthplace of the ancient Games. It was followed by the Olympic team of refugee athletes and then, the other nations in French alphabetical order.Usually during Olympic opening ceremonies, the parade of athletes takes place during a pause in the razzmatazz. But Paris shattered that tradition by having the parade and pageantry at the same time, blending sports and artistic expression.Some spectators who followed organizers’ advice to arrive well ahead of time along the ceremony route fumed over long waits to get to their seats.“Paris has been great, anything to do with the Olympics and dissemination of information has been horrible,” said Tony Gawne, a 54-year-old Texan who turned up six hours in advance with his wife.“When you spend $6,000 on two tickets, well, that’s a little frustrating,” he said.But Paris had plenty of aces up its sleeve. The Eiffel Tower, its head visible below the clouds, Notre Dame Cathedral — restored from the ashes of its 2019 fire — the Louvre Museum and other iconic monuments starred in the opening ceremony. Award-winning theater director Thomas Jolly, the show’s creative mind, was using the signature Paris cityscape of zinc-gray rooftops as the playground for his imagination.His task: Tell the story of France, its people, their history and essence in a way that leaves an indelible imprint on Olympic audiences. Refresh the image and self-confidence of the French capital that was repeatedly struck by deadly extremist attacks in 2015. Capture how Paris is also aiming to reboot the Olympics, with Summer Games it has worked to make more appealing and sustainable.It’s a big ask. So Paris went big, very big. That goes for the security, too. Large fenced-off stretches of central Paris were locked down to those without passes and the skies during the ceremony were a no-fly zone for 93 miles around.During the athletes’ waterborne adventure, they passed historic landmarks that have been temporarily transformed into arenas for Olympic sports.Concorde Plaza, where French revolutionaries guillotined King Louis XVI and other royals, now hosting skateboarding and other sports. The golden-domed resting place of Napoléon Bonaparte, the backdrop for Olympic archery, and the Eiffel Tower, which donated chunks of iron that have been inlaid in the gold, silver and bronze Olympic medals. They’ll be won in the 32 sports’ 329 medal events.Paris’ aim, said Estanguet, is “to show to the whole world and to all of the French that in this country, we’re capable of exceptional things.”

A hot topic amongst tourists and athletes at the 2024 Olympics is the decision France made to forgo including air conditioning in Olympic Village.Some countries have chosen to supply their own air conditioning units to their competitors, like Team USA. Other countries have agreed with France's decision and will not provide air conditioning to their athletes.Summertime in Paris is much more tolerable than you initially would think.The average high temperatures are in the mid 70s with overnight lows in the upper 50s and low 60s.Last year, Paris did deal with record-breaking heat as temperatures soared over 86 degrees.A key component to keeping the Olympic Village between 73 and 79 degrees is in the piping. Water pipes under the floor's surface will aid in keeping the village in more comfortable conditions without the aid of air conditioning units.This is all in an effort to make the 2024 Olympics the greenest yet.France has kept the goal of keeping carbon emissions at a minimum this year. You will notice most of the Olympic sporting venues are historic sites where they only had to construct grandstands and the competition ground, rather than building new Olympic structures.

Susan Collins distanced herself from President Donald Trump during her first Maine Senate debate with Democrat Troy Jackson, arguing she has maintained her political independence by repeatedly voting against Trump's agenda and saying that she's “not exactly his favorite senator.”Democrats are trying to flip the Maine Senate seat as they work to win control of the Senate. In January, Collins joined a handful of Republican colleagues in backing a failed effort to limit the president’s ability to unilaterally use force in Venezuela. The move prompted Trump to say on social media that they “should never be elected to office again.”Collins argued that her seniority and experience in the Senate have resulted in money and resources for Maine, saying: “Leadership matters in Washington.”She also spent Tuesday evening attempting to turn the focus of Maine’s high cost of energy and housing on Jackson, arguing that he had a larger role in making a difference when he was the state Senate president and criticizing “Augusta’s failed policies” as a way to connect Jackson’s to the state’s struggle to address affordability.Other moments showed how the two candidates were approaching their appeal to working class Maine voters. With less than a month until Election Day, Democrats are looking beyond the traditional battlegrounds as new signs emerge that the fight for control of Congress could be spreading into states Republicans once had little reason to worry about. Kansas and Florida are among the states receiving new attention, while President Donald Trump’s own campaign schedule is taking him into reliably Republican territory. RELATED STORY | Trump holds Ohio midterm rally, urging voters to consider him on the ballot during 32-day campaign tourThe shift can also be seen in campaign spending. Conservative groups have recently moved money from North Carolina, where the Senate contest was expected to be one of the year’s most competitive races, to Kansas as Democrats perform better in both states. Kansas has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century. “Since Labor Day, the numbers have only gotten worse for Republicans,” said Kyle Kondik, a nonpartisan election analyst with the University of Virginia Center for Politics. Florida is another state to watch. Democrats are increasingly campaigning there even though the state appeared on relatively few lists of major battlegrounds earlier this year. RELATED STORY | Trump takes midterm push to Nebraska amid economic concerns among farmersKondik said Florida could become an important early indicator on election night if Democrats are having an especially strong showing. “That’s a state that counts very quickly,” Kondik said. Trump, meanwhile, campaigned this week in Nebraska, a state he carried by nearly 200,000 votes two years ago. The president frequently calls polls fake, and Kondik cautioned that the current political picture could still be affected by inaccurate polling. “I am always concerned about there being some systematic polling error,” he said. Republicans currently hold 218 seats in the House, while the Senate has 53 Republicans and 47 Democrats. Democrats need 51 Senate votes to hold a majority, while Republicans need 50 because the vice president breaks ties. The final weeks of the campaign will help determine whether the activity in Kansas, Florida and other states marks a genuine expansion of the political battlefield or whether the fight for Congress ultimately returns to more familiar battlegrounds.

We protect our country.”The president's message was interrupted repeatedly by protesters, including by one who appeared to be close to the stage. In all, at least a dozen demonstrators interrupted the president. Some were led away by police.Trump stepped away from the microphone briefly after one interruption.“He’s going back home to mom,” Trump said. “But what he doesn’t know is his mom voted for Trump.”Texas has become an unexpected battleground for RepublicansThe Republican Party did not plan to devote so much money and manpower to Texas this midterm season.Texas is the nation’s most populous reliably Republican state, where Trump won in 2024 by almost 14 percentage points. But with Election Day less than a month away, Trump’s poor approval ratings, the Iran war and soaring gas prices have threatened Republicans in virtually every state.Wednesday’s appearance marked Trump’s third trip to Texas in less than a month, and party officials have devoted more than $300 million to elections in the state so far.RELATED STORY | Obama is set to get more involved in the midterms, starting with an appearance alongside Abdul El-SayedIn a sign of Trump’s poor standing, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott did not attend the evening rally. A three-term Republican governor who won reelection in 2022 by roughly 11 percentage points, even Abbott has been caught in the turbulent national currents.He’s locked in a competitive reelection race against Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa.Instead of appearing with Trump, Abbott was scheduled to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on the governor’s absence.“For years, Greg Abbott has never been shy about embracing Donald Trump, calling Trump a ‘great friend’ and championing his agenda every step of the way,” said Texas Democratic Party spokesperson Jacob Long. “But now, as Texas families get crushed by record-high prices driven by Trump’s tariffs and war with Iran, suddenly Greg Abbott has somewhere else to be.”Trump focuses on helping the Senate candidate he endorsed in GOP primaryWhile the race for governor has drawn a sudden influx of cash from Democrats, the state’s U.S. Senate race has drawn the most attention as Democrats fight for the chamber’s majority. The state has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, but candidate James Talarico’s fundraising, Trump’s low approval rating and nagging concerns about Paxton’s character have put the race squarely in play.Trump spent most of his remarks focused on the Senate contest, describing Paxton as “perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America.”RELATED STORY | Trump holds Ohio midterm rally, urging voters to consider him on the ballot during 32-day campaign tour“He was tough and he was with us all the way,” Trump said of Paxton, whom he endorsed in the state's GOP primary over incumbent Sen. “He’s a fantastic man.”Trump made no mention of the recently leaked recording of Paxton lamenting the war in Iran and rising fuel prices, while also complaining his campaign was being run by operatives in Washington.He repeatedly criticized Talarico, including on the death penalty, a point that would appeal to many conservatives in the state that leads the nation in executions.Trump restated his support for the death penalty for “large scale drug dealers, human traffickers and anyone who kills a police officer,” while acknowledging that Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army major who killed 13 people in a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad.The president approved the method of execution earlier this week and suggested that Talarico opposes it.The Talarico campaign did not immediately respond when asked about the candidate’s position on Hasan’s scheduled execution.Paxton, invited onstage near the end of the rally, heaped praise on Trump, who stood behind him: “I am so grateful that you’re here."Trump makes a big announcement, but not about the Senate raceWhile Trump promoted Paxton briefly at the beginning of his remarks, he spent almost as much time later talking up Clemens, the retired Red Sox and Yankees pitcher who has been denied a spot in Major League Baseball's Hall of Fame due to his alleged involvement with performance-enhancing drugs.Trump brought him onstage and said he'd be awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, which is the highest civilian honor — and, Trump said, “a step up” from the Hall of Fame.Clemens said he was stunned by the honor.“This supersedes anything that obviously I’ve done in my playing career,” he said, standing alongside Trump. “And to get it from this man, this president. You talking about a winner? That’s a winner right there.”

hero.headline: Vero Beach Airport Schedule Change Renews Focus On Treasure Coast Travel Options
hero.body:
A schedule change to a Breeze Airways flight at Vero Beach Regional Airport is drawing new attention to how limited transportation options make travel difficult for Treasure Coast residents. The airline's route between the New York area and Vero Beach, which previously departed from Westchester, New York in the evening, now leaves in the morning, a shift that travelers say has disrupted their routines.

Peter Masella, who spoke about getting around the region, said, "In the Treasure Coast area, Vero Beach specifically, it is difficult to get around." He pointed to the absence of a Brightline station in Vero Beach, saying residents often must travel to other cities to find additional transportation options.

The Breeze Airways schedule change has created real complications for some flyers. A New York City physician said, "I'm a physician working in New York City, and because of the change of flight for Vero Beach, I have had to rearrange my patients' schedules two days in a row." Another traveler from Westchester, New York described the new logistics as a burden, saying, "Then I have to take a taxi all the way down and around to Vero Beach. It's very inconvenient."

At the same time, Breeze Airways has been expanding its presence at Vero Beach Regional Airport. Last month the airline introduced nonstop service to Trenton, Baltimore, Pittsburgh and Atlantic City, adding to the airport's commercial flight options. Airport Director Brandon Dambeck said such changes are a normal part of how carriers manage their networks. "All of these airlines are monitoring the routes and their gauge of success," Dambeck said, explaining that airlines regularly evaluate route performance, which can lead to new destinations as well as schedule or route changes. Travelers say they welcome the additional destinations, but argue that flight times fitting their schedules matter just as much as the number of places they can fly.

hero.headline: AG Cites Fort Pierce Manager's Conviction as First Case of New Corruption Unit
hero.body:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier pointed to the conviction of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms as the first major result from the state's newly created public corruption unit, announcing at a press conference Wednesday that more than 25 active public corruption investigations are underway across Florida. Speaking at the Attorney General's Office in West Palm Beach, Uthmeier warned that additional charges against public officials are coming in the weeks ahead.

A St. Lucie County jury last week found Mimms guilty of official misconduct, a third-degree felony, while acquitting him on a bid-tampering charge. The case centered on a city-owned parcel near the historic Lincoln Theater in Fort Pierce. Prosecutors alleged that in 2024 Mimms used his position to help a nonprofit organization secure the land deal, even though his niece served on the nonprofit's board, and that he later concealed his involvement and failed to disclose the family connection. Uthmeier said the nonprofit went on to receive hundreds of thousands of dollars in grant funding from a Catholic charitable organization for a planned development on the property, but the infrastructure project never materialized.

"The facts make clear that shenanigans took place to ensure that that nonprofit ended up with the award, and ultimately the city manager covered it up," Uthmeier said. He said his office will continue investigating where the grant money went. "We'll keep digging," Uthmeier said. "I think more facts will come to light as to where that money was going."

Uthmeier said the Mimms case reflects exactly the kind of conduct the public corruption unit was built to pursue. "This is the first big announcement," he said. "You'll see many to come in the weeks ahead as we wrap up our evidence and begin to press charges against people that have abused their office, that have abused the public trust." FDLE Commissioner Larry Keefe said rooting out public corruption is now a top priority for the agency. "When the people of Florida lose their sense of trust in their institutions, it's death by a thousand cuts," Keefe said. Sentencing for Mimms is expected at a later date. "This will be the first of many, sadly," Uthmeier said. "I hope we don't have to do too many, but we'll do as many as necessary to ensure the public knows that we are protecting their trust, that we are protecting taxpayers, and that we are going to hold public officials to the oaths that they take."

hero.headline: Martin County Terminates Transit Contract, Moves to Restore MARTY Bus Service
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted Tuesday to terminate the county's contract with Martin County Transit and begin emergency negotiations with MTM Transit to restore MARTY bus service, which shut down abruptly last week and left hundreds of riders without transportation and 28 drivers without jobs. Commissioners approved the emergency action under the county's emergency procurement rules, aiming for a one-year operating agreement with MTM Transit, a company that previously ran the county's transit system.

"We're doing it under our emergency procurement rules, and we will have a one-year contract," said Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton. The proposed deal with MTM Transit would serve as a temporary fix while county leaders work out a longer-term plan for public transportation. Gorton said restoring service quickly is essential so former drivers can return to their jobs. "The next vendor needs to have a contract to be able to hire the drivers back," he said.

The sudden shutdown left transit workers scrambling. "It was shocking. This company has pulled out and left 28 employees unemployed, and not knowing what tomorrow is going to be like is very devastating," said Joey Acevedo, president of ATU Local 1577. Former MARTY bus driver Bill Lawrence said he and his coworkers are eager to get back on the road. "I'm very hopeful. We have people behind us that give us hope," Lawrence said. With paychecks and benefits on hold, Lawrence said the wait has been financially painful. "We have no income right now. I'm going to lose it if I don't have my insurance," he said.

Gorton said the county is pushing to finalize the agreement with MTM Transit as soon as possible. "Our goal is to get them finalized this week and try to stand up the service next week. It's an aggressive goal," he said. County leaders are continuing negotiations with MTM Transit and hope to complete an emergency operating contract within days. If the agreement is approved, officials say MARTY bus service could resume as early as next week, giving riders across Martin County back their transportation option and giving former drivers like Lawrence a path back to work. "So we need to get everything rolling, so we all can get back to work," Lawrence said.

hero.headline: High-Speed I-95 Chase Ends in Arrest of Suspected Fentanyl Supplier Tied to Overdose Death
hero.body:
A suspected drug trafficker linked to a fatal fentanyl overdose is in custody after investigators say he hit a law enforcement vehicle and led detectives on a high-speed chase along I-95 through St. Lucie and Martin counties. James Arthur Green, 43, was arrested following a weeks-long narcotics investigation that also uncovered his suspected role in supplying the fentanyl that killed a person.

According to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, detectives with the Special Investigations Division made multiple undercover drug purchases during the investigation, gathering evidence that identified Green as the suspected supplier of fentanyl to a person who later died of an overdose. On Oct. 13, detectives used the deceased victim's cellphone to arrange another controlled narcotics buy, placing an order for fentanyl. Investigators said Green returned to the victim's residence, delivered about two grams of fentanyl and sent a photograph showing where he left the drugs.

Later that day, detectives carried out a separate undercover operation in which Green allegedly took part in a transaction involving about two ounces of fentanyl and one pound of methamphetamine. When detectives moved to arrest him, Green fled, allegedly striking a sheriff's office vehicle before speeding onto southbound I-95. Authorities said the pursuit reached speeds of about 115 mph, and detectives reported seeing Green throw suspected narcotics and a cellphone from his vehicle during the chase.

The Florida Highway Patrol and the Martin County Sheriff's Office joined the pursuit as it crossed into Martin County. Troopers deployed stop sticks and performed a PIT maneuver near Kanner Highway, bringing the chase to an end. Investigators recovered the one pound of methamphetamine and two ounces of fentanyl tied to the controlled purchase, along with an additional 22 grams of methamphetamine, two grams of crack cocaine and one gram of fentanyl.

Through the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office investigation, Green faces charges including trafficking of fentanyl, trafficking of cocaine, four counts of trafficking methamphetamine, sale of cocaine and unlawful use of a two-way communication device. The Florida Highway Patrol separately charged him with two counts of aggravated battery on a law enforcement officer, trafficking of fentanyl, trafficking of methamphetamine, two counts of fleeing and eluding, tampering with evidence, reckless driving, dangerous excessive speeding and resisting an officer without violence. The sheriff's office said Green was already out on bond in an unrelated Miami-Dade County case at the time of his arrest and is now being held without bond. The investigation into the fatal overdose remains active.

County officials are working to finalize the agreement with MTM Transit this week and hope to resume bus service as early as next week. "Our goal is to get them finalized this week and try to stand up the service next week. It's an aggressive goal," Gorton said. For drivers like Lawrence, the timeline carries real financial stakes. hero.headline: Vero Beach Council Approves Lease for Marriott at Regional Airport
hero.body:
Vero Beach City Council approved a lease agreement Tuesday to bring a four-story, 116-room Marriott hotel to the Vero Beach Regional Airport, ending three years of negotiations over the project. Developers said the hotel will break ground next year and is expected to be completed by the end of 2028.

The hotel will sit just outside the gates of the airport terminal along Aviation Boulevard. Brian Dembeck, interim airport director, said the project will improve the experience for travelers passing through the airport. "We've been in negotiations with this for the last three years," Dembeck said. "This is something that is going to dramatically improve the passenger experience." Dembeck said passengers will be able to stay at the hotel while waiting for flights and walk straight over to the terminal.

The hotel is intended to serve more than just airport passengers. Brian Cartland, vice-president of economic development for the Indian River County Chamber of Commerce, said the project could draw new business investment to the area. "The hotel is going to serve multiple purposes," Cartland said. "This hotel is going to help target industry growth by giving those companies that are looking at the area some additional alternatives for some great high-end options."

Chad Maxey, senior vice president of Diversified Companies, the project's developer, said another major driver behind the hotel is its proximity to the Jackie Robinson Training Complex down the street. "We feel this is a great location to have a hotel that's going to be able to provide amenities to the airport and also to the families and kids that are going to play baseball," Maxey said. He said the hotel will include a "homerun dugout amenity" where families can enjoy virtual baseball. "Kids can play virtual baseball in the hotel as they're getting ready to go across the street and actually hit the diamond over there and play with the Major League Baseball players," Maxey said.

hero.headline: Martin County to negotiate $3M deal with MTM Transit to restart MARTY buses
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to let the county administrator negotiate a new one-year contract worth approximately $3 million with MTM Transit, aiming to restore MARTY bus service after it abruptly shut down last Thursday. The agreement would be reached under the county's emergency procurement rules.

MARTY service stopped last Thursday when Martin County Transit LLC, the company previously running the system, discontinued operations and cited rising costs, including fuel and maintenance. The shutdown left several drivers without jobs, including Bill Lawrence, a former MARTY bus driver who said Tuesday's vote gave him hope. "I'm hoping that we get this back on the road soon. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work," Lawrence said.

Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton told commissioners that county officials spent the past several days exploring options to restore service. "We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us," Gorton said. He said the county evaluated several proposals before settling on MTM Transit, which had previously operated the county's bus system, as its preferred choice. During the one-year emergency contract, county officials plan to work toward a standard multi-year agreement through the county's normal competitive bidding process.

Gorton said bringing back the drivers who lost their jobs in last week's shutdown is a priority in the negotiations. "We absolutely want to use those same drivers and get them back to work as quickly as possible," he said. Commissioners also authorized county administration to move forward with terminating the county's previous contract with Martin County Transit LLC. County officials said they hope to finalize negotiations with MTM Transit by the end of this week, which could allow MARTY buses to resume operating as soon as next week.

The action follows last week's abrupt shutdown of MARTY bus service, which left hundreds of riders without transportation and dozens of drivers without jobs. County officials say the shutdown disrupted transportation across the community for residents who depend on MARTY buses to reach work, medical appointments and other essential destinations.

Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said the county is using emergency procurement rules to quickly put a one-year contract in place with MTM Transit. He said restoring service depends on getting a new vendor under contract so former drivers can return to their jobs. This company has pulled out and left 28 employees unemployed, and not knowing what tomorrow is going to be like is very devastating," Acevedo said. Gorton said the county is aiming to finalize the agreement with MTM Transit this week and resume bus service as early as next week. "Our goal is to get them finalized this week and try to stand up the service next week. It's an aggressive goal," Gorton said. cards.headline: St. Lucie Fire Board Member Calls for Chief Jeff Lee's Resignation
cards.teaser: More than 74% of St. Lucie County firefighters voted no confidence in Fire Chief Jeff Lee, and board member James Clasby says it's time for him to go. Scrutiny is also growing over the reassignment of Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez, who received a 92% no-confidence vote.
cards.body:
A St. Lucie County Fire District board member is calling on Fire Chief Jeff Lee to resign after firefighters delivered an overwhelming vote of no confidence in district leadership. More than 74% of firefighters who took part in the union vote said they had no confidence in Lee. The vote is the latest fallout from a hazing investigation that led to the firing of three veteran firefighters.

Fire Board member and St. Lucie County Commissioner James Clasby said the vote should push the board to act. "I think it's a wake-up call," Clasby said. "They've sent their message, and now it's, again, up for the board to take action." Asked whether that action should include Lee's resignation, Clasby said yes. "I don't know how you could possibly recover from getting such an overwhelming vote of no confidence," he said.

The union vote also found that about 92% of participating firefighters had no confidence in Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez, and 97% said the same of district attorney Kim Sabol. Sabol has submitted notice of her retirement, effective in December. A reassignment notice shows Gonzalez is being moved from assistant chief to battalion chief, a decision Clasby questioned given the no-confidence numbers against him. "I have lots of questions about why this move happened, why you would move somebody that received over 90% no confidence into a training position that will now train everybody in the district," Clasby said. The district said Gonzalez and Lee agreed the reassignment was in the district's best interest and said the move had been under discussion for some time prior to recent events. In a statement, the district said it recognizes the results of the no-confidence vote and remains committed to addressing workplace concerns and taking appropriate action to protect the safety, well-being and trust of its firefighters.

The no-confidence vote stems from an investigation earlier this year into videos involving firefighters at Station 1A. A third-party investigator concluded the videos depicted hazing, including one showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary employees. Veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin were fired following the investigation, though all three have maintained the activity was consensual. Union representative Ryan Sapp, who represents the three firefighters in their fight for reinstatement, said previous settlement offers are now off the table and that Lee told him he does not believe a change in leadership would resolve the confidence or morale issues. The Fire Board is weighing whether it has the authority to reinstate the three firefighters and is working to overhaul how complaints against district leadership are handled, with that effort expected to continue at the board's Oct. 21 meeting.

hero.headline: Martin County to Negotiate $3M Deal With MTM Transit to Restore MARTY Bus Service
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to let the county administrator negotiate a new one-year contract worth approximately $3 million with MTM Transit, a company that previously operated the county's public bus system. The move aims to restore MARTY bus service and rehire drivers after Martin County Transit LLC abruptly shut down operations last Thursday, citing rising operating costs including fuel and maintenance.

Former MARTY bus driver Bill Lawrence was among those who suddenly lost their jobs when service stopped last week. He said Tuesday's vote gave him hope. "I'm hoping that we get this back on the road soon. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work," Lawrence said.

Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton told commissioners that county officials spent the past several days exploring options to restore service. "We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us," Gorton said. He said the county evaluated several proposals before settling on MTM Transit as its preferred option. Under the county's emergency procurement rules, the proposed agreement would run for one year while officials work toward a standard multi-year contract through the county's normal competitive bidding process.

Gorton said bringing back the drivers who lost their jobs is one of the county's top priorities in the negotiations. "We absolutely want to use those same drivers and get them back to work as quickly as possible," he said. Commissioners also authorized county administration to move forward with terminating its previous contract with Martin County Transit LLC. County officials said they are hopeful a deal with MTM Transit can be finalized by the end of this week, which could allow buses to resume operating as soon as next week.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire Board Member Calls on Chief Lee to Resign After No-Confidence Vote
hero.teaser: More than 74% of St. Lucie County firefighters who voted said they have no confidence in Fire Chief Jeff Lee, and a fire board member says he should step down. The board is set to weigh reinstating three fired firefighters at its Oct. 21 meeting.
hero.body:
A St. Lucie County Fire District board member is calling on Fire Chief Jeff Lee to resign after firefighters delivered an overwhelming vote of no confidence in district leadership. The vote is the latest fallout from a hazing investigation that led to the firing of three veteran firefighters. More than 74% of firefighters who participated in the union vote said they had no confidence in Lee. About 92% said the same of Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez, and 97% said the same of district attorney Kim Sabol.

Fire Board member and St. Lucie County Commissioner James Clasby said the vote should push the board toward action, including Lee's resignation. "I think it's a wake-up call," Clasby said. "They've sent their message, and now it's, again, up for the board to take action." Asked whether that action should include Lee stepping down, Clasby said yes. "I don't know how you could possibly recover from getting such an overwhelming vote of no confidence," he said.

The no-confidence vote stems from an investigation earlier this year into videos involving firefighters at Station 1A. A third-party investigator concluded the videos depicted hazing, including one showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary employees. Veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin were fired following the investigation. All three have maintained the activity was consensual. "It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said. "We're all still friends," Boudrias said. Their terminations sparked pushback from firefighters and community members, which led to the union vote. Union representative Ryan Sapp, who is representing the three firefighters in their push for reinstatement, said previous settlement offers are now off the table. Sapp said he recently met with Lee and district leadership, who told him a change in leadership would not resolve the confidence or morale issues.

The vote comes as the district is already undergoing leadership changes. Sabol has submitted notice of her retirement effective in December, and a reassignment notice shows Gonzalez is being moved from assistant chief to battalion chief. Clasby questioned that move given the no-confidence results against Gonzalez. "I have lots of questions about why this move happened, why you would move somebody that received over 90% no confidence into a training position that will now train everybody in the district," he said. The district said Gonzalez and Lee agreed the reassignment was in the district's best interest and that the move had been under discussion for some time before the recent controversy. In a statement, the district said it recognizes the results of the no-confidence vote and remains committed to addressing workplace concerns and taking appropriate action to protect the safety, well-being and trust of its firefighters. The Fire Board is weighing whether it has the authority to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin while also working to overhaul how complaints against district leadership are handled. That work is expected to continue at the board's Oct. 21 meeting. Sapp said the last settlement offer, which would have reinstated the three firefighters with a three-shift suspension, was not accepted.

cards.headline: Martin County Cancels Transit Contract, Fast-Tracks Deal to Restore MARTY Bus Service
cards.body:
Martin County commissioners voted Tuesday to terminate the county's contract with Martin County Transit and begin emergency negotiations with MTM Transit to restore MARTY bus service within a week, following a sudden shutdown last week that left hundreds of riders without transportation and dozens of drivers without jobs.

Commissioners approved the move under the county's emergency procurement rules, clearing the way for a one-year operating agreement with MTM Transit, a company that previously ran the county's transit system. "We're doing it under our emergency procurement rules, and we will have a one-year contract," said Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton. The agreement is meant to serve as a temporary fix while county leaders work on a longer-term plan for public transportation.

The abrupt shutdown disrupted service for residents who depend on MARTY buses to reach jobs, medical appointments and other essential destinations, and it left 28 transit employees suddenly out of work. "It was shocking. This company has pulled out and left 28 employees unemployed, and not knowing what tomorrow is going to be like is very devastating," said Joey Acevedo, president of ATU Local 1577. Gorton said rehiring those drivers depends on quickly finalizing a new contract. "The next vendor needs to have a contract to be able to hire the drivers back," he said.

Former MARTY bus driver Bill Lawrence said he and his colleagues are ready to return to work and are counting on the county to move fast. "I'm very hopeful. We have people behind us that give us hope," Lawrence said. With paychecks and benefits on hold since the shutdown, he said the financial strain is mounting. "We have no income right now. I'm going to lose it if I don't have my insurance," Lawrence said. Despite the uncertainty, he remains optimistic about getting back behind the wheel. "So we need to get everything rolling, so we all can get back to work," he said.

County officials said they are pushing to finalize the agreement with MTM Transit this week and resume bus service as soon as next week. "Our goal is to get them finalized this week and try to stand up the service next week. It's an aggressive goal," Gorton said. Negotiations with MTM Transit are continuing, and county leaders say they hope to complete the emergency contract within days, a step that would restore transportation for riders across Martin County and open a path for former drivers to return to their jobs.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Approves Costco, Rehab Hospital and Entertainment District in Southern Grove
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie City Council approved site plans for a 163,000-square-foot Costco, a 42-bed rehabilitation hospital and the first phase of the Tradition Entertainment District, all along the Southern Grove jobs corridor.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council approved three major site plans for the Southern Grove area, the city's developing jobs corridor in western Port St. Lucie. The plans include a long-awaited Costco retail store, an acute care rehabilitation hospital and the first phase of the Tradition Entertainment District.

The Costco store will span 163,000 square feet. Scott Samples, with the City of Port St. Lucie, said the project has been in the works for a long time. "This is something that we have been looking forward to for a long time," Samples said. "This is getting closer to the finish line." Samples said Costco still must close on the land and move through construction design planning and permitting before any shovels hit the ground.

Wes McCurry, president and CEO of the St. Lucie County Economic Development Council, said the Costco store marks the beginning of a new phase of growth for the area. The store will join other companies already based in Southern Grove, including Amazon, Tamco and Cheney Brothers. McCurry said the jobs already established in the corridor are now drawing new commercial development. "They see all the development that's occurring here, along with the demographics that they like to see," McCurry said. "It only makes sense that Costco opens a retail store here."

The council also approved a 5.5-acre site plan for the first phase of the Tradition Entertainment District, which is set to bring restaurants and retail to the area. McCurry said the corridor has historically lacked dining, retail and entertainment options relative to its growing population. "This area has historically been largely underserved by restaurants and retail, and especially entertainment facilities," McCurry said. "It's kind of catching up to the rooftops that are happening. You know, rooftops always drive that demand, but there's more to come." The third approved plan sets aside space for an acute care rehabilitation hospital with 42 beds in a building of more than 55,000 square feet, offering both inpatient and outpatient services. McCurry said the hospital represents an expansion of health care access for the growing area. He said the three projects reflect a master plan city leaders set for Southern Grove two decades ago. "The plan is coming together. The vision is coming together. What everyone saw 20 years ago is now starting to happen," McCurry said.

hero.headline: Misplaced Cellphone Sparks False Weapon Rumor at Vero Beach High School
hero.body:
A misplaced cellphone in the cafeteria at Vero Beach High School triggered a false weapon rumor on Monday morning, though school officials confirmed there was no credible threat to students or staff. According to the School District of Indian River County, a student had left a cellphone in the cafeteria and hurried back to retrieve it. The confusion that followed caused inaccurate information to circulate among students, and that information eventually morphed into a rumor that a weapon was present at the school.

District officials stated clearly that the reported threat was not credible at any point. Vero Beach High School Principal Serra Finnegan sent families an update clarifying what had actually happened, according to the district. The explanation was meant to stop the spread of the rumor and reassure parents that the situation did not involve any actual danger.

The district also thanked the Indian River County Sheriff's Office for its partnership in responding to the situation. Officials encouraged families to help spread accurate information instead of repeating unverified rumors, noting how quickly such stories can travel among students on campus and across social media.

No weapon was ever found, and no credible threat was identified throughout the incident. The combined response from the school district and the sheriff's office was intended to calm concerns and make clear to the school community that the rumor did not reflect any real threat at Vero Beach High School.

hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to let the county administrator negotiate a one-year emergency contract worth roughly $3 million with MTM Transit, a move aimed at restoring MARTY public bus service after its abrupt shutdown last week. The decision comes days after Martin County Transit LLC, the company that had been running MARTY, stopped service suddenly last Thursday, citing rising operating costs including fuel and maintenance.

Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton told commissioners that county officials spent the past several days searching for a replacement operator. "We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us," Gorton said. He said the county reviewed several proposals before settling on MTM Transit, a company that previously operated the county's bus system, as its preferred choice. Under the county's emergency procurement rules, the proposed deal would run for one year while officials work toward a standard multi-year contract through the normal competitive bidding process.

Commissioners also authorized county administration to begin terminating the county's existing contract with Martin County Transit LLC. Gorton said getting the former drivers back on the job is a top priority in the negotiations. "We absolutely want to use those same drivers and get them back to work as quickly as possible," he said.

Former MARTY driver Bill Lawrence, who lost his job when service halted last Thursday, said Tuesday's vote gave him hope. "I'm hoping that we get this back on the road soon. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work," Lawrence said. County officials said they hope to finalize the agreement with MTM Transit by the end of this week, which could allow buses to resume running as early as next week.

hero.headline: Martin County Terminates MARTY Bus Contract, Moves to Restore Service With MTM Transit
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted Tuesday to terminate the county's contract with Martin County Transit and begin negotiating an emergency one-year operating agreement with MTM Transit, a company that previously ran the county's transit system. The move aims to restore MARTY bus service after an abrupt shutdown last week left hundreds of riders without transportation and dozens of drivers without jobs.

Commissioners approved the action under the county's emergency procurement rules. "We're doing it under our emergency procurement rules, and we will have a one-year contract," said Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton. The proposed agreement with MTM Transit would serve as a temporary fix while county leaders work on a longer-term plan for public transportation. Gorton said restoring service quickly is essential so former drivers can return to their jobs. "The next vendor needs to have a contract to be able to hire the drivers back," he said.

The sudden shutdown disrupted transportation across Martin County for residents who depend on MARTY buses to reach jobs, medical appointments and other essential destinations. It also left 28 employees unemployed. "It was shocking. This company has pulled out and left 28 employees unemployed, and not knowing what tomorrow is going to be like is very devastating," said Joey Acevedo, president of ATU Local 1577. Former MARTY bus driver Bill Lawrence said he and his colleagues are ready to get back to work. "I'm very hopeful. We have people behind us that give us hope," Lawrence said. He also described the financial strain of being without a paycheck. "We have no income right now. I'm going to lose it if I don't have my insurance," he said.

County officials are continuing negotiations with MTM Transit and hope to finalize the emergency contract within days. "Our goal is to get them finalized this week and try to stand up the service next week. It's an aggressive goal," Gorton said. If the agreement is approved, officials say bus service could return as early as next week, giving riders across Martin County a transportation option again and giving former drivers a path back to work. Lawrence said he and other drivers are eager for that to happen. "So we need to get everything rolling, so we all can get back to work," he said.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Fire Board Member Calls for Chief's Resignation After No-Confidence Vote
hero.body:
A St. Lucie County Fire District board member is calling on Fire Chief Jeff Lee to resign after firefighters delivered an overwhelming vote of no confidence in district leadership. The vote is the latest fallout from a hazing investigation that led to the firing of three veteran firefighters earlier this year. More than 74% of firefighters who participated in the union vote said they had no confidence in Lee. About 92% said the same of Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez, and 97% said they had no confidence in district attorney Kim Sabol.

Fire Board member and St. Lucie County Commissioner James Clasby called the results a wake-up call. "They've sent their message, and now it's, again, up for the board to take action," Clasby said. Asked whether that action should include Lee's resignation, Clasby said yes. "I don't know how you could possibly recover from getting such an overwhelming vote of no confidence," he said.

The no-confidence vote stems from an investigation into videos involving firefighters at Station 1A. A third-party investigator concluded the videos depicted hazing, including one showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary employees. Veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin were fired following the investigation. All three have said the activity was consensual. "It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said. Boudrias said the firefighters involved "are all still friends." Union representative Ryan Sapp, who is representing the three firefighters in their push for reinstatement, said he recently met with Lee and district leadership to ask how they planned to respond to the vote. "His response was that he doesn't feel a change in leadership would change the confidence issue or the morale," Sapp said. Sapp said a previous settlement offer to reinstate the three firefighters with a three-shift suspension was not accepted.

The leadership shakeup comes as Sabol has submitted notice of her retirement, effective in December, and Gonzalez is being reassigned from assistant chief to battalion chief, according to a reassignment notice. Clasby questioned that move given the no-confidence vote against Gonzalez. "I have lots of questions about why this move happened, why you would move somebody that received over 90% no confidence into a training position that will now train everybody in the district," he said. The district said Gonzalez and Lee agreed the reassignment was in the district's best interest and that the move had been under discussion "for some time prior to recent events." In a statement, the district said it recognizes the results of the no-confidence vote and remains committed to addressing workplace concerns and taking appropriate action to protect the safety, well-being and trust of its firefighters. The Fire Board is weighing whether it has the authority to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin and is working to overhaul how complaints against district leadership are handled, with that work expected to continue at the board's Oct. 21 meeting. Sapp said rebuilding trust in leadership could prove difficult given the vote's results, but added, "this is a great department. We have great men and women that work here. In light of all this bad publicity we've had, I promise you these members, these employees that I have, they genuinely enjoy serving this community and do the absolute best they can do."

Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said the county is acting under its emergency procurement rules to move quickly. cards.headline: St. Lucie Fire Board Member Calls on Chief Lee to Resign After No-Confidence Vote
cards.teaser: More than 74% of St. Lucie County firefighters voted no confidence in Fire Chief Jeff Lee, prompting a fire board commissioner to call for his resignation ahead of an Oct. 21 meeting on reinstating three fired firefighters.
cards.body:
A St. Lucie County Fire District board member is calling on Fire Chief Jeff Lee to resign after firefighters delivered an overwhelming vote of no confidence in district leadership. The vote is the latest fallout from a hazing investigation that led to the firing of three veteran firefighters earlier this year. More than 74% of firefighters who participated in the union vote said they had no confidence in Lee. About 92% said the same of Assistant Chief Brian Gonzalez, and 97% said the same of district attorney Kim Sabol.

Fire Board member and St. Lucie County Commissioner James Clasby said the results should push the board to act. "I think it's a wake-up call," Clasby said. "They've sent their message, and now it's, again, up for the board to take action." Asked whether that action should include Lee's resignation, Clasby said yes. "I don't know how you could possibly recover from getting such an overwhelming vote of no confidence," he said.

The no-confidence vote stems from a third-party investigation into videos involving firefighters at Station 1A. Investigators concluded the videos depicted hazing, including one showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary employees. Veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Chris Baldwin were fired following the investigation. All three have said the activity was consensual. "It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said. "We're all still friends," Boudrias said. Their terminations drew pushback from firefighters and community members, which led to the union's no-confidence vote.

Union representative Ryan Sapp, who is representing the three firefighters in their push for reinstatement, said previous settlement offers are now off the table, including one that would have reinstated the three with a three-shift suspension. Sapp said he recently met with Lee and district leadership to ask how they planned to respond to the vote. "His response was that he doesn't feel a change in leadership would change the confidence issue or the morale," Sapp said.

The vote comes as the district is already undergoing leadership changes. Sabol has submitted her retirement notice, effective in December, and a reassignment notice shows Gonzalez is being moved from assistant chief to battalion chief. Clasby questioned that move given the no-confidence results against Gonzalez. "I have lots of questions about why this move happened, why you would move somebody that received over 90% no confidence into a training position that will now train everybody in the district," he said. The district said Gonzalez and Lee agreed the reassignment was in the district's best interest and that the move had been under discussion for some time before the recent controversy. In a statement, the district said it recognizes the results of the no-confidence vote and remains committed to addressing workplace concerns and taking appropriate action to protect the safety, well-being and trust of its firefighters. The Fire Board is weighing whether it has the authority to reinstate Boudrias, Hutchinson and Baldwin while also working to overhaul how complaints against district leadership are handled, with that work expected to continue at the board's Oct. 21 meeting.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Council Approves Lease for Marriott Hotel Near Airport
cards.teaser: The Vero Beach City Council signed off on a lease agreement to build a four-story, 116-room Marriott near Vero Beach Regional Airport, a project tied to airport growth and the nearby Jackie Robinson Training Complex.
cards.body:
The Vero Beach City Council on Tuesday approved a lease agreement to bring a four-story, 116-room Marriott hotel to the area around Vero Beach Regional Airport. The hotel would sit just outside the terminal gates along Aviation Boulevard.

Brian Dembeck, interim airport director, said the project has been in negotiations for three years. "This is something that is going to dramatically improve the passenger experience," Dembeck said. He said passengers will be able to stay at the hotel next door while waiting for flights and then walk straight over to the terminal.

The hotel is intended to serve more than just airport travelers. Brian Cartland, vice-president of economic development for the Indian River County Chamber of Commerce, said it could help draw more businesses to Vero Beach and the surrounding area. "The hotel is going to serve multiple purposes," Cartland said. "This hotel is going to help target industry growth by giving those companies that are looking at the area some additional alternatives for some great high-end options."

Chad Maxey, senior vice president of Diversified Companies, the project's developer, said the hotel will also meet lodging demand from the nearby Jackie Robinson Training Complex. "We feel this is a great location to have a hotel that's going to be able to provide amenities to the airport and also to the families and kids that are going to play baseball," Maxey said. He said the hotel will include a "homerun dugout amenity" where kids can play virtual baseball before heading across the street to the diamond to play with Major League Baseball players. Developers said construction is expected to break ground next year, with completion targeted for the end of 2028.

hero.headline: UF/IFAS Extension Sets Fall Plant Sale Saturday in Fort Pierce
hero.teaser: The UF/IFAS Extension St. Lucie County Fall Plant Sale brings Florida-Friendly and native plants, workshops and garden tours to its Fort Pierce office Saturday, with a Friday accessibility event for those with mobility challenges.
hero.body:
The UF/IFAS Extension St. Lucie County Fall Plant Sale returns Saturday, Oct. 17, offering Florida-Friendly plants, including many native species, along with gardening advice for shoppers. The sale runs from 10 a.m. at the Extension office, 8400 Picos Road in Fort Pierce.

Quart-size plants are priced at $4, one-gallon plants at $7 and three-gallon plants at $12, all including tax. Shoppers can also take part in workshops and garden tours offered throughout sale hours, including a composting workshop scheduled from 10:30 to 11 a.m. An Ask an Expert session will also be available during the sale.

Ahead of the main event, the Extension office will host Mobility Day on Friday for people with accessibility challenges, running until noon. The event gives those with mobility issues a chance to shop and explore the sale offerings before the larger Saturday crowd arrives.

Proceeds from the sale and any donations collected will support educational programming through the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences Extension in St. Lucie County. Additional details about the sale, including plant selection and scheduling, are available through the St. Lucie County event calendar.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Police Still Hunting Driver Who Killed Scooter Rider, Fled Crash on Okeechobee Road

The crash happened shortly before 9 p.m. on October 11 just west of South 25th Street, according to Major Michael Santiago with the Fort Pierce Police Department. Santiago said the scooter rider was stopped at a red light behind a Toyota pickup truck when the eastbound van failed to stop and struck him from behind, throwing him into the truck ahead. The scooter rider was pronounced dead at the scene. St. Lucie County Fire District crews were dispatched at 8:51 p.m. and arrived four minutes later, but no other patients were transported.

According to a police news release, the driver then fled northbound on foot. cards.article_text: Fort Pierce police are searching for a driver who they say hit and killed a man riding a scooter before fleeing the scene, crashing into a salon and running away on foot Sunday night. The deadly crash happened shortly before 9 p.m. on October 11 along Okeechobee Road, just west of South 25th Street. According to Major Michael Santiago with the Fort Pierce Police Department , a man riding a scooter was stopped at a red light behind a Toyota pickup truck when a white van traveling eastbound failed to stop and struck him from behind. "That in turn led to a domino effect where the motorcyclist was ejected from the scooter itself and was thrown into the vehicle in front of the scooter," Santiago said. Obtained 911 recordings capture the frantic moments following the crash. In one call, a person inside the Toyota pickup truck described the aftermath. "We got hit, and it's like, there's blood all over our car," the caller told a dispatcher. Another caller reported seeing the white van crash into the nearby building while trying to get away. Lucie County Fire District officials said crews were dispatched at 8:51 p.m. and arrived four minutes later. The scooter rider was pronounced dead at the scene. No other patients were transported. But investigators say the van driver did not remain at the scene. See also: No lawyer, no law degree: Port St. Lucie man takes on Flock cameras in federal court Instead, Santiago said the driver reversed, made a U-turn, briefly traveled westbound in the eastbound lanes of Okeechobee Road, crossed the median and lost control before crashing into Kings & Queens Unisex Salon. "After he crashed into the business, he fled on foot," Santiago said. According to a police news release, the driver ran northbound after crashing into the salon, located at 2508 Okeechobee Road. Police responded to multiple 911 calls reporting the crash around 8:52 p.m. and immediately established a perimeter, searching for the driver using K-9 units and assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office aviation unit. Despite their efforts, they were unable to locate him. Two additional vehicles involved in the crash remained at the scene, according to police. The department's Traffic Homicide Unit, Crime Scene Investigations and other personnel processed the scene as part of the ongoing investigation. By Monday afternoon, the van had been removed, but significant damage remained. Broken concrete and debris were piled outside the entrance, which was boarded up and surrounded by caution tape. Salon owner Sheila Hampton said she received a phone call about the crash and arrived to find extensive damage to her business. "They just called me at the last minute and I just seen a hole in my wall. Hampton said she was unable to open the salon Monday and was concerned about when she would be allowed to resume business. And I'm just hoping tomorrow will be a better day," she said. Despite the damage to her business, Hampton also expressed sympathy for the family of the man who died. "My condolences from King and Queen Salon. We give out our condolences to the family," she said. "This shouldn't have ever happened." Police searching for driver Santiago said witnesses described the driver as a Hispanic man wearing a dark top and light-colored pants or shorts. Investigators believe he may have been injured in the crash, based on evidence recovered at the scene. Police have recovered the van and identified its registered owner, but have not confirmed who was driving. Santiago said the registered owner lives approximately one to one-and-a-half miles from the crash scene. He also said the owner stopped communicating with investigators after officers began asking who had access to the vehicle. Police have not ruled anyone out as they continue pursuing leads. Investigators are also searching for surveillance footage that could help identify the driver. As of Monday afternoon, Santiago said they had not obtained video showing the suspect himself. "We are desperately needing the public's help in identifying who was behind the wheel of this box van," Santiago said. He urged anyone who saw the white van in the area Sunday night, recognized someone who may have been driving it or captured video of the incident to come forward. Police said the victim's identity had not yet been confirmed as of Monday, and confirmation was still pending before next of kin could be notified. No arrest had been announced as of Monday afternoon. Anyone with information about the crash or the driver's whereabouts is asked to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or submit a tip through Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers .

hero.headline: Martin County Commissioners OK Deal to Restore MARTY Bus Service
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to let the county administrator negotiate a one-year contract worth roughly $3 million with MTM Transit to restore MARTY public bus service after it abruptly shut down last Thursday. The vote came days after Martin County Transit LLC, the company that had been operating MARTY, halted service and cited rising operating costs, including fuel and maintenance, as the reason.

For former MARTY bus driver Bill Lawrence, Tuesday's decision brought a sign of hope after he and several other drivers suddenly lost their jobs when service stopped last week. "I'm hoping that we get this back on the road soon. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work," Lawrence said.

During Tuesday's meeting, Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton told commissioners that county officials had spent the past several days searching for a way to resume service. "We reached out to a number of vendors; a number of vendors reached out to us," Gorton said. He said the county evaluated several proposals before settling on MTM Transit, a company that has previously operated the county's bus system, as its preferred option. Under the county's emergency procurement rules, the proposed agreement would run for one year while officials work toward a standard multi-year contract through the county's normal competitive bidding process.

The vote gives county administration the green light to begin negotiations with MTM Transit, a company that previously operated the county’s public bus system. We need our employees, our drivers, to get back to work,” Lawrence said. The company cited rising operating costs, including fuel and maintenance, as reasons for its decision to discontinue service. Under the county’s emergency procurement rules, the proposed agreement would be a one-year contract costing approximately $3 million. During that year, county officials would work toward establishing a standard multi-year contract through the county’s normal competitive bidding process. One of the county’s priorities during negotiations is bringing back the drivers who lost their jobs following last week’s shutdown. “We absolutely want to use those same drivers and get them back to work as quickly as possible,” Gorton said. Commissioners also authorized county administration to move forward with terminating its previous contract with Martin County Transit LLC. County officials say they are hopeful negotiations with MTM Transit can be finalized by the end of this week, potentially allowing buses to begin operating again next week. hero.headline: Vero Beach Council Approves Lease for 116-Room Marriott at Regional Airport
hero.body:
Vero Beach City Council approved a lease agreement Tuesday to bring a four-story, 116-room Marriott hotel to the Vero Beach Regional Airport, capping three years of negotiations over the project. The hotel will sit just outside the terminal gates along Aviation Boulevard.

Interim airport director Brian Dembeck said the project is designed to improve conditions for travelers passing through the airport. "We've been in negotiations with this for the last three years," Dembeck said. "This is something that is going to dramatically improve the passenger experience." Dembeck said the hotel's location will let passengers stay nearby and walk straight to the terminal when it's time to fly. "They're going to have a hotel right next door that they can come, they can stay, wait for their flight, and then go right over to the terminal."

The hotel's backers say its impact will reach beyond the airport. Brian Cartland, vice president of economic development for the Indian River County Chamber of Commerce, said the new lodging option could help draw businesses to Vero Beach and the surrounding area. "The hotel is going to serve multiple purposes," Cartland said. "This hotel is going to help target industry growth by giving those companies that are looking at the area some additional alternatives for some great high-end options."

Chad Maxey, senior vice president of Diversified Companies, the project's developer, said the hotel is also meant to serve the Jackie Robinson Training Complex down the street. "We feel this is a great location to have a hotel that's going to be able to provide amenities to the airport and also to the families and kids that are going to play baseball," Maxey said. He said the hotel will include a "homerun dugout amenity" for young guests. "Kids can play virtual baseball in the hotel as they're getting ready to go across the street and actually hit the diamond over there and play with the major league baseball players," Maxey said. Developers expect to break ground on the project next year, with completion targeted for the end of 2028.
