hero.headline: Martin County Advances Data Center Moratorium, But New Project Would Be Exempt
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted unanimously Tuesday to move forward with a one-year moratorium on new data center development as officials decide how to regulate the facilities going forward. The vote came one day after the county received its first-ever application for a data center in unincorporated Martin County, a hyper-scale facility of more than 950,000 square feet proposed on a lot off Kanner Highway west of I-95. Because that application was submitted before the moratorium was introduced, the project would not be subject to the new restrictions if they take effect.

Tuesday's vote marked the first of two required hearings on the moratorium. Commissioners are scheduled to take up the measure again on Oct. 27, when another vote will be needed before any pause on new data center projects could take effect. Commissioner Edward Ciampi said the moratorium gives the county room to gather input before moving forward. "An opportunity to say, 'pause,' let's hear from people, let's have the opportunity for experts to come and speak to us on both sides," Ciampi said. Commissioner Eileen Vargas said the county should take as much time as necessary before allowing more data centers to be built. "If it takes a year, a year and a half, two years, whatever it takes, whatever it takes, we should be doing this," Vargas said.

Residents who spoke at the meeting raised concerns about wildlife, water use and noise tied to large-scale data center development. Sergei Kelley told commissioners the facilities threaten rural land and the animals that depend on it. "For me it's wildlife so these areas are in largely rural or large plots of land and so you take that area and develop it and these facilities are massive, millions and millions of square feet, no animals can live there anymore, or the hum is going to affect the animals," Kelley said. Martin County resident Scott Butler pointed to the amount of water the facilities require. "The fear of the use of all this water we have," Butler said, adding residents need a clearer picture of "what these data centers are going to use."

Other residents urged commissioners to slow down before approving any new industrial development. One resident told commissioners that "once land is converted into industrial use the consequences can remain long after." Another said the county needs "serious studies completed in order to go forward with something of this consideration." The hyper-scale proposal off Kanner Highway is moving forward under current county rules even as commissioners weigh whether to restrict future projects. The Oct. 27 vote will determine whether the one-year moratorium takes effect for data center applications submitted after Monday.

hero.headline: Florida executes James Robertson as DeSantis withdraws warrant for Thompson
hero.body:
Florida executed James Robertson on Tuesday, nearly 18 years after he strangled his sleeping cellmate in what he told investigators was a deliberate attempt to land on death row. In the same week, Gov. Ron DeSantis withdrew a death warrant for a separate death row inmate, William Lee Thompson, marking the first time DeSantis has pulled back a signed death warrant.

Robertson, 63, declined to offer any last words before he received a three-drug injection and was pronounced dead about 10 minutes later. He had pleaded guilty to first-degree murder for strangling Frank Hart in 2008 and waived all appeals. Hart was killed just eight days before he was due to be released from prison. Hart's daughter, Rebecca Hart, read a statement at Florida State Prison saying her father was not just a piece of Robertson's story. "When someone you love is taken from you in such a violent way, the world keeps moving, even when a part of yours feels like it has stopped," she said. "Other people go on with their lives, but you carry your loss into every tomorrow." Robertson first went to prison in 1980 at age 17 for burglary and assault, and convictions for escape, battery and weapons offenses behind bars kept adding to his sentence. Hart had been sent to prison in 2003 following a sexual battery conviction. Jordan Kirkland, a spokesperson for the Florida Department of Corrections, said before the execution that the state has a "sound lethal injection process and protocol" designed to be humane and dignified. Florida carries out executions using a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart.

Robertson was originally supposed to be one of two Florida prisoners executed Tuesday, but DeSantis withdrew the death warrant for Thompson, 74, last week without giving a reason. The governor had already stayed Thompson's execution temporarily last month pending a psychiatric evaluation. Thompson's attorneys say he has dementia and failing health and have asked that he be transferred to a medical facility. Thompson remains on death row, and a new warrant could still be signed against him in the future. He was convicted of first-degree murder, kidnapping and sexual battery in the 1976 killing of 23-year-old Sally Ivester, and DeSantis is the third Florida governor to sign a death warrant in his case after Bob Graham and Bob Martinez both scheduled his execution in the 1980s before years of appeals and stays intervened.

Robertson's execution was Florida's 17th of 2026. DeSantis oversaw 19 executions in 2025, the most by any Florida governor in a single year since the state reinstated the death penalty in 1976, and he leaves office in January. Two more executions are already scheduled, not counting Thompson's case. William Reaves, 77, convicted of fatally shooting a sheriff's deputy in 1986, is set to be executed on Oct. 20. Jesse Guardado, 64, convicted of robbing and killing a woman to buy drugs in 2004, is scheduled to follow in November. DeSantis has made few public comments about the unprecedented pace of executions under his administration, saying previously that his goal is to deliver justice to victims' families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out.

Florida has executed more than half of the 31 people put to death nationwide so far this year, out of 47 total executions in the United States. In July, the state executed two prisoners in a single day, the first state to do so in nearly a decade. Robertson's execution came amid heightened national attention on capital punishment, following the botched execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee two weeks earlier, when she survived two lethal doses of pentobarbital and was rushed to a hospital. The Pentagon also said last week it would livestream the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan, a decision that drew criticism from lawmakers in both parties.

hero.headline: Florida executes James Robertson as DeSantis withdraws warrant for William Lee Thompson
hero.body:
Florida carried out the execution of James Robertson on Tuesday, while Gov. Ron DeSantis withdrew a death warrant for a separate death row inmate, William Lee Thompson, in what records show is the first such withdrawal in state history. Robertson, 63, received a three-drug lethal injection at Florida State Prison near Starke starting at noon. He had pleaded guilty to first-degree murder and waived all appeals in the 2008 strangling of his cellmate, Frank Hart, telling investigators the killing was unprovoked and that he wanted to be sentenced to death rather than serve out his prison term.

Robertson was supposed to be one of two prisoners executed Tuesday, but DeSantis withdrew Thompson's death warrant last week without giving a reason. The governor had previously issued a temporary stay of Thompson's execution last month pending a psychiatric evaluation. The withdrawal does not change Thompson's sentence. He remains on death row, and a new warrant could be signed for him in the future. DeSantis is the third Florida governor to sign a death warrant for Thompson, following Bob Graham and Bob Martinez in the 1980s, when years of appeals and stays spared him from Florida's electric chair. Thompson, 74, was convicted of first-degree murder, kidnapping and sexual battery in the 1976 killing of 23-year-old Sally Ivester. His attorneys say he suffers from dementia and failing health and have asked that he be moved to a facility equipped to provide adequate medical care.

According to court records, Robertson was incarcerated at Charlotte Correctional Institution, north of Fort Myers, when he tied together several socks and strangled Hart while Hart slept in December 2008. Robertson first went to prison in 1980 at age 17 for burglary and assault, and subsequent convictions for escape, battery and weapons offenses extended his sentence over the years. Hart had been sent to prison in 2003 following a sexual battery conviction. Robertson pleaded guilty, waived the penalty phase that would have let a jury weigh a death sentence or life in prison, and was sentenced to death by a judge. He later waived all post-conviction proceedings and told a judge earlier this month that he understood his execution date and did not want to pursue appeals to the Florida Supreme Court or U.S. Supreme Court. Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty said the case shows the death penalty can drive violence rather than deter it. The group's legal and policy director, Maria DeLiberato, said in a statement that Hart deserved to be safe in state custody and that his loved ones deserve compassion.

Robertson's execution was the 17th in Florida this year, with two more already scheduled, not counting Thompson. William Reaves, 77, is set to be executed Oct. 20 for fatally shooting a deputy in 1986. Jesse Guardado, 64, is scheduled for execution in November for robbing and killing a woman in 2004 to buy drugs. If both executions proceed as planned, Florida would match its 2025 total of 19 executions, the most by any Florida governor in a single year since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976, with eight weeks still remaining in 2026.

Only one other Florida inmate remains alive after DeSantis signed a death warrant for him. James Dailey, 80, was scheduled to die in late 2019 for the murder of a 14-year-old girl, but a federal judge halted the execution amid arguments over his guilt. The stay was later lifted, but DeSantis has not signed a new warrant for Dailey. DeSantis has said his goal is to bring justice to victims' families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out, saying he would not proceed if he believed someone was innocent. Florida carried out more than half of the 30 executions nationwide last year and in July became the first state in nearly a decade to execute two prisoners in a single day.

Robertson told investigators that the attack was unprovoked and that he killed his cellmate so that he would be sentenced to death, rather than having to live out his days in prison.Robertson was 17 years old when he went to prison in 1980 for burglary and assault. Years of convictions for escape, battery and weapons while in prison kept adding time to his total sentence. Hart was sent to prison in 2003 following a sexual battery conviction.Robertson pleaded guilty and waived a penalty phase, where a jury would recommend the death penalty or life in prison. A judge sentenced Robertson to death, and he later waived all post-conviction proceedings. Robertson reiterated his position during a hearing earlier this month, telling a judge that he understood his execution had been scheduled and that he didn't want to make any final appeals to the Florida Supreme Court or U.S. Supreme Court.While proponents of the death penalty have long claimed that it is a deterrent, Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty released a statement saying that this case demonstrates the opposite."Frank Hart deserved to be safe in state custody, and his loved ones deserve our compassion," the group's legal and policy director, Maria DeLiberato, said in the statement. "When someone commits murder to try to secure his own execution, we have to confront the conditions that contributed to that decision and the reality that the existence of the death penalty may have caused the very violence it purportedly prevents."Meanwhile, DeSantis is the third Florida governor to sign a death warrant for Thompson. Bob Graham and Bob Martinez both scheduled executions for Thompson in the 1980s, but years of appeals and stays allowed him to avoid the electric chair, the state's method of execution at the time. The 74-year-old death row inmate was convicted of first-degree murder, kidnapping and sexual battery in the 1976 killing of 23-year-old Sally Ivester.Thompson will remain on Florida’s death row, and a new death warrant could be signed for him in the future. His attorneys have said he suffers from dementia, and his health is failing. They said he should be relocated to an adequate medical facility to get the care he needs.Only one other Florida inmate remains alive following a death warrant signed by DeSantis. James Dailey, 80, was scheduled to die in late 2019 for the murder of a 14-year-old girl, but a federal judge halted the execution as attorneys argued against his guilt. The stay was eventually lifted, but DeSantis didn't sign a new death warrant. The state halted all executions during the COVID-19 pandemic and didn't restart until 2023.DeSantis, who leaves office in January, oversaw 19 executions in 2025, more than any other Florida governor in a single year since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Robertson would be the state's 17th execution of 2026, with two more already scheduled, not counting Thompson.William Reaves, 77, is scheduled to be executed on Oct. 20, followed by Jesse Guardado, 64, on Nov. Reaves was convicted of fatally shooting a deputy after dropping a gun in front of the law enforcement officer in 1986. Guardado was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.If Robertson, Reaves and Guardado are all executed as planned, that would match the state's 2025 total, with eight weeks remaining in 2026.DeSantis has made few public comments about the unprecedented number of executions but explained previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out."I felt I owed it to them to make sure this ran very smoothly. If I honestly thought someone was innocent, I would not pull the trigger," the governor said last year.A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half of the 30 total executions in the U.S. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Council Approves Site Plan for Costco Store in Southern Grove
hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a site plan application Monday for a new Costco store in the Southern Grove district, moving the long-planned project closer to construction. City leaders agreed earlier this year to sell the land to Costco for $6 million.

The new store will sit east of Southwest Village Parkway and south of the newly constructed Marshall Parkway. It will be built next to the Costco distribution center that is currently under construction in the same area.

The site plan approval is the latest step in a project that pairs a retail store with the nearby distribution facility, both located in the growing Southern Grove district. City leaders finalized the land sale agreement with Costco earlier this year before bringing the site plan to a council vote.

With the site plan now approved, the project moves forward alongside the distribution center construction already underway in Southern Grove. The store and distribution center are expected to anchor further commercial growth in the fast-developing western Port St. Lucie corridor.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Family Seeks Animal Cruelty Charges After Dog Killed on Goodman Avenue
cards.teaser: Surveillance video shows a truck dragging the family's German shepherd down Goodman Avenue after striking him last Tuesday. Animal control is investigating the case as a hit-and-run.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie family is pushing for animal cruelty charges after their German shepherd, Titus, was struck and killed by a truck in a hit-and-run on Goodman Avenue last Tuesday. Michelle Baker and Dillon Baker, the dog's owners, say animal control is investigating the case as a hit-and-run, and they believe the driver's actions amount to a crime.

The incident happened around noon when the family's dogs got loose after hopping the fence and running down the road. The Bakers tried to track the dogs using GPS collars but could not reach them in time. Surveillance footage shows a silver truck hitting Titus, stopping briefly, then continuing to drag the dog down the road before running him over. The driver did not return to the scene.

"I want justice served because you didn't stop; you killed my dog after you hit him," Michelle Baker said. Dillon Baker said the driver appeared to know he had hit something. "He knew he hit something because he stopped, then he kept going," he said. Michelle Baker said the way Titus died was senseless. "My dog did not deserve to go out like that," she said. She argued the incident should be treated as a serious offense. "That's a crime, that's a full-on crime, it's murder," she said.

Michelle and Dillon Baker are now trying to explain Titus' death to their two children, ages 11 and 2. At the family's home, another of their dogs, Gypsy, witnessed the incident and has not been the same since. The Bakers have a message for the driver who hit Titus. "Pay attention, pay attention and care about what's on the road in front of you," Michelle Baker said. Animal control's investigation into the hit-and-run remains open.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Council Approves Costco and Two Other Southern Grove Projects
hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council approved three major site plans for the Southern Grove jobs corridor in western Port St. Lucie, including the long-awaited Costco retail store. The 163,000-square-foot Costco is one of three projects cleared at the meeting, alongside a 5.5-acre first phase of the Tradition Entertainment District and a 42-bed acute care rehabilitation hospital.

"This is something that we have been looking forward to for a long time," said Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie. Samples said Costco still must close on the land and move through construction design planning and permitting before any shovels hit the ground. "This is getting closer to the finish line," he said.

Wes McCurry, president and CEO of the St. Lucie County Economic Development Council, said the Costco store is just the beginning of a new phase of growth in the area, which already includes Amazon, Tamco and Cheney Brothers. McCurry said the jobs already in place in Southern Grove are now drawing new commercial development. "They see all the all the development that's occurring here, along with the demographics that they like to see," McCurry said. "It only makes sense that Costco opens a retail store here."

The Tradition Entertainment District's first phase will bring restaurants and retail to an area McCurry said has lacked those options. "This area has historically been largely under-served by restaurants and retail, and especially entertainment facilities," McCurry said. "It's kind of catching up to the rooftops that are happening. You know, rooftops always drive that demand, but there's more to come." The rehabilitation hospital will offer inpatient and outpatient services in a building of more than 55,000 square feet. "Growing area needs services, and that's just another component of services that are coming into the area is expanded healthcare access," McCurry said.

McCurry said the three approvals mark progress toward the city's long-term vision for Southern Grove. "The plan is coming together. The vision is coming together. What everyone saw 20 years ago is now starting to happen," he said.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce Ends Crabby's Dockside Lease Over Nearly $334,000 Debt
hero.body:
Fort Pierce city commissioners voted unanimously to terminate the lease with Winking Starfish, the former operator of Crabby's Dockside, and begin searching for a new operator for the waterfront restaurant at the Fort Pierce Marina. The city now says Winking Starfish owes nearly $334,000 in rent, taxes, and late fees, after recalculating a balance it had previously put at more than $418,000.

Crabby's Dockside, located along Avenue A at the marina, closed in February. Winking Starfish had identified a potential new operator for the restaurant, but city officials said the proposal sought favorable terms, which led the city to move toward terminating the lease instead.

City Manager Richard Chess told commissioners that the city would allow interested restaurateurs to compete for the location rather than negotiate with a single successor operator. The city plans to set requirements for potential operators, with the city commission making the final decision on a new tenant. Chess also said any new agreement would combine rent and other payments into one amount based on the property's market value, a change from the prior lease structure.

Mayor Linda Hudson emphasized the importance of the site to the marina's operations. "Our marina is very, very successful, and we're very proud of it, and that location, that Crabby's location, is a very critical part of the marina," Hudson said.

Florida 511 advised drivers to use caution and anticipate slower travel through the area. Both I-95 and the turnpike are heavily traveled routes through St. Lucie County, and blockages near the Becker Road interchange have the potential to back up traffic for commuters and other motorists passing through the region. Drivers traveling through the Becker Road area on I-95 or the turnpike were encouraged to stay alert for continued delays following the two incidents.

hero.headline: Misplaced Cellphone Sparks False Weapon Rumor at Vero Beach High School
hero.body:
A misplaced cellphone in the cafeteria at Vero Beach High School triggered a false weapon rumor on Monday morning, though school officials said there was never a credible threat to students or staff. According to the School District of Indian River County, a student had left a cellphone behind in the cafeteria and hurried back to grab it. That simple moment created confusion, and as word spread through the school, the story shifted and grew until it became a rumor that a weapon was involved.

District officials moved quickly to clarify that the alleged threat had no basis in fact. Principal Serra Finnegan sent an update to families to address the misunderstanding and set the record straight about what had actually happened. The explanation was meant to calm any fears among parents and students who may have heard the rumor before learning the full picture.

The district also publicly thanked the Indian River County Sheriff's Office for its partnership in helping address the situation as it unfolded. Officials asked families to help stop the spread of misinformation by sharing only verified details rather than passing along unconfirmed rumors, a request aimed at preventing similar confusion in the future.

The incident is a reminder of how fast rumors can travel in a school setting, especially in a crowded, fast-moving environment like a cafeteria. What began as an ordinary moment, a student rushing to retrieve a forgotten phone, spiraled into a more serious-sounding claim once inaccurate details started circulating among students. No injuries, arrests, or disciplinary actions were reported in connection with the rumor.

hero.headline: Jupiter Nurse Arrested, Charged With Stealing Fentanyl at Tradition Hospital
hero.teaser: A Cleveland Clinic Tradition ICU nurse has been arrested on felony charges after police say she stole fentanyl from a critically ill patient's IV line. Port St. Lucie police say a family member witnessed the theft before detectives confirmed it through surveillance footage.
hero.body:
A Jupiter woman who worked as an intensive care unit nurse at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital has been arrested on felony charges after Port St. Lucie police say she stole fentanyl from a critically ill patient's IV infusion while on shift. Leslie Pope, 54, was taken into custody in Jupiter on Oct. 8, following a police investigation into the alleged theft.

According to investigators, a family member of the patient reported seeing Pope use a syringe to withdraw fluid from the patient's fentanyl infusion line, place the syringe in her pocket and leave the room. Police said Pope was not assigned to care for the patient at the time.

Detectives said Pope returned to the patient's room the following evening and again approached the IV equipment. The family member intervened during that encounter. Investigators later reviewed surveillance footage that they say showed Pope manipulating protective caps on the IV equipment, though authorities said they could not determine whether any additional medication was removed during the second incident.

Pope now faces felony charges of grand theft of a controlled substance, possession of a controlled substance without a prescription and fraudulently obtaining a controlled substance. The Port St. Lucie Police Department led the investigation into the alleged diversion at the hospital, located in the Tradition area of Port St. Lucie.

cards.headline: Coast Guard Tows Disabled Boat With Four Aboard Near Fort Pierce Inlet
cards.teaser: A Coast Guard Station Fort Pierce crew towed a disabled 15-foot vessel carrying four people to safety near the inlet during rainy weather Sunday.
cards.body:
A Coast Guard Station Fort Pierce boat crew assisted four people aboard a disabled 15-foot vessel near the Fort Pierce Inlet on Sunday after the boat's engine became inoperative. The incident unfolded amid rainy conditions, according to the Coast Guard.

The crew provided a manual bilge pump to the boaters as a precaution against flooding before towing the vessel safely to the Stan Blum Boat Ramp.

"Our Coast Guard crews stay prepared through continuous training, qualifications and physical fitness, ensuring they remain Semper Paratus, Always Ready, to respond to maritime emergencies across the Southeast's 1.8 million square mile area of responsibility," the agency posted Monday on Facebook.

The Fort Pierce rescue came a day after a Coast Guard Station Miami boat crew rescued one person in the water after a passing personal watercraft operator waved them down and alerted them to an overturned hydrofoil near Flagler Memorial Island.

hero.headline: Developer Sues Indiantown Over Stalled $25 Million Data Center Plat
hero.body:
Silver Fox 606 LLC has filed a lawsuit against the Village of Indiantown, its village council, planning board, and local residents, seeking emergency injunctive relief to keep its $25 million data center project moving forward. The complaint, which includes a verified petition for a writ of prohibition, accuses village officials of illegally derailing the project after a newly elected council took office in 2026.

Silver Fox bought the more than 600-acre property at 13820 SW Silver Fox Lane in 2025 after zoning verifications confirmed that computer and data processing facilities were permitted as an as-of-right use in Heavy Industrial districts. The lawsuit alleges that the new village council moved to stall or ban data center development despite earlier municipal marketing efforts that had actively recruited similar tech infrastructure to the area. Indiantown's Community and Economic Development Director administratively approved the Silver Fox plat on September 17. A local resident later filed an administrative appeal seeking to overturn that approval.

Silver Fox's legal team argues that the village's planning, zoning, and appeals board has no legal jurisdiction to review the plat approval, citing state statutes that render recorded plats unassailable without the landowner's consent. The lawsuit also points to a September 1 emergency council meeting at which the village manager and the village's long-serving village attorney were ousted. Silver Fox alleges the Village Council violated Florida's Sunshine Law during those personnel changes, raising accountability questions about how the decisions were made.

The developer is asking the court for emergency injunctive relief, a preliminary injunction blocking any stop-work orders or retroactive reviews of the project, and declaratory judgments affirming its vested development rights. The lawsuit frames the dispute as a test of whether an administratively approved plat can be unwound by a council and resident appeal after the fact, with Silver Fox maintaining that its approval was final and legally binding before the political shakeup in Indiantown took hold.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Man Fights City's 126-Camera Network in Federal Court
hero.body:
A Port St. Lucie resident is representing himself in a federal lawsuit against the city, Mayor Shannon Martin and surveillance company Flock Safety, challenging a combined network of 126 license plate cameras he says violates residents' constitutional rights. Steven Greer, a former surgeon who later worked on Wall Street, filed the suit in August and has since amended it. His complaint alleges Port St. Lucie operated 53 Flock cameras along with 73 Axon license plate readers.

Greer argues the cameras, which photograph passing vehicles and record identifying information along with time and location, let police reconstruct a person's movements without a warrant. He says this violates the Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable searches and seizures. "I was appalled at what I learned," Greer said. His complaint also cites two cases involving the cameras, including the arrest of Fort Pierce Officer Josepher Crutchfield, who was accused of searching his ex-girlfriend's vehicle 382 times, and a woman who was mistakenly jailed after her vehicle was wrongly linked to a deadly hit-and-run before charges against her were dropped. Greer contends those incidents point to a larger problem with the surveillance system itself.

The lawsuit also raises a Second Amendment argument, pointing to Flock cameras reportedly installed at the entrance to the Ocala Shooting Range in Marion County. Greer argues that recording visitors to a gun range could discourage people from exercising their right to bear arms. "When I saw that case where they have Flock cameras in gun ranges, I said, 'Whoa, that's a Second Amendment violation,'" Greer said. "The key buzzword is chilling. You know, if they scare you away from using your gun rights that's a violation." His complaint additionally challenges the city's handling of public records requests, alleging officials withheld information about camera locations and system audit logs, and raises claims under Florida's constitutional privacy protections along with questions about the legality of public spending on the network.

Port St. Lucie has already voted to remove 18 of its 53 Flock cameras, but Greer says that is not enough because a future administration could reverse a voluntary decision. "The end result is to get a consent decree, where the city and Flock agrees to pull the cameras forever," he said. His amended lawsuit seeks a court declaration that the city's surveillance program is unconstitutional, an injunction limiting the network's operation or data sharing without a warrant backed by probable cause, access to disputed public records, statutory damages and litigation costs. Greer said his main goal is a binding court order rather than money. "I'm not running for office. I'm not seeking attention," he said. "It's my way of doing something." A federal judge has not ruled on whether Port St. Lucie's camera program is unconstitutional, and the case still faces potential motions to dismiss.

While he has no formal legal training, he says his years working as a surgeon and later on Wall Street prepared him for the technical research and writing involved in representing himself. The CBS12 News I-Team has been reporting on Flock cameras since last year, examining how the technology is used by law enforcement and more recently, allegations of misuse. In Fort Pierce, Officer Josepher Crutchfield was arrested after investigators accused him of searching his ex-girlfriend's vehicle 382 times. In another case, a woman was arrested and jailed after investigators mistakenly linked her vehicle to a deadly hit-and-run crash. The charges against her were later dropped. Law enforcement agencies, however, defend license plate readers as valuable investigative tools, crediting the technology with helping identify suspects, recover stolen vehicles and solve crimes. "I know that police have always argued these Flock cameras really help solve crimes. What would be your response to that?" Bente asked. "That's their number one defense. It's not true," Greer said. His assertion is disputed by law enforcement agencies that have documented cases in which license plate reader information helped investigators. Whether the technology is useful in solving crimes is a separate question from whether particular searches are constitutional. Greer's lawsuit also raises an argument not typically associated with traffic cameras: the right to bear arms. He points to Flock cameras reportedly installed at the entrance to the Ocala Shooting Range, a public gun range in Marion County. Greer argues that recording who visits a shooting range could discourage people from exercising their Second Amendment rights. You know, if they scare you away from using your gun rights that's a violation." The complaint also challenges the city's handling of public records requests, alleging officials withheld information about camera locations and system audit logs. It includes claims under Florida's constitutional privacy protections and questions the legality of public spending on the network. Greer has also raised First Amendment concerns following a Sept. Lucie City Council meeting. He told the I-Team that the number of police officers present made him feel intimidated and could discourage residents from speaking out. I'm looking around, I see police officers all over the place," Greer said. Meanwhile, the legal debate over Flock is playing out across the country. In Oklahoma, a federal judge ruled Oct. 1 that a warrantless search of approximately a month of license plate location records violated the Fourth Amendment, suppressing evidence obtained following the search. The ruling concerned the specific circumstances of that case and did not establish that all Flock searches are unconstitutional. Law enforcement agencies have continued to defend the technology, while privacy advocates argue that large networks of searchable cameras allow police to monitor ordinary drivers on a scale that wasn't previously possible. Florida is already seeing changes. The Florida Department of Transportation revoked permits for automated license plate readers on state highway rights-of-way, requiring their removal from those locations. Lucie also voted to remove 18 of its 53 Flock cameras. But for Greer, taking down some cameras isn't enough. hero.headline: More Than 200,000 Customers Have Power Back After Hurricane Isaias
hero.body:
More than 200,000 customers across the Florida Panhandle had their power restored as of Sunday afternoon, Gov. Ron DeSantis said, as crews continued cleanup from Hurricane Isaias. The storm made landfall Friday night near the Panhandle as a Category 2 hurricane, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands of residents. About 430,000 customers remained without power as of Saturday morning, but that number has dropped sharply since then. DeSantis said Florida Power and Light is expected to largely finish restoration by Monday, while Choctawhatchee Electric Cooperative, which had about 46,000 customers still without power at the time of Sunday's press conference, is targeting Tuesday for full restoration.

"I know it's frustrating to lose power and some of you have been without it for a couple of days now," CHELCO CEO Steve Rhodes said. "Be assured we're working around the clock to recover from this devastating hurricane."

DeSantis held Sunday evening's press conference at Grayton Beach State Park in Santa Rosa Beach, one of 24 parks that have reopened since the storm. The park had been closed after a bridge washout left a 50-foot-long, 15-foot-deep gap that cut off access and threatened to harm Western Lake, according to the Florida Department of Transportation. Crews worked overnight, bringing in 600 cubic yards of sand to repair the bridge in less than 18 hours, and DeSantis said the park was expected to reopen Sunday night. The governor said the storm caused widespread damage across Northwest Florida, driven mainly by falling trees, debris and wind rather than storm surge. Two storm-related deaths have been confirmed in Escambia County.

The hardest-hit counties by power outages included Santa Rosa County, where about 90% of customers lost power, along with Holmes County at 89%, Washington County at 86%, Walton County at 85%, Escambia County at 75% and Okaloosa County at 53%. DeSantis said the state plans to submit a request for a federal major disaster declaration, which requires reaching a certain damage threshold before it can be approved by the president. "I think clearly, just given the amount of trees that fell down on different things, there's going to be more than enough," he said. A major disaster declaration would open a range of federal assistance programs for individuals and public infrastructure, including funding for emergency and permanent recovery work, according to FEMA. State emergency officials said Saturday they had not received any requests for large-scale search and rescue deployments.

hero.headline: Church and Neighbors Rally After Port St. Lucie House Fire Injures Renter
hero.teaser: A garage fire on Carmelite Street in Port St. Lucie's Northport Village neighborhood burned renter Nigel Laidlow and displaced his family, but church members and neighbors have stepped in to help them recover.
hero.body:
A house fire in Port St. Lucie's Northport Village neighborhood injured a renter and displaced his family Friday afternoon, and members of a local church and neighbors have since rallied to help them begin cleaning up. The fire broke out on Carmelite Street near St. Lucie County Fire District crews, who responded around 1:30 p.m. and arrived to find heavy fire coming from the garage.

According to the family, the fire started in the kitchen before spreading through the garage. They said a propane tank later exploded, causing additional damage and impacting a neighbor's garage doors across the street. When firefighters extinguished the flames, they left behind a charred garage door, blackened walls and belongings covered in soot.

Renter Nigel Laidlow was inside the home when the fire broke out and suffered burns to his legs. He was transported for medical treatment. "I don't even know how to describe it. It was really surreal," Laidlow said. "I would've never thought a little fire would turn into this."

By Saturday, family photos, furniture and other belongings were spread across the front yard as loved ones worked to salvage what they could. Members of the Fort Pierce Seventh-day Adventist Church spent the day helping move and sort through the damaged items. "We have a really strong support system, especially from my church," Laidlow said. Despite the loss, he said he is grateful his family survived. "This right here is something not anybody would like to deal with. Not in a lifetime," he said. The family is now focused on recovering and determining its next steps, and the cause of the fire remains under investigation.

hero.headline: Flash Flood Warning Hits Stuart, Hobe Sound, Palm City and Coastal Martin County
hero.body:
A Flash Flood Warning is in effect for northeastern Martin County until 7 p.m. as thunderstorms continue to dump heavy rain across the coast. As of 5:23 p.m., Doppler radar showed storms producing additional heavy rainfall over the warned area. Between 2 and 3 inches of rain had already fallen, with another 1 to 2 inches possible before the storms move out.

Flash flooding is either already happening or expected to develop shortly across the warning area. Communities at risk include Stuart, Jupiter Island, Port Salerno, Hobe Sound, Palm City, Sewall's Point, Witham Field, Hobe Sound Beach and the Hobe Sound Wildlife Refuge. The warning applies to small creeks and streams as well as urban areas, highways, streets, underpasses and other spots known for poor drainage or low elevation.

The threat stems from thunderstorms capable of producing intense, fast-moving rainfall. That kind of rain can quickly overwhelm drainage systems and cause water to pool or rise in places that normally handle wet weather without issue, raising the risk of sudden and dangerous flooding on roads and in neighborhoods.

Residents in and around Stuart, Port Salerno, Hobe Sound, Palm City, Sewall's Point and Jupiter Island should stay alert for rising water through the evening hours. Drivers are urged to avoid flooded roadways and underpasses, since floodwaters can be deeper and move faster than they appear. The Flash Flood Warning remains active until 7 p.m., and conditions could change quickly as the storms continue to track through the region.

hero.headline: DeSantis: Over 200,000 Customers Have Power Back After Hurricane Isaias
hero.body:
More than 200,000 customers across the Florida Panhandle had their power restored as of Sunday afternoon, Gov. Ron DeSantis said, as crews continue cleanup efforts following Hurricane Isaias. Florida Power and Light is expected to be largely finished with restoration by Monday, and CHELCO, which still had about 46,000 customers without power at the time of DeSantis's Sunday evening press conference, is targeting Tuesday to have service fully restored. The state also plans to submit a request for a federal major disaster declaration given the widespread damage.

Isaias made landfall in the Panhandle Friday night as a Category 2 hurricane. Hundreds of thousands of people lost power in the storm's aftermath, with 430,000 customers still without electricity as of Saturday morning. DeSantis said crews are making steady progress and that 24 state parks have reopened. The governor confirmed two storm-related deaths in Escambia County. State emergency officials said Saturday they had not received any requests for large-scale search and rescue deployments.

DeSantis said the storm caused widespread damage across Northwest Florida, mostly from falling trees, debris and wind rather than storm surge. Some of the hardest-hit counties included Santa Rosa County, where about 90% of customers lost power, along with Holmes County at 89%, Washington County at 86%, Walton County at 85%, Escambia County at 75% and Okaloosa County at 53%. Because of the scale of the damage, the state intends to request a major disaster declaration from the federal government, a designation that must be approved by the president. hero.headline: Port St. Lucie House Fire Injures Renter, Displaces Family in Northport Village
hero.body:
A house fire Friday afternoon on Carmelite Street in Port St. Lucie's Northport Village neighborhood injured a renter and displaced his family, while neighbors and church members quickly stepped in to help with cleanup. St. Lucie County Fire District crews responded to the home around 1:30 p.m. and arrived to find heavy fire coming from the garage.

According to the family, the fire started in the kitchen before spreading through the garage. A propane tank later exploded, causing additional damage and striking a neighbor's garage doors across the street. When firefighters extinguished the flames, they left behind a charred garage door, blackened walls and belongings covered in soot.

Renter Nigel Laidlow was inside the home when the fire broke out and suffered burns to his legs. He was transported for medical treatment. "I don't even know how to describe it. It was really surreal," Laidlow said. "I would've never thought a little fire would turn into this."

By Saturday, family photos, furniture and other belongings were spread across the front yard as loved ones worked to salvage what they could. Members of the Fort Pierce Seventh-day Adventist Church spent the day helping move and sort through the damaged items. "We have a really strong support system, especially from my church," Laidlow said. Despite the loss, Laidlow said he is grateful his family survived. "This right here is something not anybody would like to deal with. Not in a lifetime," he said. The family is now focused on recovering and determining its next steps, and the cause of the fire remains under investigation.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Residents Escalate to EPA Over ALF Project Near Contaminated Site
hero.teaser: Port St. Lucie's City Council already approved the major site plan for a 150-unit assisted-living facility next to a petroleum-contaminated property, but residents say an engineering letter shows cleanup plans had to be revised because of the project. Neighbors have now contacted the EPA and Florida Department of Health seeking answers.
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie's City Council has approved the major site plan for a 150-unit assisted-living facility planned next to a petroleum-contaminated property, a decision residents are now pushing back on by contacting federal and state environmental agencies. The project, known as PSL Westmoreland ALF, is planned for 7.1 acres within the Rivella planned unit development along Southeast Morningside Boulevard near Southeast Westmoreland Boulevard. The three-story facility would include assisted-living units and a memory care component. Residents say they have reached out to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Florida Department of Health seeking more information about the neighboring property's contamination history.

An engineering letter obtained by residents adds new detail to their concerns. The letter, from BTEX Engineering, discusses a March 2026 meeting with environmental officials about the neighboring contaminated property and states that the proposed remediation approach should be changed because of concerns about surrounding properties, including the planned assisted-living facility. The letter also says vapors would need to be captured during the remediation process.

Resident David Lipps said the issue is not about what is being built on the site, arguing that nearby businesses and other facilities could also be affected by environmental concerns tied to the contaminated property. Resident Charlie D'Agata said residents have raised objections at City Council meetings for about two years and questioned why a developer would be allowed to build near a property he described as contaminated.

Construction on the assisted-living facility has not begun. Although the City Council approved the project's major site plan in September, the developer must still submit construction plans for technical review, followed by additional reviews involving the South Florida Water Management District and other agencies. The environmental history of the neighboring property and the extent of any potential impact on surrounding land remain central questions for residents, who say they want clearer answers about how any risks would be addressed as the project moves forward.

cards.headline: Flooding at Port St. Lucie's California and Savona costs pizza shop thousands
cards.body:
Recurring flooding at the intersection of California and Savona boulevards in Port St. Lucie has cost a nearby pizza shop thousands of dollars in lost revenue, and city officials say a permanent fix is still years away. The water has receded since this week's flooding turned the intersection into what looked like a lake, but business owners in the shopping plaza there say the problem keeps coming back.

Joe Dascoli, who works at Estella Pizzaria near the intersection, said the flooding this week forced the shop to close early. "We were actually calling it the California River, as a joke," Dascoli said. "It becomes like an island around here." The shopping plaza housing the pizza shop becomes cut off when the roads flood, he said. "It's an ongoing thing that you know should be resolved," Dascoli said. During this week's flooding, customers could not get into the shop and orders could not go out. "We've lost thousands of dollars just in revenue and people not being able to come in," Dascoli said. "Some of our drivers, their cars aren't capable of going through the floods, so we have to stop deliveries."

City officials confirmed they are rolling out a pilot program that will install water level sensors at flood-prone locations across Port St. Lucie. Scott Samples with the city said the sensors will send alerts to Public Works and police when an area starts seeing rapid flooding. "There'll be alerts that'll be able to go to Public Works and the police to say, 'Hey, this area is seeing rapid flooding,' so they might be able to respond quicker," Samples said. The sensor program is meant to speed up the city's response to flash flooding rather than prevent it.

For a long-term fix, Samples pointed to a large-scale drainage project planned for the Oak Hammock neighborhood. The project calls for two new retention ponds, baffle boxes to collect runoff, and raised sections of roadway at California and Savona boulevards. Samples said the project is currently in the data collection phase and has not yet moved into design. "This is one of the highest priorities that we have in terms of capital investment projects, and so it's going to take time," Samples said.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Fire on Carmelite Street Injures Renter, Church Helps Family Recover
hero.body:
A fire that tore through the garage of a Port St. Lucie home Friday afternoon injured a renter and displaced a family, prompting neighbors and church members to help with the cleanup. The fire broke out on Carmelite Street in the Northport Village neighborhood. St. Lucie County Fire District crews responded around 1:30 p.m. and arrived to find heavy fire coming from the garage.

According to the family, the fire started in the kitchen before spreading into the garage. They say a propane tank later exploded, causing additional damage and affecting a neighbor's garage doors across the street. By the time firefighters extinguished the flames, the home had suffered significant damage, including a charred garage door, blackened walls and belongings covered in soot.

Renter Nigel Laidlow was inside the home when the fire started and suffered burns to his legs. He was transported for medical treatment. "I don't even know how to describe it. It was really surreal," Laidlow said. "I would've never thought a little fire would turn into this."

By Saturday, family photos, furniture and other belongings were spread across the front yard as loved ones worked to salvage what they could. Members of the Fort Pierce Seventh-day Adventist Church spent the day helping move and sort through the damaged items. "We have a really strong support system, especially from my church," Laidlow said. Despite the loss, he said he is grateful his family survived. "This right here is something not anybody would like to deal with. Not in a lifetime," he said. The family is now focused on recovering and determining its next steps, and the cause of the fire remains under investigation.

cards.headline: Flooding at Port St. Lucie Intersection Costs Pizza Shop Thousands
cards.teaser: Repeated flooding at California and Savona boulevards forced Estella Pizzaria to close early and halt deliveries this week, as the city rolls out a sensor pilot program while a long-term drainage fix remains years away.
cards.body:
Flooding at the intersection of California and Savona boulevards in Port St. Lucie turned the roadway into what neighbors called a lake earlier this week, forcing a nearby pizza shop to close early and lose thousands of dollars in revenue. The water has since receded, but the shopping plaza near the intersection, home to Estella Pizzaria, has become what workers describe as an island during floods.

"We were actually calling it the California River, as a joke," said Joe Dascoli, who works at Estella Pizzaria near the intersection. "It becomes like an island around here." Dascoli said the flooding on Thursday forced the shop to close early. Customers could not get inside and orders could not go out. "It's an ongoing thing that you know should be resolved," Dascoli said. "We've lost thousands of dollars just in revenue and people not being able to come in," he said. "Some of our drivers, their cars aren't capable of going through the floods, so we have to stop deliveries."

The city of Port St. Lucie says it is starting a pilot program using water level sensors at flood-prone areas around the city. Scott Samples with the city said the sensors will send alerts to Public Works and police when an area is experiencing rapid flooding, allowing crews to respond faster. The program is aimed at helping the city react more quickly to flash flooding like what hit the California and Savona intersection this week.

Samples said a long-term fix depends on a large-scale drainage project planned for the Oak Hammock neighborhood. That project calls for two new retention ponds, baffle boxes to collect stormwater runoff, and raised sections of roadway at California and Savona boulevards. The project is currently in the data collection phase and has not yet moved into design. "This is one of the highest priorities that we have in terms of capital investment projects, and so it's going to take time," Samples said.

hero.headline: Martin County Employee Rescues Teen in Rip Current at Unguarded Bob Graham Beach
hero.body:
A Martin County employee rescued a teenage girl caught in a rip current Thursday afternoon at unguarded Bob Graham Beach, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. Paramedics took the girl to a hospital with minor drowning-related injuries after the rescue, officials said.

Around 3 p.m., Amy Offenbach saw three girls swimming in a rip current as thunderstorms moved through the area, according to the county. Offenbach, who works in the county's Growth Management Department and surfs in her free time, noticed one of the girls struggling. Officials said Offenbach commandeered a surfboard and brought the teen to shore. The county said the girl had lost consciousness after choking on water.

Offenbach then drove the teen to Jensen Beach, where members of Martin County Ocean Rescue provided medical care before Martin County Fire Rescue transported her to the hospital. Bob Graham Beach does not have lifeguards, officials said.

The rescue highlights the danger of rip currents, particularly at unguarded beaches and when storms move through the area. Officials advise swimmers caught in a rip current not to fight the current directly. Instead, they should float, signal for help and swim parallel to shore when able.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Details Flood Fixes After California/Savona Water Hits Pizza Shop
cards.teaser: Estella Pizzaria says flooding at California and Savona boulevards cost it thousands in lost business this week. City officials outlined a new sensor pilot program and a long-term drainage project for the area.
cards.body:
Flooding at the intersection of California and Savona boulevards in Port St. Lucie shut down a nearby pizza shop this week and cost it thousands of dollars in lost revenue, prompting city officials to detail both short-term and long-term fixes. The water has since receded, but earlier this week the intersection was underwater, with neighbors sharing video of roadways that looked like rivers.

Joe Dascoli, who works at Estella Pizzaria near the intersection, said employees joked about calling it the "California River" because the shopping plaza where the restaurant sits turns into an island during heavy flooding. The flooding forced the shop to close early on Thursday. Dascoli said customers could not get in and deliveries could not go out, and some drivers could not get their cars through the water. "We've lost thousands of dollars just in revenue and people not being able to come in," Dascoli said. "It's an ongoing thing that you know should be resolved," he added.

City of Port St. Lucie representative Scott Samples said the city is starting a pilot program that will install water-level sensors at flood-prone areas around the city. The sensors will send alerts to Public Works and police when an area is seeing rapid flooding, allowing crews to respond more quickly. "There'll be alerts that'll be able to go to Public Works and the police to say, 'Hey, this area is seeing rapid flooding,' so they might be able to respond quicker," Samples said.

Samples said the city's long-term solution is a large-scale drainage project for the Oak Hammock neighborhood. The project calls for two new retention ponds, baffle boxes to collect runoff, and raising sections of roadway at California and Savona boulevards. Samples said the project is still in the data collection phase before it moves into design. "This is one of the highest priorities that we have in terms of capital investment projects, and so it's going to take time," he said.

hero.headline: Martin County Employee Rescues 3 Girls From Rip Current at Bob Graham Beach
hero.body:
A Martin County employee helped rescue three girls caught in a rip current Thursday afternoon at Bob Graham Beach near Jensen Beach, an unguarded stretch of shoreline where no lifeguards were on duty. Amy Offenbach, who works in Martin County's Growth and Development Department, said she arrived at the beach around 2 p.m. to surf when she noticed three girls about 25 yards offshore clinging to the same surfboard.

Offenbach, an avid surfer, said something about the scene immediately caught her attention. "The ocean could be very gentle and calm, but it can also be very heavy and crash very hard," she said. She grew concerned when one of the girls appeared distressed. "That kind of struck me as strange," Offenbach said. "The other one seemed a little agitated." A girl on the beach then told Offenbach she believed her friends needed help. "By that time the girls were waving in the water like they needed help, so immediately I just went into rescue mode," Offenbach said.

Offenbach and a friend paddled out to reach the group. When she got to the girls, she said one of them appeared to be in serious distress. "I looked at her, and she seemed kind of dazed and confused," Offenbach said. "I said, 'Get up on the board.'" She gave her surfboard to two of the girls and told them to hold on and kick toward shore, then placed the third girl on her soft-top board and paddled her back to the beach. Offenbach, who has some lifeguard training, quickly recognized the girl needed medical attention once they reached land. "The girl that I rescued said that she blacked out under the water," Offenbach said. "She inhaled water, and she had a severe headache." Because Bob Graham Beach has no lifeguards, Offenbach drove the girl to a nearby lifeguard station, where an ambulance was called.

Offenbach said she has not been able to reconnect with the girl or learn more about her condition. She hopes the rescue reminds beachgoers to understand ocean conditions before entering the water, and she encourages people to swim at guarded beaches when possible, check rip current forecasts and use flotation devices or boards when appropriate. "I'm just really happy that I was in the right place at the right time," she said. Offenbach said the ocean, while a place she loves to spend time, can be dangerous. "It can be very treacherous."

hero.headline: Vero Beach Man Arrested in August Shooting Death of Ex-Girlfriend
hero.body:
A 33-year-old Vero Beach man has been arrested on a first-degree murder charge in the August shooting death of his former girlfriend, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. Matthew Allen Waggle was taken into custody Oct. 5 on an active warrant and is being held without bond in connection with the killing of Dawn Marie Kriskewic.

Deputies responded to the 500 block of 1st Street in Vero Beach after 911 callers reported a woman lying in the roadway. They found Kriskewic with injuries consistent with gunshot wounds and began CPR before she was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she was pronounced dead.

Investigators identified Waggle as Kriskewic's former boyfriend. A coworker told detectives that Kriskewic had expressed concerns about Waggle before her death and that he had previously threatened consequences if she called police when he came to retrieve his belongings. Surveillance footage reviewed by detectives showed a person identified as Waggle near the area around the time of the shooting, and additional footage showed him walking through the area before and after it. Investigators said footage also showed him discarding a shirt, which they later recovered.

Investigators recovered a rolling suitcase containing men's clothing and a tactical vest with a "security" patch near the crime scene. A Ruger pistol was found on a neighboring property along with a note stating that another person had given Waggle permission to use the firearm for firearm qualifications, according to the affidavit. A judge signed the first-degree murder warrant for Waggle, and he was taken into custody at the Indian River County Sheriff's Office.

cards.headline: MARTY Bus Service Halts Without Warning Across Martin County
cards.body:
MARTY public transit service across Martin County stopped abruptly Thursday, leaving riders who depend on the buses without transportation as county officials work to find a fix. Martin County officials said they received no advance warning that service would stop. The system's operator, Martin County Transit LLC, had requested a significant increase in its contract, saying rising insurance, fuel and maintenance costs had caused significant financial losses since it took over operations in July 2025. Negotiations between the county and the company failed to produce an agreement.

County officials said Martin County Transit LLC submitted a 180-day notice to terminate its contract approximately two weeks ago. Despite that notice, the company told the county Thursday morning that it was discontinuing service immediately, catching officials off guard and cutting off bus routes countywide without notice to riders.

George Stokus, assistant Martin County administrator, said the county is pursuing both short-term and long-term solutions to restore service. "We are doing everything we can humanly do right now to restore service as soon as we can," Stokus said. "It's just not an easy operation or switch to turn it back on. It's going to take some time, and we are working to get to that." County officials said they are coordinating with community partners, including United Way, to help residents affected by the shutdown. No timeline has been given for when MARTY service might resume, and officials said updates will be posted on social media as a solution is reached.

The suspension caught riders by surprise. Leticia Chaclan, of Martin County, waited for her bus in Stuart on Thursday, but it never arrived. She said she had been riding MARTY for years and called it essential for many in the community. "We really need the bus," she said. "Especially people within the Hispanic community, who don't have a driver's license, and need it to go to places like the clinic, to go to the hospital, and for other things we need. It's very necessary, and we use the bus a lot. In my case, I don't drive. But I really need the bus, and I use it a lot. I don't drive, and we go everywhere to shop." Steven Godell, another rider, said he resorted to riding his bicycle Thursday after the bus failed to show. "It's crazy, but I will move on and do something different," he said.

hero.headline: DeSantis Confirms 2 Deaths in Escambia County as Isaias Recovery Continues
hero.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis confirmed Saturday that two people died in Escambia County from causes related to Hurricane Isaias, as more than 430,000 customers across Florida remained without power following the storm's landfall in the Panhandle. Speaking from Destin, DeSantis said the Category 2 hurricane came ashore in Okaloosa County Friday night and caused widespread damage across Northwest Florida, primarily from falling trees and debris.

Escambia County Sheriff Chip Simmons said in videos posted to Facebook that one woman died after a tree fell on her home. A man died after using a generator that was not properly ventilated inside a garage, Simmons said. Four other people inside the same home were hospitalized. "What I saw was both from the structural perspective, I think our structures handled the storm very well," DeSantis said. "The problem is that the storm knocked over a lot of trees."

State emergency crews have completed roughly 180 missions through the Florida Division of Emergency Management, according to DeSantis. Nearly 10,000 power accounts have already been restored, but about 430,000 customers remained without electricity Saturday morning, including roughly 325,000 within Florida Power & Light's service area. Officials said debris removal remains one of the biggest obstacles to restoring power. "The folks have been out since daylight," DeSantis said. "Some of it is that you've got to get the debris out of the way before the linemen can connect it." The Florida Department of Transportation began clearing roads and bridges before sunrise, and the Florida Highway Patrol has completed dozens of debris-clearing missions. State officials said 85 traffic signals have been restored using generators. Northwest Florida Beaches International Airport has reopened to commercial traffic, while airports in Pensacola and Fort Walton Beach remained closed Saturday but were expected to resume operations soon. Florida Division of Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said more than 16,000 utility workers have been mobilized to restore power in the region.

Perdue warned that flooding risks remain even after the storm has passed, noting that several rivers, including the Shoal River in Okaloosa County, are still rising and are not expected to crest for several days. "We want to make sure we keep enough resources on hand in case search and rescue is needed," Perdue said. State leaders urged residents to avoid flooded roads and standing water. Attorney General James Uthmeier said a small number of price-gouging complaints have already been filed, and residents who believe businesses are overcharging for fuel, food or other emergency supplies can file complaints with his office. Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia warned residents about post-storm scams, including unlicensed contractors and fraudulent roofers, and urged people not to sign contracts or provide deposits before verifying credentials. The state plans to set up insurance assistance hubs in affected areas within 48 hours to help residents file claims. Businesses can report storm damage through the state's survey at FloridaDisaster.biz. DeSantis said recovery efforts will continue across the Panhandle, where damage stretches from the Alabama state line to the eastern Panhandle. "We're going to get through this," DeSantis said. "There's damage, and that's going to be difficult for people whose property was damaged, but I also feel like this is very surmountable for us if we all just work together and get the job done."

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Garage Fire Injures Renter, Community Rallies to Help Family
hero.body:
A fire that tore through the garage of a Port St. Lucie home Friday afternoon injured a father and displaced his family, prompting neighbors and church members to step in and help with cleanup. The fire broke out on Carmelite Street in the Northport Village neighborhood. St. Lucie County Fire District crews responded around 1:30 p.m. and found heavy fire coming from the garage.

According to the family, the fire started in the kitchen before spreading into the garage. They said a propane tank later exploded, causing additional damage and affecting a neighbor's garage doors across the street. When firefighters put out the flames, they left behind a charred garage door, blackened walls and belongings covered in soot.

Renter Nigel Laidlow was inside the home when the fire started and suffered burns to his legs. He was transported for medical treatment. "I don't even know how to describe it. It was really surreal," Laidlow said. "I would've never thought a little fire would turn into this."

By Saturday, family photos, furniture and other belongings were spread across the front yard as loved ones worked to salvage what they could. Members of the Fort Pierce Seventh-day Adventist Church spent the day helping move and sort through the damaged items. "We have a really strong support system, especially from my church," Laidlow said. Despite the loss, he said he is grateful his family survived. "This right here is something not anybody would like to deal with. Not in a lifetime," he said. The family is now focused on recovering and figuring out its next steps, and the cause of the fire remains under investigation.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Launches Flood Sensors as California/Savona Fix Looms
cards.teaser: After flooding shut down a pizza shop and turned the intersection into what neighbors call the "California River," Port St. Lucie is rolling out water-level sensors while a larger drainage project remains years away.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie is starting a pilot program using water-level sensors at flood-prone areas, including the intersection of California and Savona boulevards, after this week's flooding forced a nearby pizza shop to close early and cost it thousands of dollars in lost revenue. The water at the intersection has receded, but earlier this week the roadway looked like a lake.

Joe Dascoli, who works at Estella Pizzaria near the intersection, said the flooding has become a recurring problem. "We were actually calling it the California River, as a joke," Dascoli said. "It becomes like an island around here." That island is the shopping plaza where the pizza shop sits. Dascoli said customers could not get in and orders could not get out during this week's flooding, and some delivery drivers could not get their cars through the water. "We've lost thousands of dollars just in revenue and people not being able to come in," Dascoli said. "It's an ongoing thing that you know should be resolved."

Scott Samples with the city of Port St. Lucie said the new sensor pilot program will send alerts to Public Works and police when an area starts seeing rapid flooding, allowing crews to respond faster. The sensors are meant to address immediate flooding risks while the city works on a longer-term solution.

That long-term fix is a large-scale drainage project for the Oak Hammock neighborhood, which includes building two new retention ponds, installing baffle boxes to collect runoff, and raising sections of roadway at California and Savona boulevards. Samples said the project is currently in the data collection phase and has not yet moved into design. "This is one of the highest priorities that we have in terms of capital investment projects, and so it's going to take time," Samples said.

hero.headline: Martin County Employee Pulls Drowning Girl From Water at Unguarded Stuart Beach
hero.teaser: Amy Offenbach grabbed a surfboard and paddled out to rescue a choking, limp girl at Bob Graham Beach, which had no lifeguards on duty at the time.
hero.body:
A Martin County employee is being praised for rescuing a girl from drowning Thursday afternoon at Bob Graham Beach in Stuart, where no lifeguards were on duty. Amy Offenbach had come to the beach to surf when she saw three girls struggling in the water. "It was just by chance that we were here and thank God that we were at the right time," Offenbach said.

Offenbach, who has years of lifeguard training, said her instincts took over immediately. "I took off my clothes, grabbed the board, and started paddling," she said. "I immediately went into rescue mode." Authorities said one of the girls was choking on water. Offenbach used her surfboard to stabilize the child as she brought her out of the water.

"Once she was on the board, she was kind of limp. Her body wasn't doing anything else," Offenbach said. She said the girl's forehead felt cold, which prompted her to rush the child to the nearest lifeguard stand down the road. The girl was then taken to the hospital with minor drowning injuries.

Offenbach, a Martin County employee, said she does not feel the need for recognition, even as others have called her a hero. She said she was simply acting on instinct as a mother. "I have a 14-year-old son myself, and I can't imagine him not coming back from hanging out at the beach with his friends," she said. "I'm just really thankful that her parents have their child," Offenbach said. The incident is a reminder to use caution at beaches that do not have lifeguards on duty.

hero.headline: Treasure Coast High Freshman Dies After Being Struck on Port St. Lucie Boulevard
hero.body:
A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student has died after being struck by a vehicle while walking to school in Port St. Lucie on Wednesday morning. The Port St. Lucie Police Department confirmed the death in a news release issued at 8 p.m. Friday, three days after the crash near the intersection of Southwest Port St. Lucie Boulevard and Southwest Squirrel Avenue.

Chief Leo Niemczyk announced the student's death in a statement headlined "14-YEAR-OLD PEDESTRIAN SUCCUMBS TO INJURIES FOLLOWING CRASH." "The Port St. Lucie Police Department extends its deepest condolences to the student's family, friends, classmates, and all those affected by this heartbreaking loss. Our thoughts are with them during this incredibly difficult time," the department said.

Police said a preliminary investigation found the freshman was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near the edge of the roadway when he was struck from behind by a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man. According to investigators, the driver initially believed he had hit a construction barrel and did not realize he had struck a person. The driver later made a U-turn at the next safe location, returned to the scene, turned on his hazard lights and found the teenager unconscious on the side of the road.

Police said the driver has remained cooperative with investigators and that they have not observed any signs of impairment. Authorities stressed that the assessment is preliminary and could change as the investigation continues. Detectives are still examining the circumstances surrounding the crash.

hero.headline: Nearly 450,000 Without Power in Florida After Hurricane Isaias, No Confirmed Deaths Yet
hero.body:
Nearly 450,000 utility customers remained without power across Northwest Florida on Saturday morning after Hurricane Isaias made landfall in the Panhandle, and state officials said no storm-related fatalities had been confirmed as recovery efforts continued. Gov. Ron DeSantis delivered the update during a statewide briefing, saying the storm came ashore near Destin at 9:30 p.m. Friday as a Category 2 hurricane with sustained winds of about 105 mph. Wind gusts reached as high as 116 mph near Santa Rosa Sound, and storm surge pushed water levels about 5.5 feet above normal in some areas.

DeSantis said there have been no confirmed fatalities, though state officials are still looking into a possible death in Escambia County linked to a fallen tree. The storm has since weakened into a post-tropical cyclone and moved out of Florida, but DeSantis warned that flooding remains a concern, particularly in parts of the Panhandle and Big Bend, where 4 to 8 inches of rain are expected through the weekend.

More than 16,000 linemen were staged ahead of the storm and began restoration work as early as 3 a.m. Saturday. By 7 a.m., about 448,000 customer accounts were without electricity statewide, including roughly 323,000 Florida Power & Light customers and about 110,000 customers served by electric cooperatives. Santa Rosa County was among the hardest hit, with about 90% of customers without power, followed by Holmes County at 89%, Washington County at 86%, Walton County at 85%, Escambia County at 75% and Okaloosa County at 53%. The Florida Department of Transportation and Florida Highway Patrol ran overnight "cut and toss" operations to clear roads of fallen trees and debris, and officials said all state-owned bridges had been inspected and reopened by 6 a.m. Northwest Florida Beaches International Airport resumed commercial operations Saturday morning, while Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport and Pensacola International Airport remained closed.

hero.headline: Treasure Coast High Student, 14, Dies After Being Struck Near SW Port St. Lucie Blvd
hero.body:
A 14-year-old Treasure Coast High School student has died after being struck by a vehicle while walking to school in Port St. Lucie. The Port St. Lucie Police Department said the crash happened Wednesday morning near the intersection of SW Port St. Lucie Boulevard and SW Squirrel Avenue.

A preliminary investigation found the teen was walking northbound along Port St. Lucie Boulevard near the edge of the roadway when he was struck from behind by a 2002 Ford Excursion driven by a 72-year-old man. Detectives are continuing to examine the circumstances surrounding the crash.

The Port St. Lucie Police Department extended condolences to the student's family, friends, classmates and all those affected. "Our thoughts are with them during this incredibly difficult time," the department said in a statement.
